# Application of Contemporary Measurement and Calculation Methods for Structural Analysis and Monitoring of Heritage Buildings

Łukasz Bednarz1, Artur Górski2  , Jerzy Jasieńko1, Eugeniusz Rusiński2 and Marcin Rutkowski1, 2

(1)

Zakład Materiałów Budowlanych, Konstrukcji Drewnianych i Zabytkowych, Wydział Budownictwa Lądowego i Wodnego, Politechnika Wrocławska, Wroclaw, Poland

(2)

Zakład Komputerowego Wspomagania Projektowania, Instytut Konstrukcji I Eksploatacji Maszyn, Wydział Mechaniczny, Politechnika Wrocławska, Wroclaw, Poland

Artur Górski

Email: artur.gorski@pwr.edu.pl

Abstract

An analysis of the condition of the structure of heritage buildings is a complex and time-consuming process. This is why contemporary numerical, optic or laser technologies are used more and more frequently to prepare detailed inventories, generate models or monitor the condition of such buildings. Computer technologies, enabling development of advanced analysis of complex physical relations in heritage buildings using the FEM, are of particular interest and importance.

Marcin Rutkowski: Freelancer, budowlaniec.\u200Bnet

## 1 Introduction

An analysis of the condition of the structure of heritage buildings is a complex and time-consuming process. This is why contemporary numerical, optic or laser technologies are used more and more frequently to prepare detailed inventories, generate models or monitor the condition of such buildings. Computer technologies, enabling development of advanced analysis of complex physical relations in heritage buildings using the FEM, are of particular interest and importance.

## 2 Analysis of the Structural Condition of Heritage Buildings

An analysis of the structural condition is a complex task and needs to be implemented with reference to a wide range of issues. Determining the types of analysis necessary for a given building depends on its structural type, materials used and its heritage value. The analysis needs to consider the following aspects: the static behaviour of the structure in its original condition and following the strengthening intervention, as well as the status and direction of stress, the value of displacement, and weather load, service load, thermal load etc., impact of load modifications, the condition of materials used (depending on type: strength, hardness, moisture analysis etc.) in relation to both the ultimate limit state and serviceability limit state. An analysis of the structural condition of a heritage building can be carried out in a simplified or in a more comprehensive way, depending on the accuracy of results needed and the type of completed and planned interventions. The wide range of analysis is used not only to observe the strain of the structure, but also to investigate the microclimate of the building's interior and the condition of the building materials used. Analytical data provides a basis for further monitoring of the building–for defining the scope of monitoring and the equipment needed. The data can be also used to plan necessary repairs and strengthening.

The analysis of heritage buildings should begin with analysis of available historical documentation, the geotechnical conditions of the building, the size and scale of cracking, assessment of moisture conditions and micro-climate, assessment of plaster condition and mycological analysis. The next stage involves a detailed inventory, development of a model of the building for carrying out static and dynamic calculations essential for verifying the condition of the existing structure. Comprehensive evaluation of the condition of a heritage building needs to include analysis and observations regarding both the structure and the building materials used. Technologies used for preparing inventories, numerical analysis, selecting strengthening and monitoring methods of buildings, with a special emphasis on heritage buildings are presented in what follows.

## 3 Inventory Preparation

A 3D spatial laser scanner is the perfect tool for carrying out a detailed inventory of a heritage building. The device generates a cloud of points. When processed, a very accurate 3D image of the structure is generated. An inventory obtained in this way can be used for further design and planning work.

Laser scanning enables remote measurement of hundreds of thousands of points per second, with millimetre precision. Each of the points is characterised not only by its X, Y, Z coordinates, but also a record of the intensity of the reflected signal or its RBG colour. Using a cloud of points provides for realistic visualisations as accurate spatial measurements can be transferred to a virtual reality, providing also a basis for advanced spatial modelling and reverse engineering.

3D scanners are used for 3D scanning. They are usually optical electronic devices developed for use in so-called reversed design, which is a process of industrial design based on using structures that already exist. Spatial scanning uses a coordinate-based measurement technique, which enables relatively high precision and contact-free identification of the spatial dimensions of physical objects. The method involves measurement procedures based on the values of the coordinates of measurement points, which describe the body of the scanned object. Spatial scanning is one of the techniques or methods, which is helpful in developing 3D structures and in processes involving digitalization of fragile structures, which are susceptible to mechanical damage.

A 3D scanner is a device used for precise and comprehensive measurements, surveys and documentation. The device creates detailed projection of the geometry of the physical world at minute intervals and defines it in virtual space. A 3D scanner provides the most effective method for collecting 3D documentation. The use of 3D scanning can successfully replace the tiresome process of collecting data using traditional tape-measures, range-finders and cameras, which are prone to measurement errors, may involve some safety risks and which require additional tasks and actions, as well as time—often many months.

A 3D laser scanner takes minutes to create a detailed 3D projection of places and structures of high complexity. It recreates the physical world and defines it in a virtual space. The resulting image comprises millions of 3D points, enabling an exact recreation of existing physical structures. With the capability of scanning up to a million points per second, a laser scanner provides the most effective method for collecting 3D documentation. The direct result of scanning is a 'cloud of points', comprising a set of millions of points. These points constitute an accurate 3D model of the scanned object.

The 3D scanning technique, when used for generation of visualisations and 3D models in conjunction with the CAD environment, can provide for a more accurate analysis of the condition of the buildings and a more precise assessment of their technical condition.

## 4 Model Generation

A numerical model of a structure is always its approximation. The transfer process from the actual physical structure is strictly defined. Importantly, it is determined by a number of variable factors, which depend on the nature of the problem under investigation. In order to avoid any errors, the procedure described above needs to be correctly selected and implemented, [1]. The first step involves identification of the problem—determination of a physical phenomenon, forces, material properties, and the answers which are being sought. Analysis of these issues is of key importance for selecting an appropriate structural model and calculation method—correct implementation of the process of collecting and processing data is crucial to this step. The Finite Element Method (FEM) is the calculation method, which was selected for the project. According to the procedure, the numerical method is not applied to the physical problem, but to its conceptual model (which is a simplified physical model with redundant features removed). So called redundant features include, for example, the detailed geometry, which is omitted in the model as its influence on the final result is negligible. Every decision regarding a simplification of a model needs to be reasonable and justified, of course. Having developed a conceptual model, the next step involves definition of a structural model, comprising of three basic elements: geometry (points, lines, surfaces, solids), mathematical description of the physical phenomena being investigated (usually in the form of a system of partial differential equations) and the description of materials and loading.

An ideal solution to solving the physical, engineering problem requires a capability for describing and solving the problem using systems of differential equations with closed solutions. Unfortunately, the number of such problems is very limited, both in terms of solutions to systems of equations and to their size. For this reason, a number of numerical methods are applied to obtain approximate solutions, with an accuracy that is satisfactory and reliable enough for using these methods in science and engineering. These methods include the finite difference method, parametric methods and the boundary element method, [2]. Currently, the Finite Element Method is regarded as the most effective, [3]. Two critical issues related to this method include the calculus of variation and the discretization (dividing a whole problem into elements).

Several examples of analyses of existing historical buildings are presented in what follows. The results obtained from the numerical models contributed in a significant way to developing recommendations regarding these buildings, especially in relations to repair and strengthening and the scope of further monitoring of their condition.

One of the simplest ways of analysing an heritage building involves modelling its sections in relation to flat distortion (plates and beams), (Fig. 1), or modelling sections of the building – as in modelling a groin vault in relation to spatial distortion (shell) divided into rectangular and triangular finite elements (Fig. 2).

Fig. 1

A flat distortion model (plates and beams), divided into triangular and quadrilateral finite elements

Fig. 2

A spatial distortion model (shell) divided into rectangular and triangular finite elements—a groin vault

Modelling the whole structure (Fig. 3) using a simplified spatial model (Fig. 4) is a highly advanced method. The model comprises such details as: different materials (brick, stone, timber), niches and openings in walls, sections of structural elements (thickness of walls, vault spans and beam sections). The assumptions related to loading were based on the weight of the elements of the building in the form and materials as they are today. The calculations were based on the assumption that the building will continue be used as it has been used to date, i.e. the floors from the first floor up will be used for residential purposes, and the groundfloor as a commercial space. A simulation model was created to indicate possible deformation of the building and the directions of potential destruction.

Fig. 3

The actual building

Fig. 4

A simplified spatial model of the building

The model was used to analyse stresses in the building using the FEM method. A Concrete Damage Plasticity (CDP) model was applied, with averaged parameters for the materials of brick walls, stone walls and for the elastic model of these materials. The behaviour of the model under loading characteristic for a normal use of the building was determined. The results obtained in the analysis are presented in Figs. 5, 6.

Fig. 5

Displacement of structural elements of the building

Fig. 6

The distribution of stress in the arcades in front of the building

The stress distribution in the arcade in front of the building demonstrates uneven loading of the pillars, which translates into different impacts onto the ground below.

The method of modelling a load-bearing structure of the roof and vaulted ceilings of a building (Fig. 7) as a simplified spatial model was used to analyse the situation presented below. Numerical analysis of the generated 3D model of the load-bearing roof structure and vaulted ceilings was carried out to design an appropriate strengthening for the structural elements. The model served to analyse the situation before and after the strengthening intervention.

Fig. 7

A model of the load-bearing roof structure and vaulted ceilings of the building

Based on the results of the numerical analysis (Fig. 8) it was assumed that the PBO-FRCM strengthening system, as described in, inter alia, [4–7], would provide for the expected increase of the load-bearing capacity of the structure and would consolidate the structure. Repair work, as well as consolidation and strengthening interventions were recommended, along with development of a monitoring system for determining the condition of selected structural elements with respect to their possible distortion or deformation during the repair intervention and the normal use of the building.

Fig. 8

Results of numerical analysis—vertical displacements, before and after the strengthening intervention

In the case of a reinforced concrete dome (Fig. 9) the geometry of the structure was obtained from various sources (e.g. 3D scans), which enabled the generation of a fully integrated model of the structure, which could later be used for further analysis. The geometric data was merged with measurement data, resulting in a comprehensive design of a system for monitoring the safety of the building. The results of measurements were interpreted using the FEM method. A model was generated to allow identification of critical elements and to description phenomena related to the use of the building (such as appearance of extreme, unaccounted for loading or vibrations).

Fig. 9

A model and the third main stresses in the ribs and circumferential beams

The original structural drawings, material analyses, inventories and building design drawings provided the source of information related to geometry, reinforcement, the characteristic features of the structure and structural changes introduced after the building had been completed. BIM models, generated on the basis of digital models obtained from 3D scans, were also used.

## 5 Strengthening

The results obtained from numerical analyses can be used to make decisions regarding repair work and strengthening interventions in heritage buildings. In this regard, interest has been growing in new technologies and methods which can be used in restoration of public-owned buildings. A task that contemporary engineers specialising in structural strengthening have to face more and more frequently relates to maintaining building structures in serviceable condition, which have been partially or significantly destroyed. Current trends in structural strengthening involve application of innovative methods for repairing and stabilizing structures. In this respect, composite materials represent one of the most recent scientific advancements.

Conventional strengthening methods, such as shotcrete or additionally reinforced concrete or steel structures, result in increasing load-bearing capacity and rigidity of the structure. They can also cause irreversible changes to the aesthetics of the building. When a significant increase of the load-bearing capacity of the structure is necessary, composite materials can be used as an alternative solution to conventional methods of strengthening existing buildings. The mechanical parameters of fibres used in composite material strengthening systems reduce tensile and bending stresses, while at the same time allowing for increased loading of the structural element. Tests have demonstrated that fibre-based composite materials can be applied successfully to repair existing steel, masonry, timber and reinforced concrete structures and to appropriately safeguard them.

Historically, organic fibres have been used in strengthening interventions. In recent years, there have been renewed attempts to make use of biological—bio-composite—materials, such as jute, linen (Fig. 10), hemp (Fig. 12) or broom in strengthening heritage buildings.

Fig. 10

Linen fabric

Fig. 11

C-FRCM carbon fibre mesh

Fig. 12

Hemp fibre fabric

Tensile strength is the overriding factor to be taken into account in the selection of an appropriate strengthening system. For this reason, fibrous FRP (Fibre Reinforced Polymer) composite materials with a polymer (thermoplastic and thermosetting resins) warp or with a mineral FRCM (Fibre Reinforced Cementitious Matrix) warp, reinforced with carbon, basalt, graphite, glass, boron, aramid fibres or steel, are of crucial importance.

FRCM (Fibre Reinforced Cementitious Matrix) systems are an alternative solution to the FRP systems. They comprise a fibre mesh [e.g. C-FRCM mesh made of carbon fibre (Fig. 11) or PBO-FRCM mesh made of PBO (polyparaphenylene-benzobisoxazole) fibre (Fig. 13)] in a mineral warp without epoxy resins.

Fig. 13

PBO-FRCM fibre mesh

Attempts to generate FEM models of composite strengthening systems for heritage structures have been undertaken, inter alia, in [7–9].

## 6 Monitoring

Monitoring refers to a system of methods and techniques used to measure the condition of a structure. Monitoring activities can be classified according to a variety of criteria, e.g. the goal of the monitoring, the type of measurements (static, dynamic), the nature of testing (destructive, quasi-destructive or non-destructive methods), time of monitoring, etc. The best results can be obtained using a hybrid system comprising techniques for assessment of static or dynamic behaviour of the structure over time, enabling tracking of changes in the geometry of the structure (which can occur also as a result of delayed phenomena) and non-destructive tests of building materials.

The examples presented in the paper are focused on monitoring the geometry of the buildings investigated. Ongoing monitoring of buildings was recommended as there has been a lack of earlier detailed data on changes to the geometry of the buildings, as well as to the displacements and cracking of their structural elements. The digital documentation generated represents a valuable tool for preservation of heritage buildings. Models generated on the basis of this documentation have been used to assess the condition of structures and to identify factors contributing to their destruction.

It is possible to detect displacements and propagation of cracking of 3D elements by repeating 3D scanning and superimposing successive images upon each other. This technique is an effective tool for monitoring of the condition of a structure, without physically accessing the structural elements of the building. Thanks to its millimetre precision, such technology can be also applied also to register surface degradation of, e.g., brick or stone masonry surfaces, [10].

## 7 Conclusions

Due to the complex character of the examples cited in this paper, the analyses presented did not allow unambiguous definition of the stresses present in sections of the structural elements in the buildings investigated. However, the analyses identify patterns and suggest the approach to be used in such situations with its focus on higher-stress areas which may require intervention.

Analysis of a number of patterns (loading variations, forced displacements, changes to the support conditions) enables simulation of structural behaviour and identification of overly-stressed sections. Additional information related to the expected scope of maintenance work and potential strengthening intervention needed can be provided through analysis of the quantity and the quality of loading patterns combined with a critical perspective on the chances of their occurrence during use of the structure.

The most effective way of determining on-going structural behaviour is through on-going monitoring, involving a regular registration of cracking and deformations, geodetic measurement of reference points and the ever more popular repeated 3D laser scanning of the geometry of the building investigated.

# Synthesis and Structural Analysis of High Strength Composite Flexible Landing Gear Legs

Paweł Borkowski1  , Adam Dacko1 and Mirosław Rodzewicz1

(1)

Institute of Aeronautics and Applied Mechanics, Warsaw University of Technology, Nowowiejska 24, 00665 Warsaw, Poland

Paweł Borkowski

Email: pbork@meil.pw.edu.pl

Abstract

The problem considered was to develop, synthesize and design a flexible landing gear leg, subject to some restrictions resulting from requested loads and boundary conditions. The problem was already undertaken by many researchers, e.g. in monographs written by Currey (Aircraft Landing Gear Design: Principles and Practices, 2004, 1) and Thuis (The development of composite landing gear components for aerospace applications, 2004, 2) and in journals and conference papers (Ganorkar and Deshbhratar, Design Optimization of landing gear of an aircraft, 2014, 3; Goyal and Laksminarayan, Design, Analysis and Simulation of a composite main landing gear for a light aircraft, 2002, 4; Yu-xiu et al., The dynamics research on the composite undercarriage of the Unmanned Aerial Vehicle, 2015, 5; Niezgoda et al., Selection of dynamics characteristics for landing gear with the use of numerical model, 2002, 6). It was assumed that two roving "concentrated constant cross-section booms" would be created. FE simulations allowed to determine the flexible leg deformations, stress distribution and Failure Indices (using maximum stress theory) (Spencer, Novel Optimization Strategy for Composite Beam Type Landing Gear for Light Aircraft, 2013, 7). The foam core inset was tested as a means of mass reduction. FE program ANSYS was used for the analysis (Ansys Theory Reference, 2013, 8).

## 1 Introduction

The gyrocopter airframe was shaped in the way that allowed for flexible leg rotation relative to axis x, "parallel to flight direction" (see Figs. 1 and 2). The continuous, single "wheel-to-wheel beam" flexible leg was attached to the airframe by four bolt connections (two at each side of the fuselage). The bolted connection, due to elastic bushings, had a freedom of displacement and rotation relative to the fuselage.

Fig. 1

Flexible landing gear leg mounted on the fuselage

Fig. 2

Flexible leg of the gyrocopter (only the right side shown)—"enveloped-on-dry" technology

Landing gear leg loads were defined according to proper standards and regulations. In FE analysis the single, complex load case was considered. This load case contained superposition of all force components (see Table 1). The most dangerous case was assumed, when the sidewise force was acting outwards, increasing the top fibers compression, that resulted from the vertical forces of hard landing.

Table 1

Load values (per side) acting at the flexible landing gear leg

Complex load case description | Load value (N)

---|---

Force—vertical, upwards | 15,450

Sideways force—outwards | 3430

Force—horizontal, to the rear | 5500

## 2 Materials Used and Manufacturing Technology Options and Assumptions for Computational Model

In the designed structure number of details was to be determined: manufacturing technology, type of composite material, the means of load application, mass of the resulting design as well as "basic geometry", i.e. variation of cross-section parameters and dimensions span-wise.

It was decided, that the flexible leg could be manufactured in two variants: "enveloped-on-dry" (see Fig. 2) or "enveloped-on-wet" (see Fig. 3).

Fig. 3

The flexible leg cross-section for "on the wet" manufacturing technology

The first variant of the flexible leg was to be manufactured in three stages. In the first stage, the "omega-shaped" internal wall (see Fig. 2) would be formed in the first form, along with creation of external, constant cross-section "booms". The booms do not use "drop-off" due to the feature of constant cross-section. After removing from the form, the component would be reversed "upside-down", and in the second form, the middle portion of the roving inset would be formed. This insert, due to variable cross-section—would use material drop-offs. As the third, last operation, the whole component would be "enveloped-on-dry".

The second variant of design and manufacturing technology (see Fig. 3) required two separate forms for upper and lower part of the landing gear flexible leg. The leg would be manufactured in a single stage. After placing the enveloping layers in the form, and bending the excess of enveloping outside, the roving would be laid inside the forms, using drop-offs in both of them. Subsequently, both halves would be closed by their envelops and compressed together, enveloped for curing.

The landing load was applied through the wheel (not modeled) to the circular hole in the landing leg. The wheel shaft, mounted in the circular hole (dia of 35 mm) transmitted the load to the composite. The connection of wheel shaft with composite was modeled by MPC solution (MultiPoint Constraint of rigid beam RBE type), where the slave nodes were located at the surface of the hole.

The flexible landing gear leg is mounted on a gyrocopter, which due to additional equipment has elevated center of gravity location. That means, that the low located mass of the landing gear flexible leg improves dynamic stability features. Hence, the minimization of mass was not of prime importance in the design.

Moreover, that decided also on choosing glass-based composites. It is heavier than carbon based, but on the other hand is much more flexible and not that brittle. That also improves safety for the pilots in the case of hard landing (or crash landing). The glass based composites were preferred by the cooperating manufacturer.

The glass-epoxy materials chosen for the project are summarized in the Tables 2 and 3 [9], where Ex, Ey, Ez are the Young's moduli in directions x, y, z and respectively: ν—the Poisson's ratios, G—the shear moduli. The allowable stress limits were the tensile (+) and compressive (−) and shear stresses with respect to assumed coordinate systems with y axis oriented along the span of the leg and x axis directed parallel to flight direction.

In FE modeling, the roving portions were modeled using HEXA brick elements (SOLID45), while the fabric was modeled by QUAD4 elements (SHELL181). Element coordinate systems for the flexible leg were tailored to fit the shape of the leg. The layered composite details (thickness and orientation of layers) were defined using the SECTIONS option [8].

Boundary Conditions, allowing for rotation of the flexible leg relative to the fuselage, were modeled using MPC solution (rigid RBE type). The independent node was located 30 mm above the surface of the leg, while connected dependent nodes formed "an umbrella" touching the flexible leg at the edge of metal washer, connected to the flexible leg (see Fig. 4).

Fig. 4

RBE defining the support allowing rotation

The modeled support allowed the flexible leg to move horizontally and to rotate in the yz plane (see Fig. 2)—as was required by the modeled connection. The FE analysis used only half of the whole structure, using proper symmetry conditions. The nonlinear analysis was run using ANSYS software. Due to size of the problem (40,998 nodes, 49,106 elements) and dominating solid elements, the iterative solver was chosen (PCG).

## 3 Results

The below presented and compared results concern some chosen cases of numerical simulation, for the flexible lending gear legs of previously optimized shape and dimensions. Comparisons quoted here are aimed at presenting results for different manufacturing technologies.

The first manufacturing option

was named "enveloped-on-dry".

In the first manufacturing option (enveloped-on-dry, see Fig. 2.), the omega-shaped wall consisted of 7 plies of Krosglass 300 fabric, laid at 45° direction to the leg axis. The enveloping was done by 3 layers of the same fabric, also at 45° orientation. The roving total volume in the whole flexible leg was 8178.84 cm3, what at assumed RR-305 roving density of 2 g/cm3 resulted in overall roving mass of 16.36 kg.

The deflection of right-hand-side flexible leg part is presented in Fig. 5, while Fig. 6 presents normal (bending) stress component in roving elements (for clarity limited to the range of ±800 MPa.

Fig. 5

Fig. 6

Normal (bending) stress component in roving elements (MPa)

Figures 7 and 8 present the Failure Index (based on theory of Maximum Stress). For clarity, the range was limited to the range 1–3, i.e. indicating areas, where failure criterion is EXCEEDED. The most of the structure, shaded grey, was satisfying the criterion. The allowable index of 1 was on the top, compressed surface. The FI on she shell elements (walls) is presented for the mostly stressed layer. As the maximum value is 0.9 it means the criterion is not exceeded in shell elements.

Fig. 7

Fig. 8

The second manufacturing option

was named "enveloped-on-dry" plus reinforcing 1D glass fiber fabric.

As the name of manufacturing technology implies, the component is reinforced by additional 4 layers of 1-D glass fabric at both top and bottom surfaces of the flexible leg—just before using enveloping (as previously, 3 layers of 45° fabric). The results for this manufacturing solution are presented in Figs. 9, 10, 11, 12. The "stressing" of the structure is lower (what means lower FI values), but it is at expense of lost flexibility. In short words—this solution results in stronger, but stiffer structure.

The third manufacturing option

was named "enveloped-on-wet".

The manufacturing technology principle was outlined in Fig. 3. The walls were created by 4 layers of Krosglass 300 fabric, laid at 45º to the leg axis. That means that the "boundary" layer between top and bottom halves joined at final stage, consisted of 8 layers of Krosglass 300 fabric. The results for this manufacturing technology case are presented in Figs. 13, 14, 15, 16.

## 4 Conclusions

Figure 17 presents side-by-side comparison of flexibility of landing gear leg for three analyzed manufacturing solutions.

Fig. 17

Comparison of deflection for different manufacturing technologies. Vertical component (mm)

For all manufacturing cases the critical area was top surface of the leg. The FI values were slightly exceeded (The exception were local concentrations, where FI was in the range 2 or 3). The stress state of the structure is generally lowest for solution #2—"enveloped-on-dry" plus reinforcing 1D glass fiber fabric. Additional 4 layers of fabric for a leg fully packed with roving resulted in FI below 1.0, white FI in added fabric slightly exceeded 1.0. Maximum FI for walls was about 0.95.

Walls in vicinity of bolts fixing the leg to the fuselage generally lowered local stresses in the structure. The leg enveloped "on-wet" and the leg "on-dry" without additional layers were characterized by similar stressing in the roving parts and wall parts of the structure.

## 5 Final Observations

Validation and verification of the obtained results definitely requires experimental confirmation. The material data is "literature—based" and real life material values can differ, so they require experimental confirmation.

# The Influence of the Type of Used Connections on the Results of Analyzes Carried Out in CATIA System

Dawid Cekus1  , Dorian Skrobek1  and Daniel Różalski2

(1)

Institute of Mechanics and Machine Design Foundations, Czestochowa University of Technology, Dąbrowskiego 73, 42-201 Częstochowa, Poland

(2)

P.P.H.U. Roz-Met Daniel Różalski, Jasna 49, 42-100 Kłobuck, Poland

Dawid Cekus (Corresponding author)

Email: cekus@imipkm.pcz.pl

Dorian Skrobek

Email: skrobek@imipkm.pcz.pl

Daniel Różalski

Email: danielrozalski@wp.pl

Abstract

In the paper the existing in CATIA system the types of connections that may occur between the components have been characterized. These connections specify the boundary interaction between bodies and can simulate the real connection behavior. Use in the same place another connection has a significant impact on the results of analyzes. The stress analyses of the excavator jib together with the bucket for the different types of connection properties have been presented as the examples.

## 1 Introduction

Modeling is the process of searching for the best representation of a real object that imitates behavior of a system in operating conditions. However, during the construction of models, the optimization of simplicity of a model as well as an accuracy and a faithfulness to a real object is necessary. If we strive to achieve the simplest model, the accuracy of the model response will be poor. Otherwise, a better response will be obtained using a more complex model.

In many cases the details of each individual connection can be ignored if an overall stiffness or strength assessment is to be made and the connection is assumed reasonably continuous. However there may be doubts about the local flexibility and load paths developed with this assumption. It may be that the assessment of local behavior of the connector is essential to a safety case. In some cases the interaction between the connectors and the surrounding structure is critical, as in the case of pre-loaded bolts [1].

In CATIA system a several different kinds of connection properties that may occur between the components exist. The complexity of the model and the quality of the system response depend on their type.

The work presents the influence of the type of connection on the results of the static analysis. The exemplary research have been carried out for the excavator jib together with the bucket. A geometrical and computational model have been built on the basis of the existing object produced by CASE and JCB (Fig. 1) [2].

Fig. 1

Excavator produced by CASE and JCB

These considerations should be considered primarily as an engineering problem, which can try as a basis to introduce new more complex types of connections. It would represent scientific contribution in the above-mentioned software.

## 2 Connection Properties

Connection properties are assembly connections used to specify the boundary interaction between bodies in an assembled system. In CATIA program [3–7] in the Generative Assembly Structural Analysis (GAS) product [8–11], which is a tool to perform structural analysis of assemblies, four different kinds of connection properties can be defined:

  * face-face connection:

    * a slider connection is the link between two bodies which allows sliding in tangential planes,

    * a contact connection is the link between two bodies which allows movement until contact is made,

    * a fastened connection allows two bodies to behave as a single body,

    * a fastened spring connection forms elastic connection between faces,

    * a pressure fitting connection is the link between two bodies where interferences or overlaps are,

    * a bolt tightening connection is a connection that takes into account pre-tension in bolt-tightened assemblies,

  * distant connection:

    * a rigid connection links two bodies as infinitely rigid. Only the rigid connection relations do not take into account the elastic deformability of the interfaces,

    * a smooth connection links two bodies with elastic deformation,

    * a virtual rigid bolt tightening connection and a virtual spring bolt tightening connection are connections that take into account pre-tension in a bolt-tightened assembly in which the bolt is not included,

    * a customized user-defined connection property allows user to specify elements and the properties associated,

  * welding connection:

    * a spot welding connection, a seam welding connection, a surface welding connection are the link between two bodies, using point/line/surface analysis connections or point/line/surface analysis connections within one part,

  * point base connection:

    * a nodes to nodes connection property and a node interface property enables to transmit the degrees of freedom between mesh parts.

When in the model is no contact feature (either virtual or real), no pressure fitting property and no bolt tightening (being virtual or not) feature then the problem is linear and the frequency and stress analyses can be performed. When the displacement is a non linear function of the load then only the static analyses can be carried out. Therefore this paper presents only the stress tests.

## 3 The Computational Model

The geometrical model of the excavator jib together with the bucket (Fig. 2) has been built with dozens of solid elements and even greater number of constraints. It was also assumed that all elements of the model were made from the steel.

Fig. 2

The geometrical model of the excavator jib together with the bucket

In order to show the effect of the type of used connection on the results of static analysis three computational models have been performed.

The first computational model (Fig. 3a) is characterized in that the individual parts are interconnected only with the use of the rigid connections. This is the easiest way and the least corresponding to the reality.

Fig. 3

The applied connections in the computational models

In the second computational model (Fig. 3b) the rigid connections occurring between elements joined with the screws have been replaced by the pressure fitting connections and the slider connections. Furthermore in the hydraulic cylinder between the piston and the cylinder the smooth connections have been applied.

In the third computational model (Fig. 3b), all the connections with the second model have been taken into account, and also the seam welding connections located in the excavator arm as well as the virtual bolt tightening connection occurring in the place of joining the bucket with forearm and forearm with the arm of excavators have been used.

The strength tests have been carried out for various model configurations. In each analysis the gravitation has been taken into account and all degrees of freedom in the supports have been taken away.

The first position is a position in which the excavator extracts the ground from the excavations (Fig. 4a). The load in the form of a force of 7000 N has been imposed perpendicular to the surface of bucket.

Fig. 4

The work configurations of the excavator

In the second position the excavator arm carries the material (Fig. 4b). A load of 1200 N has been applied to the inner side of the excavator bucket (perpendicular to the base).

In the third configuration, the emptying the contents of the scoop takes place (Fig. 4b).

## 4 Sample Numerical Results

On the basis of the proposed computational models the strength analyses of the system have been carried out.

In the Figs. 5 and 6 the von Missess stresses and the displacements for configuration illustrating transfer of material and for the proposed types of connection properties have been shown.

Fig. 5

The stress distribution in the computational models

Fig. 6

The displacement distribution in the computational models

In the Tables 1 and 2 the maximum values of stresses and displacements in other cases of duty cycle of the excavator have been collected.

Table 1

The maximum stresses in the excavator jib together with the bucket

Connection properties | Maximum stresses (N/m2)

---|---

1st configuration | 2nd configuration | 3rd configuration

1st computational model | 4.59 × 107 | 4.49 × 106 | 7.82 × 105

2nd computational model | 5.89 × 107 | 5.19 × 107 | 5.57 × 107

3rd computational model | 5.78 × 107 | 5.61 × 107 | 6.37 × 107

Table 2

The maximum displacements in the excavator jib together with the bucket

Connection properties | Maximum displacements (m)

---|---

1st configuration | 2nd configuration | 3rd configuration

1st computational model | 7.68 × 10−4 | 7.09 × 10−5 | 1.36 × 10−5

Based on the obtained results can be stated that the biggest stresses and displacements occur for the case when the emptying the ground of the excavator takes place and for the computational model in which the rigid connections, the pressure fitting connections, the slider connections, the smooth connections, seam welding connections and the virtual bolt tightening connection have been applied.

The use of the elastic deformability of the interfaces (second and third computational model) significantly increase the values of the maximum stresses and displacements.

## 5 Conclusions

The paper presents the influence of the kind of connection on the results of stress analysis conducted in CATIA system. The sample research have been carried out for the excavator jib together with the bucket.

Based on the conducted considerations it can be concluded that the kind of the connection significantly impact on the quality of the model. When only the rigid connections—that are the simplest to apply (linear computations)—are use, then the model does not represent correctly the real object. Therefore, this type of connection should only be used at the preliminary analyzes. Introducing the flexible connections (non-linear calculations) much more complex calculation model is obtained, at the same time the results better reflect the real object.

It should be have in mind that the results of FEA describe the behavior of the system in an approximate way, they are always burdened with some error, which in the case of correct use of CAE analysis can be considered negligible [12, 13].

Also keep in mind that worked out numerical models should be validated and submit the identification procedure [14].

# Modeling and Stress Analysis of an Industrial CNC Plotter

Dawid Cekus1  , Dorian Skrobek1  and Tomasz Zając2

(1)

Institute of Mechanics and Machine Design Foundations, Czestochowa University of Technology, Dąbrowskiego 73, 42-201 Częstochowa, Poland

(2)

Kimla, Bałtycka 30, 42-202 Częstochowa, Poland

Dawid Cekus (Corresponding author)

Email: cekus@imipkm.pcz.pl

Dorian Skrobek

Email: skrobek@imipkm.pcz.pl

Tomasz Zając

Email: tomasz.zajac@gmail.com

Abstract

In the paper a geometrical and computational model as well as results of stress analysis of an industrial CNC plotter have been presented. The research of the designed device have been divided into two parts: the static analysis of a frame with a plotter gate, and the static analysis of an axle assembly Z. The obtained results have been used in the design stage of an industrial plotter for a Polish company producing CNC machines.

## 1 Introduction

Industrial plotters are used both for a flat work that is cutting of shapes from materials in the form of sheets, and for the three-dimensional processing during the carrying out of casting moulds [1–3].

In this paper the geometrical and computational model as well as the static analysis of the industrial CNC plotter have been presented. The dynamic calculations presented in the article [4] and the results shown below have been implemented by Kimla, a Polish company producing CNC machines.

## 2 The Computational Model

The designed machine tool is intended to processing materials such as non-ferrous metals, plastics, composite materials and wood. The following range of axis machine: X = 1500 mm, Y = 3100 mm, Z = 500 mm was adopted.

The geometrical (Fig. 1) and computational models (Figs. 2, 3) of CNC plotter have been worked out in SolidWorks software [5, 6]. Due to the complicated geometry the most of components have been modeled as the solid elements. Only the profiles of machine frame have been performed as the surface elements. The geometrical model (Fig. 1a) takes into account all parts of the machine tool, such as: a frame, a T-groove table, a gate, an axle assembly Z, or a support.

Fig. 1

The industrial CNC plotter: a the geometrical model, b the simplified geometry: 1—a frame, 2—a gate, 3—an axle assembly Z, 4—a support

Fig. 2

The computational model of the frame with the plotter gate: 1—the load from the axle assembly Z, 2—the gravity, 3—the force from the machine cutting, 4—the load from worked material, 5—the load from the engines, 6—the fixed restraint

Fig. 3

The computational model of the axle assembly Z: 1—the load from accessories, 2—the gravity, 3—the spindle weight, 4—the fixed restraint

The geometry of the computational models has been considerably simplified (Fig. 1b). All elements that have no impact on the stiffness and strength of the structure have been removed. In the place of deleted objects with the significant weight the equivalent loads have been applied. In addition, to simplify the finite element mesh all holes with a small diameter and gaps necessary for the welding structure have been removed. This all operations make it possible to reduce the computation time without a significant influence on the results.

The material has been assigned individually to each part. It was assumed that, apart from the drivers made cast steel (Young's modulus: 200000 N/mm2, Poisson's ratio: 0.32, mass density: 7800 kg/m3), the machine elements are made from carbon steel (Young's modulus: 210000 N/mm2, Poisson's ratio: 0.28, mass density: 7800 kg/m3).

The stress research has been conducted in two phases. The first concerned the static analysis of the frame with the plotter gate. The static analysis of the axle assembly Z was the second stage. The division of the studies into two parts shortened the computational time.

In the first case the computational model (Fig. 2) [7–11] assumes that:

  * all six degrees of freedom have been taken away on the surfaces of machine feet, which come into contact with the ground,

  * the axle assembly Z, the cover plates, the profiles of the table, the conductors and the engines have been replaced by the equivalent loads,

  * the load resulting from the material mounted on the table, the gravitational force, and the friction between elements have been taken into account.

The computational model [7–10] of the axle assembly Z (Fig. 3) assumes that:

  * all six degrees of freedom have been taken away on the rear surface of the plate fixed to the support of CNC plotter,

  * the spindle, the accessories and the cover plates have been modeled with the help of equivalent loads,

  * the contact between the carriages and the blocks and the gravity have been considered.

## 3 Results of Stress Analyses

The static analyses make it possible to estimate how the load of table and the load from the machine cutting forces influence on the work of machine.

In the case of CNC plotter from the mechanical point of view the stresses and the displacements occurring in the machine are significant. For example the smaller value of displacements the better material machining.

The stress analyses have been carried out in the linear-elastic range of material. To the calculations the FFE Plus solver has been used. It is characterized by a much faster problem solving in comparison with the Direct Sparse solver, as well as it is more stable.

In the Figs. 4, 5, 6, 7 the results of the static analysis have been presented. The Figs. 4 and 5 concern the research of the frame with the plotter gate whereas the Figs. 6 and 7 concern the study of the axle assembly Z.

Fig. 4

The reduced stress: a in the nodes, b in the elements

Fig. 5

The displacements: a resultant, b along the Y axis

Fig. 6

The reduced stress: a in the nodes, b in the elements

Fig. 7

The displacements: a resultant, b along the Y axis

On the basis of obtained results can be notice that the displacements does not exceed 0.17 mm for the frame, 0.06 mm for the plotter gate, and 0.002 mm for the axle assembly Z. Moreover the yield point of materials has not been exceeded in both analyses. This all confirms that the structure was designed correctly.

## 4 Conclusions

Using CAD/CAE software for instance SolidWorks the carrying out of tests is possible before implementation of machines to production. The analyzes make it possible to examine the assemblies in terms of strength and movement possibilities. This helps to accelerate and reduce significantly the cost of making a prototype.

The carried out of static analyses of the model of the industrial CNC plotter confirm that the designed construction will be work correctly. Displacements of the main part of machine are little, and the yield point of materials has not been exceeded.

The obtained stress results with the dynamical calculations presented in the paper [4] has been implemented by Kimla, a Polish company producing CNC machines (Fig. 8).

Fig. 8

The industrial CNC plotter BPF 1530 [12]

# Numerical Identification of Effort of Load Carrying Structure of Adjustable Stand

Robert Czabanowski1

(1)

Department of Off-Road Machine and Vehicle Engineering, Wroclaw University of Technology, Lukasiewicza 7/9, 50371 Wroclaw, Poland

Robert Czabanowski

Email: Robert.Czabanowski@pwr.edu.pl

Abstract

The works is the numerical analysis of the state of stress and deformation of load bearing structure of adjustable stand. Numerical calculations were carried out by finite element method. Obtained distributions of stresses positively verified analyzed load carrying structure. The results of numerical tests showed the possibility of structure optimization, e.g., to reduce weight of the adjustable stand.

Keywords

Finite element methodLoad carrying structureNumerical identification

## 1 Introduction

The adjustable stand is of an auxiliary device used in the process of assembly and disassembly of the parts on traverses used to their transport. Therefore stands are used in pairs, as shown in Fig. 1. Adjusting the position of support of stand using the screw gear with gear-motor is executed without load. Vertical moving of the traverse (lifting and lowering) is done with the help of a crane. For this reason, the device is not subject to the requirements for lifting devices [1], but of course must meet the standards for the design of steel structures [2].

Fig. 1

A pair of adjustable stands with traverse (a the same supports position, b allowable difference of supports position)

Depending on the technological requirements allowed to irregular load distribution traverse cooperating with stands and differences in the position of supports both from the stands. For this purpose, control system allows to change the position of supports both stands at the same time or separately each stand. Due to the different positions of supports and the possible non-uniform load distribution on the traverse is required to conduct an analysis of effort of load carrying structure of the stand.

## 2 Construction and Working Conditions for the Adjustable Stand

Adjustable stand (Fig. 2) is built with a steel frame (1) made of a normal channel sections supported on a steel plate anchored to the floor. In the frame are mounted linear guides (2), with which it cooperates shaped from sheet metal support (3). The movement of the support (without load) is realized with the help retaining sleeve (6) and a screw gear (4) with a gear-motor (5). In this screw gear was used, primary (7) and safety (8) nut. Screw mechanism (4) carries the load on the frame via the bearing assembly (9). The nominal capacity of the analyzed equipment is 25 kN. The frame is made of steel S235 while the linear guides and support of steel S355.

Fig. 2

Adjustable stand (1 frame, 2 linear guides, 3 support, 4 screw mechanism, 5 gear motor, 6 retaining sleeve, 7 primary nut, 8 safety nut, 9 bearing assembly)

### 2.1 Load Condition of the Adjustable Stand

Due to the character of the work (changing the position of supports can only be operated without load) load stand can be considered as quasi-static. Load condition determined by the supports position and load distribution on the traverse. For technological reasons, it is permissible difference the position of the supports equal to half the lifting height. The permissible non-uniform the load distribution on the traverse are presented as equivalent concentrated force offset from the traverse center. Table 1 shows the analysed operating conditions of the adjustable stands.

Table 1

Permissible operating conditions of adjustable stands set

Position of supports | Load distribution on traverse

---|---

Uniform | Non-uniform

The same |   |

Allowable difference |   |

F*—equivalent concentrated force resulting from the weight of the load and traverse

### 2.2 Discrete Model of Carrying Structure of Adjustable Stand

Using the program Geomagic Design was built a geometrical model of adjustable stand (Fig. 2), which was used to build discrete models for numerical strength analysis. For this purpose, they made the necessary simplification of the structure of the details that are irrelevant to a correct assessment of the effort of the body, e.g.: removed small parts used to mount the limit switches. The discrete models are shown in Figs. 3 and 4. For modeling are used solid 10-node elements with three degrees of freedom in the node. Discrete model of support consist of 243,573 elements and 418,048 nodes while discrete model of frame and linear guides consist of 636,164 elements and 1,078,531 nodes.

Fig. 3

The discrete model of support

Fig. 4

Discrete model of the frame and linear guides

## 3 Numerical Analysis of Effort of Bearing Structure

Numerical research of effort of carrying structure stand was made by finite element method using the NE/Nastran for Windows [3], solving problems as static [4, 5], the calculations were made for standard ambient temperature and pressure (SATP: temperature: 25 °C, absolute pressure: 100 kPa).

### 3.1 Boundary Conditions and Analyzed States of the Load Bearing Structure

Analyses were performed to isolate from the structure the support, the boundary conditions are defined so as to give a true and take into account its interaction with the linear guides and primary nut (Fig. 5). In guiding sleeves (A in Fig. 5) received degrees of freedom so as to reflect in interaction with the linear guides (lack of mobility in the radial direction). On the spherical cap (B in Fig. 5: B) of retaining sleeve deprived of the ability to move in the radial direction of the sphere (a model of interaction of support with the primary nut). The analysis included in Table 1 load conditions. A method of modeling loads of the support shown in Fig. 6.

Fig. 5

The boundary conditions for strength analysis of support (description in the text)

Fig. 6

Loading methods of the support (a by uniform load distribution on horizontal traverse: perpendicular force on a part of supports plate, b by non-uniform load distribution on sloping traverse: the resultant force on the outer edge of the support plate)

The obtained values of reaction were used to define loads of guide lines and the frame. Linear guides are loaded forces that balance the moment which generates an eccentric load of support. The reactions at the ends of linear guides are carried on a frame which also carries screw axial force by the bearing assembly. The frame was fixed by fixing of all degrees of freedom on the contact surface the steel plate with substrate. A method of load and restraint of the frame and guides lines shown in Fig. 7. In order to take account of interaction between the frame and guide line defined on the ends of the linear guide contact zone (assumed friction coeff. of 0).

Fig. 7

Load of frame and a linear guide (a) and the boundary conditions of frame (b)

### 3.2 Selected Results of Numerical Calculations

The Figs. 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 show example calculation results: reduced stress hypothesis according to Huber and total displacement (all values in basic SI units: Pa and m).

Fig. 8

Distributions of reduced stresses in support for uniform load distribution on horizontal traverse

Fig. 9

Distributions of reduced stresses in support for non-uniform load distribution on sloping traverse

Fig. 10

Total displacements of the support (a uniform load distribution on horizontal traverse, b-non-uniform load distribution on sloping traverse)

Fig. 11

Distributions of reduced stresses in frame and guide lines for non-uniform load distribution on sloping traverse

Fig. 12

Total displacements of the frame and guide lines for non-uniform load distribution on sloping traverse

The resulting stress values (160 MPa for support and approx.125 MPa the frame) do not exceed the limit values for the used materials, the safety factor has a value of approx. 2. The resulting displacement is also small, and frame deflection does not exceed 1/1000.

## 4 Conclusions

The work was performed strength analysis carrying structure of adjustable stand. The results positively verify the selection of materials and dimensions of the components of carrying structure of adjustable stand. This gives the required supply stability needed for the occurrence of overloads which frequently occur in the industrial environment. Possible optimization can affect the dimensions and thickness of the sheet metal ribs the lower part of the structure for reduce weight of the adjustable stand.

# Selected Aspects of Technical Condition State Assessment of Spreaders Operating in Lignite Mines

Jerzy Czmochowski1  , Przemysław Moczko1  , Damian Pietrusiak1  , Grzegorz Przybyłek1  and Eugeniusz Rusiński1

(1)

Department of Machine Design and Research, Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, Wroclaw University of Science and Technology, Wrocław, Poland

Jerzy Czmochowski

Email: jerzy.czmochowski@pwr.edu.pl

Przemysław Moczko

Email: przemyslaw.moczko@pwr.edu.pl

Damian Pietrusiak (Corresponding author)

Email: damian.pietrusiak@pwr.edu.pl

Grzegorz Przybyłek

Email: grzegorz.przybylek@pwr.edu.pl

Eugeniusz Rusiński

Email: eugeniusz.rusinski@pwr.edu.pl

Abstract

On the basis of spreader A2RsB 15400 the method for technical condition state assessment of machines, after many year of operation, in lignite mines is presented. In purpose to identify the structure hot spots and cracks, both numerical and experimental methods were applied. Additionally, the dynamic behavior of the structure was assessed with use of the experimental methods. The paper presents the meaningful results chosen from the assessment procedure.

## 1 Introduction

The age of many machines still operating in lignite mines is over 30 years. After such a long period of constant operation, fatigue cracks of crucial elements of load carrying structures are observed [2, 11]. Perfect example is brakeage of the tensile member supporting the counterweight boom of bucker wheel excavator KWK-1400 [10], cracks in the undercarriage support pillars of excavators SRs-2000 [17], cracks in the front part of the bucket wheel boom of SchRs-4600 [18] excavator, brakeage of the end part of the axis in crawler set of spreaders ZGOT-11500 (Fig. 1) and A2RsB-12500 (Fig. 2) [19], and cracks in welded connections of spreader A2RsB-15400 (Fig. 3) structure. Load carrying structures of the machines of that type should be periodically controlled and assessment of its technical condition should be done. This allows to point potential areas of cracks initiation [6, 20]. Worth noting is also the fact that the machines operate in geological conditions different than assumed in the design process. Mostly, those conditions are much more harder. Considering this fact, identification of actual loads is one of the most important thing. While the machines were designed years ago, only now the complex discrete models are built in purpose to assess the state of stress, both static and fatigue. On the basis of complex numerical and experimental testing it is possible to prognose the future operation time [11, 20].

Fig. 1

Brakeage of the end part of the axis in the crawler set of spreaders ZGOT-11500

Fig. 2

Brakeage of the crawler axis A2RsB-12500

Fig. 3

Cracks in welded connections of spreader A2RsB-15400

Actual strategy of the mining companies is to acquire information about the technical condition of most working machines. The main scope is the degradation of load carrying structures of spreaders and bucket wheel excavators. Realization of this task requires planned, organized structure of the investigations realization. It must be consistent with the operation and maintenance plan in the company. The procedure is based on already developed and presented methods [11, 15]. Below, presented is the investigation procedure which was applied to the A2RsB 15400 spreader (Fig. 4). According to the method developed in Department of Machine Design and Research of Wroclaw University of Technology, following steps were taken:

Fig. 4

Spreader A2RsB 15400

  * analysis of the historical failures and repairs of the loads carrying structure

  * analysis of the structure modifications

  * long term measurements of the dynamic effects

  * superstructure vibrations measurements

  * finite element analysis of static and fatigue

  * Non Destructive Testing (NDT) of the elements prone to crack

  * recommendations for the control procedure of prone to fatigue crack areas

## 2 Spreader Superstructure Vibration Measurements

In purpose to verify vibrations level of the spreader during operation, the on-site measurements were taken [3, 4, 7, 9, 12, 13]. Additionally, the acquired data were compared with the dynamic factors values defined by the standard [8]. The measurement points were selected in such way to assure most reliable results (Fig. 5). Two points were selected on the discharge boom, two on the front mast, three on the rear mast, three on the counterweight boom and one point in the central area of the superstructure [14]. Measurements were taken during dump and during travel (two superstructure position—parallel and perpendicular to the travel direction). The exemplary accelerations spectrum acquired at discharge boom is presented in Fig. 6.

Fig. 5

Placement of measurement points on the spreader superstructure

Fig. 6

Acceleration spectrum—discharge boom, point 2

On the basis of acceleration measurements, the vibration energy (RMS) was determined and compared with the normative values [8] which are the recommendation for design. Values over the normative threshold are observed some points placed on the discharge and counterweight boom (Table 1). In case of the central part of the superstructure, for which standard do not define the dynamic factor level, the measured factor level is the range between 15.63 and 22.55. Experimentally obtained values were applied to the numerical model for the fatigue calculations.

## 3 Finite Element Analysis

The strength calculations with use of finite element method are the crucial part, while enables identification of the structural hot-spots. In case of complex object, like for example spreaders, it is a difficult task to do. Model presented in the paper consists of the beam and shell elements. The trusses were modeled as a wireframe geometry and then meshed with the beam elements. The areas which consist of the large steel plates the surface geometry was developed and transformed to the shell element type [16]. The model was developed on the basis of technical drawings delivered by the customer. Developed model included all structural modification in design made during years of operation.

The elements of the structure which are assembled on the load carrying structure i.e.: motors, conveyors, pulleys, drums, axes, bucket wheel etc. were included in the model as lumped mass. Plenty of special elements like constraints, rigid or springs were used in purpose to represent all supports and connections in modeled structure (Figs. 7 and 8).

Fig. 7

Wireframe-surface model of spreader A2RsB-15400

Fig. 8

Part of finite element beam-shell model of the central part of the A2RsB-15400 spreader superstructure

The guidelines and instructions of loads combination are stated in the standard [8] and in the stability proof of the machine which defines position of all elements and the structure center of gravity. Loads which derive from the superstructure turn and machine travel are defined on the basis of the power of motors and experimental measurements.

The stress state in structure is define by the Huber-Mises theorem. The fatigue stress state is defined on the basis of the range of stress alternations. Exemplary static stress distribution is presented in Fig. 9 and fatigue stress range is presented in Fig. 10.

Fig. 9

Huber-Mises stresses in central part of spreader superstructure—H1a load case

Fig. 10

Range of fatigue stresses in the central part of spreader superstructure—H1b load case

On the basis of finite element analysis, areas with excessive stress level were localized. Those areas are potential regions of the cracks initiations those were selected for periodical control. Additionally, they were examined with use non-destructive testing—defectoscopy.

## 4 Non Destructive Testing

The non-destructive testing was done in purpose to localize possible cracks which could initiate in operation time. Under testing were welded connections which were previously pointed out in numerical simulations. Special attention was paid for the central part of the structure while it is the element exposed for the highest loads alternation. Systematically, all connections were controlled to checks its proper manufacture and cracks occurrence [1, 5, 11].

The investigation was done with use of the magnetic particle testing method. For the detection of scattered magnetic field, the magnetic-sensitive dust in spray was used. Tested area was magnetized with use of solid magnets. Before that it was cleaned and covered with the dedicated paint. That treatment allows high quality cracks detection. In consequence of performed test, the cracked and corroded elements were detected (Fig. 11).

Fig. 11

Non-destructive testing: cracks in the supports of the superstructure central part: a right side, b left side

## 5 Summary and Conclusions

The complex analysis of the load carrying structure of spreader A2RsB-15400 was done within the technical condition state assessment procedure.

It was performed according to the methodology developed by Department of Machine Design and Research at Wroclaw University of Technology. Those investigation revealed many elements which can cause operational problems and are potential causes of defects and dangerous failures. Presented procedure of the technical condition state assessment should be introduced as a standard procedure for all machines which age reached 30 years. The expenses for numerical and experimental testing should be treated as an investment for future safe and failure free operation.

# The Optimization of Three-Involute Tooth Outline with Taking into Consideration Multi-valued Logic Trees

A. Deptuła1  and P. Osiński2

(1)

Opole University of Technology, Opole, Poland

(2)

Wroclaw University of Technology, Wroclaw, Poland

A. Deptuła (Corresponding author)

Email: a.deptula@po.opole.pl

P. Osiński

Email: piotr.osinski@pwr.edu.pl

Abstract

The paper presents the application of multivalent logic trees with weighting factors in optimizing the three-involute tooth profile. The elaborated concept of the pump of the poly-involute outline sets new directions of development, and thus the applications of gear units. The process of optimization has been carried out with regard to the five basic criteria. Based on our calculations designed a whole range of gear for the involute

Keywords

Gear pumps prototypeMulti-valued decision treesQuine-McCluskey algorithmImportance rank of decision parametersOptimizationThree-involute tooth profile

## 1 Introduction

The gear pump constructions have been developed for over 400 years. Johannes Kepler was the creator of the first gear unit and he patented his solution in 1604. The primary application of the patented solution at that time was to pump water in dehydrated mines [1–3]. The valveless and self-priming gear construction resistant to numerous contaminations present in the water removed from shaft wells very quickly replaced used at that time and hard to use piston pumps. The author of this solution saw a wider application of his invention. He did not exclude using his idea to remove bilge water on ships, force the water flow in park and garden fountains but also to compress air in the construction of blowers and exhausters. The improvement of internal tightness is connected with the minimization of energy losses, increasing the transferred power and energy efficiency of the generator [4–10]. Presented in this article theoretical considerations and measurements developed for units of model and prototype deny the thesis of the end of the technical capabilities of the pumps with the wheels of an incision using a perimeter. Developed the concept of the pump outline poly involute new directions of development, and thus the applications and gear units. The paper proposes a new method of optimizing the outline using multivalent logic trees.

## 2 The Research Object

Were studied structures pumps model and prototype, which outline the tooth has been optimized with the use of multivalent logic trees. Wrocław University of Technology in co-operation with the company HYDROTOR S.A. designed the units. The experimental pump has been designed with taking into consideration technological possibilities of the company HYDROTOR S.A [11, 12]. Based on our calculations and technological capabilities Hydrotor SA (Implementing entity structure) designed a whole range of gear pumps for involute. Then they developed the technology of the new outline. Before performing an optimized kinematics of the wheel checked by polyvalent trees logic meshing three-involute profile on wheels printed in 3D. Shown in Fig. 1—wheel model were equivalent to wheels designed for pumps of the second group with a capacity of unit q = 8 cm3/rev.

Fig. 1

Wheels three involute made in 3D printing technology

The surface contour of a three-involute made in technology: grinding and shaving. Optimising production technology contributed to lower production costs and increase its productivity.

## 3 Measuring Rig

The static characteristics of the pump with multi-evolvental profile were determined using the rig shown in Fig. 2. In the rig, tested pump 1 is driven by 100 kW DC motor 2 working in tandem with SCR control system 20. The Pxob-94a motor and the DSI-0360/MN-503 thyristor control system make possible the smooth changing of pump rotational speed from 0 to 2000 rpm [13].

Fig. 2

Schematic of test rig: 1 tested pump, 2 driving DC motor, 3 feed pump, 4 AC motor, 5 suction filter, 6 cut-off valve, 7, 8 safety valves, 9, 10, 11 cut-off valve, 12 drain filter FD1-10-200-10 with overflow valve and electrical visual signaling (10 μm), 13, 14 manovacuometer 15 pressure gauge, 16 flowmeter with microammeter, 17 measuring microphones, 18 sound chamber, 19 measuring shaft, 20 tank

Preliminary pressure pump 3 and tested pump 1 are protected by safety valves 7 and 8. Tested pump 1 is loaded through throttle valve 10. The pump's actual delivery Q rz is measured by HO3/4x5/8 f—my Hoffer turbine flowmeter 16 with a measuring range of 0–100 dm3/min. Instantaneous flow rates are recorded: MINItrol type E S730 DRT f-my KEP. Pump output torque M is measured by Mt1000 torque sensor 19 with a measuring range of 0–1000 Nm and a Beta 2000 recording system. The pump's number of revolutions n is controlled on the driving motor shaft by a measuring system consisting of a photocell and digital counter 22. For this purpose a disc with holes in it is mounted on the motor shaft. There is a light source on one side of the disc with holes and a photocell on its other side. The photocell counts the number of electronic pulses dependent on the shaft rotational speed. This set is used solely to fix the prescribed speed of the driving system. Temperature t of the liquid in the tank was measured by a set of thermistors (sensor PU 381/1).

The maximum forcing pressure was limited by the measuring range of torque meter 21. The static characteristics were tested at a constant working fluid temperature of 50 °C.

## 4 Optimization of the Three-Involute Tooth Profile Including the Multi-Valued Logic Trees

The process of optimization has been carried out with regard to the five basic criteria:

  1. I.

Manufacturability,

  2. II.

Obtain a minimum compression ratio,

  3. III.

The occurrence of small changes dynamic forces in the engagement,

  4. IV.

Obtain a minimum ratio of pulsation efficiency,

  5. V.

Ensure high energy efficiency.

The profile, selected in the optimization process, is characterized by the occurrence of two ordinary evolvents and one extended evolvent. The analysis includes the basic geometrical relationships gear (Fig. 3).

## 5 Conclusions

The process of optimization has been carried out with regard to the five basic criteria: manufacturability tool, obtain the minimum compression ratio, the occurrence of small changes dynamic forces in the engagement, obtaining a minimum pulse rate performance and ensure high energy efficiency. From the point of view of the accepted conditions criterion adopted several alternative combinations outlines three-involute profile has been indicated by X 1. Were selected in the optimization profile is characterized by the presence of two involute ordinary and one involute extended. The outline of the tooth is optimized using a multi-valued logic trees. After the optimization technology of pumps prototype is smaller dispersion of results in the course of performance. Use of technology backlashless the optimized design of the three-involute resulted in the reduction of noise at a level of from 3 to 7 dB (A) for the bulk of the pump side mono-involute.
