Hydraulic oil used as material for fluid domain has following properties:

  * Density—950 kg/m3

  * Kinematic viscosity—37 mm2/s.

### 2.2 Comparison of Experimental and Simulation Results

Results from simulation have been compared with experimental studies presented in [6] for defined positions of gears and equal operating parameters of the pump (rotational speed—500 rpm and discharge pressure—0.55 MPa).

Figure 3 shows velocity vectors plot from CFD simulation results and photo from high speed camera taken during the visualization investigations of the gear pump [6]. In both cases strong disturbances in form of characteristic turbulence of the flow are visible. In this area, except of change of the flow direction, fluid velocity increase. At the same time the pressure in the turbulence zone decrease what is visible on the pressure distribution plot in Fig. 3a.

Fig. 3

Comparison of a simulation, b visualization results

The solution obtained using CFD is in the agreement with results from experimental investigations. Therefore the CFD model can be used for further analysis of fluid flow phenomena in gear pumps.

## 3 Operating Parameters and Their Influence on the Flow

The fluid flow analysis was performed for different operating parameters of the pump such as gears rotational speed and discharge pressure while maintaining the same value of radial gap. All of the cases and sets of parameters considered during research are shown in Table 2. For each set of parameters numerical simulation was performed and then the pressure distribution and velocity vectors in the area of gears engagement were plotted. This enables the analysis of fluid flow processes that appear in this region as well as investigating the intensity of cavitation phenomenon.

Table 2

Analyzed sets of parameters

Rotational speed (rpm) | Outlet pressure (MPa) | Gap (mm)

---|---|---

2000 | 15 | 0.05

10

5

1000 | 5

500 | 5

0.55

### 3.1 The Influence of Rotational Speed

Simulations for different rotational speed of gears, maintaining the discharge pressure equal 5 MPa, were performed. Pressure and velocity contours obtained for considered rotational speeds are shown in Fig. 4. In all cases the characteristic vortex appears, which intensity depends on the operating parameters of the pump. It can be noticed that with increasing of rotational speed the fluid velocity increase and the observed vortex is more intensive. At the same time, in the area of fluid flow disturbances negative pressure is present, what is shown in Fig. 5. Its value increase while increasing the gear rotational speed. For better visualization of the results the upper value of pressures was set to 0 Pa what enables to observe the whole range of negative pressure in this area.

Fig. 4

Velocity vectors for different rotational speeds a 2000 rpm, b 1000 rpm, c 500 rpm

Fig. 5

Pressure distribution for different rotational speeds a 2000 rpm, b 1000 rpm, c 500 rpm

Taking into account results shown in Figs. 4 and 5 it can be concluded that cavitation phenomenon in the zone of gear engagement increases with increasing of rotational speed of gears. This is due to the simultaneous increase in fluid velocity and local pressure drop.

### 3.2 The Influence of Discharge Pressure

In the next step the influence of the pressure in the discharge channel on the flow in the gear meshing zone was investigated. Obtained results for discharge pressure equal 5, 10 and 15 MPa, in the form of pressure and velocity distribution contours, are shown in Fig. 6. It is visible, that the flow disturbances of the hydraulic fluid become less intensive while increasing the discharge pressure. Pressure distribution plots of the analyzed area shown in Fig. 7 confirm assumptions about decreasing cavitation intensity with higher discharge pressure.

Fig. 6

Velocity vectors for different values of discharge pressure a 15 MPa, b 10 MPa, c 5 MPa

Fig. 7

Pressure distribution for different values of discharge pressure a 15 MPa, b 10 MPa, c 5 MPa

The impact of the value of discharge pressure on fluid flow phenomena in the engagement area can be observed on contours in Figs. 6 and 7. It has to be mentioned that in all considered cases both negative pressure values and velocities are lower than values observed for pump operating at different rotational speeds. This suggest less impact of the pressure in discharge channel on cavitation.

## 4 External Gear Pump 3D CFD Model

Two-dimensional CFD model presented in previous sections allows to investigate the influence of different pump operating parameters on cavitation intensity in the meshing zone. However, there are some other factors that affect the fluid flow in that area, for example pressure-relief grooves.

In order to investigate the influence of pressure-relief grooves on pressure and velocity distribution in the area of gears engagement 3D CFD model was prepared. All boundary conditions and simulation parameters remain as in 2D model.

Simulations were performed for geometry of the pump with and without pressure-relief grooves.

Results from the 3D CFD model have been compared with experimental results [6]. Velocity vectors plotted for plane cutting the oil volume for geometry without pressure relief grooves were similar to the photo taken during the flow visualization [6]. Plane chosen for pressure and vector distribution contours analysis and volume rendering is shown in Fig. 8.

Fig. 8

Pressure distribution a volume b cutting plane

## 5 The Influence of Pressure Relief Grooves

Results obtained for discharge pressure of 5 MPa and rotational speed of gears equal 2000 rpm are shown in Figs. 9 and 10. It is visible that pressures in the area of gears engagement for the gear pump without relief grooves are higher. Moreover, higher negative pressure values can be observed for the construction without pressure-relief grooves. The trapped volume between gears changes during the rotation of the gears. From the begin of the engagement of the second gear pair up to the central position of both gear pairs the trapped volume decrease what causes increasing of the pressure (Fig. 9). From the central position up to the end of the engagement of the previous gear pair the trapped volume increases. Due to changes of the trapped volume occurs the pressure overdue in the first phase and the under pressure in the second phase (Fig. 10) of the engagement area of two gear pairs.

Fig. 9

Pressure contours for geometry a without relief grooves, b with relief grooves (p = 5 MPa, n = 2000 rpm)—trapped volume is decreasing

Fig. 10

Pressure contours for geometry a without relief grooves, b with relief grooves (p = 5 MPa, n = 2000 rpm)—trapped volume is increasing

Taking into account plots shown in Figs. 9 and 10 it can be concluded that pressure-relief grooves significantly reduce the high pressure and negative pressure in trapped volume. It has to be mentioned that he pressure distribution slightly change according to the cutting plane due to asymmetric orientation of inlet and outlet channels.

## 6 Summary

The paper presents numerical simulation results for the fluid flow during the engagement of gears in an external gear pump. A comparison of results obtained by two different methods—traditional visualization method [6] and CFD technique—confirmed that the prepared CFD model reflects the basic phenomena that occurs during the fluid flow.

Simulations made for six different cases lead to the conclusion that operating parameters of the pump unit have a significant effect on the cavitation intensity. The resulting pressure distribution and vector plots in the area of gears engagement show that fluid flow turbulences and thereby the negative pressure increase with increasing of rotational speed and decrease while reducing the outlet pressure. Furthermore, the comparison of the results reveals that changes in discharge pressure in the outlet channel affects the intensity of cavitation less than the rotational speed change.

3D CFD model allowed to investigate the impact of the pressure-relief grooves on pressure in the meshing zone. The pressure-relief grooves significantly reduce the high pressure and negative pressure occurring in trapped volume. In further investigations the pressure pulsation of the gear pump as well as the mass flow rate for different operating conditions and different geometry of the pressure relieve grooves will be analyzed.

# Preliminary CFD Analysis of the Influence of the Geometry of the Selected Element on the Fluid Flow in the Tank of the Hydraulic System

Klaudiusz Klarecki1  and Dominik Rabsztyn1

(1)

Institute of Engineering Processes Automation and Integrated Manfacturing Systems, Gliwice, Poland

Klaudiusz Klarecki

Email: klaudiusz.klarecki@polsl.pl

Abstract

The article analyses the influence of the geometry of the downflow and suction lines and perforated baffle on the even flow of the working fluid in the tank of the hydraulic system. During the tests, more attention was paid to identifying the influence of the shape of wires on the phenomena connected with the flow of the fluid in the tank. We considered typical, and recommended by producers of the elements and hydraulic systems, construction forms of pipes introduced vertically into the tank, and comparing them to the pipes cut at a right angle. Since for simulation testing only one construction form was adopted, in this respect the results are only basic. Analyzing the results of simulation, it has been observed that the evenly perforated baffle does not bear significant influence on the equal distribution of fluid flow in the tank.

## 1 Introduction

When constructing tanks for the working fluid of hydrostatic drive systems, one needs to consider a variety of guidelines for the selection of: minimum usable capacity of the tank, minimum working fluid level, the form and number of baffles, geometric features [4, 5] suction and downflow lines and many others [6–11, 13, 15].

For the purposes of this article, it has been decided to verify the guidelines for the geometry of suction and downflow lines in hydraulic tanks. As far as those two are concerned, it is advised that they are positioned vertically, and their end shall be cut at 45° angle or bent at right angle (so that the stream flows in/out horizontally, parallel to the bottom of the tank) [1, 14]. It is worth observing that for most small and average hydraulic power packs, where most of the elements are mounted on the hydraulic tank's lid (including the electric motor-pump unit and downflow filter) suction and return lines have the tips cut at 45° angle [2].

The aim of the tests was to confirm the accuracy of commonly followed guidelines regarding constructing suction and return lines. In order to avoid costly prototype testing it has been decided to perform preliminary analysis with CFD (Computational Fluid Dynamics) simulation [3] using the Siemens NX 8.5 suite [16].

## 2 Test Plan

For the preliminary analysis of the problem it has been decided to take the following guidelines:

  * dimensions of the part of the tank filled with fluid 1200 × 800 × 600 mm (D × S × W), fluid volume V = 576 dm3,

  * flow rate 192 dm3/min (it has been assumed to be of threefold displacement of the pump per 1 min [1]),

  * hydraulic oil with kinematic viscosity of 37.5 mm2/s.

Taking into consideration the adopted flow rate value, the suction pipe was adjusted so that the average flow speed inside the pipe does not exceed 1 m/s [12]. The basic variant of the tank for modeling has been presented, in its simplified form, in Fig. 1. Distance from the bottom of the tank to the middle of end section of the lines has been adopted as no less than 120 mm [7, 14].

Fig. 1

Drawing of the basic variant of a tank for CFD modeling

Four variants of lines have been prepared:

  * ends cut perpendicularly,

  * ends cut at 45° angle,

  * ends bent at right angle and cut perpendicularly,

  * ends bent at right angle and cut at 45° angle.

For each of the variants, two versions have been prepared: with a baffle in the middle of the tank in the form of the perforated tile with 20 × 20 mm square perforations distributed evenly every 10 mm (total area of perforations—1976 cm2 which is 41.2% of the cross-section of the tank) and without the baffle.

Models for CFD analysis have been created on the basis of 3D geometric models, being the result of removing the part of fluid block that it has common with the tank. Then, 3D finite element mesh was generated, Tetrahedral type (4 nodes), for which the material with the properties of hydraulic oil was adopted, according to the assumptions. The inlet and outlet flow rate were adopted as boundary conditions (both set at 192 dm3/min). The plane of symmetry and ambient pressure were adopted as conditions for the fluid level in the tank. It was not possible to model the free liquid surface by directly introducing the condition of zero flow velocity in orthogonal direction to the nodes of that surface.

## 3 Results of CFD Simulation

8 simulations have been performed for the prepared models (4 variants of geometry with baffle and 4—without the baffle). In each case, the focus was on these three factors:

  * the fluid stream line between downflow and suction,

  * distribution of velocity in the plane of the middle cross-section of the tank (in the direction perpendicular to that plane),

  * distribution of vorticity on the wall of the tank's bottom.

Same of obtained results have been graphically represented on Figs. 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7.

Fig. 2

Fig. 3

Stream lines for the flow in the tank for bend with a cut at 45° angle suction and return lines, without baffle

Fig. 4

Distribution of orthogonal flow velocity in the middle plane of the tank for perpendicular cut of the suction and return lines, with baffle

Fig. 5

Distribution of orthogonal flow velocity in the middle plane of the tank for the flow in the tank catted at 45° angle, without baffle

Fig. 6

Distribution of flow vorticity at the bottom of the tank for the flow in the tank catted at 45° angle, with baffle

Fig. 7

Distribution of flow vorticity at the bottom of the tank for the flow in the tank bend with a cut at 45° angle, without baffle

On the basis of the results of CFD analysis, as shown in Table 1, it may be observed that both the angle of cutting the ends of suction and downflow lines (45° or 90°) and the presence of perforated baffle has no qualitative influence on the form of stream line of the fluid flowing in the hydraulic tank. The stream of the running fluid intensively hits the bottom of the tank, and then flows to the suction line, concentrating in the lower part of the tank.

Table 1

---|---

Yes | No

Perpendicular cut | 0.44 | 0.40

Cut at 45° angle | 0.45 | 0.43

Bend | 0.34 | 0.31

Bend with cut at 45° angle | 0.31 | 0.30

We have observed significantly different results for suction and downflow pipes bent at 90° angle, whereas the way their ends were cut was not that important. In these cases, the downflow stream hits the side wall of the tank, and then concentrates by this wall and flows to the suction line.

Before analyze the results of CFD simulations it may be noticed that in case of even flow of the fluid in the whole volume of the tank, we should obtain the average flow velocity in the middle cross-section:

  * for tanks with a baffle (A = 1976 cm2, Q = 192 dm3/min) vsr = 16.2 mm/s,

  * for tanks without a baffle (A = 4800 cm2, Q = 192 dm3/min) vsr = 6.7 mm/s.

In case of ideally even flow in the tank, we would achieve the indicator value w Z equal to 1, extremely uneven flow (for local velocity aiming at 4) would result in 0. The obtained values of indicator wZ have been shown in Table 1.

As can be easily seen, due to the criterion of value w Z , it is preferable to take the pipes cut at 45° angle.

A surprising conclusion is the fact that the perforated baffle with evenly distributed perforations did not significantly influence the equal flow distribution.

## 4 Conclusions

On the basis of the obtained results it may be observed that traditional geometric forms of suction lines and downflow lines in particular do not guarantee even flow of the working fluid in tanks of hydraulic systems. At the same time, it has been proven that cutting the pipes at 45° angle provides more satisfactory results than the alternative solution that is also more difficult from the technological point of view.

Another observation was related to the influence of perforated baffle with evenly distributed perforations on the fluid flow in the tank. According to the results presented in Table 1, it is insignificant. Obviously, it would be incorrect to conclude that the baffle is redundant. The study showed that there is a need to come up with such geometry of the baffle that would allow obtaining more even flow of the fluid in the tank. For such a baffle, it is necessary to assume irregular distribution of perforations and possible even additional surfaces (such as grills) working analogically to the steering wheel paddles in centrifugal machines, allowing shaping the stream line in hydraulic fluid.

Another step in the process of geometry optimization in tanks of the hydrostatic systems should be the study of interactions between the inlet/outlet direction for suction and downflow lines, geometry of the baffle or a few baffles and the phenomena of hydraulic fluid flow in the tanks.

As far as the places of contamination deposits in tanks are concerned and their connection with the geometry of suction and downflow lines and the baffle, it seems that it is crucial to carry out experimental tests in order to find the relation between their results and the results of the CFD simulation.

## 5 Summary

The article presents preliminary conclusions of CFD model tests, regarding constructing the tanks of hydrostatic systems. They are as follows:

  * choosing between two generally adopted methods of shaping downflow and suction lines, it is more satisfactory to use the solution that is simpler from execution point of view—cutting the end of vertical lines at 45° angle,

  * perforated baffle with evenly distributed perforations does not bear significant influence on shaping stream line of the working fluid flowing in the tank.

The study has also provided premises for further simulation and experimental tests regarding optimization of the hydraulic tanks structure.

# A Review of Fused Deposition Modeling Process Models

Piotr Komarnicki1

(1)

Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, Wrocław University of Technology, 50-370 Wrocław, Poland

Piotr Komarnicki

Email: piotr.komarnicki@pwr.edu.pl

Abstract

Recently, a large growth may be observed in the field of additive manufacturing. This technology allows for fabrication of geometrically complex functional parts directly from CAD models, without the necessity to use any tooling. The most common additive manufacturing methods utilized by the industry are based on extrusion of thermoplastic polymers (FDM—fused deposition modeling), however in present commercial applications the ability to control such processes is limited. In order to increase the capabilities of the FDM technology, it is crucial to develop accurate models of the key elements of the system and comprise them in process planning and monitoring/control algorithms. The purpose of this paper is to review and evaluate FDM process models proposed in literature.

Keywords

Additive manufacturingFused deposition modelingProcess modeling

## 1 Introduction

Additive manufacturing (AM), also known as layered manufacturing, rapid manufacturing, direct digital manufacturing or solid freeform fabrication, is a technique of fabricating three-dimensional objects directly from a digital model. As the parts are built in a layer-by-layer fashion, using additive manufacturing enables creation of geometrically complex parts that are extremely difficult or impossible to make using conventional subtractive or forming processes. By far the most widely used additive manufacturing systems are those based on extrusion, such as fused deposition modeling [3].

Currently, the applications of AM are shifting more and more towards end-use parts, which are highly demanding in terms of dimensional tolerances and mechanical properties, requiring predictable and repeatable operation of manufacturing systems. In order to satisfy these requirements, process variability and sensitivity to process variations must be reduced and the relationships between process parameters and end-part properties need to be determined [4].

Despite the fact that FDM and similar techniques have been present in the industry for more than 20 years there is still room for improvement in regards to processing science [2]. To enable development of advanced control schemes and possibly drive the development of new hardware equipped with closed-loop adaptive control systems and new types of sensors, it is essential to make use of process models that accurately describe system dynamics [7].

The objective of this paper is to review and evaluate fused deposition modeling process models related to material feed mechanism and liquefier dynamics.

## 2 Materials and Methods

Feedstocks for the FDM process are amorphous thermoplastic polymer filaments, which are commercially available as a wire with a diameter of about 1.75 or 3 mm. The filament is fed into the resistive-heated liquefying chamber, where it melts and then is extruded. FDM process employs a pinch roller mechanism to move material through the system. It consists of two rollers, which function is to create friction sufficient to grab the filament and push it into the liquefier. Energy is provided by stepper motors connected to one or both of the rollers. As the continuous solid filament is pushed into the heated chamber it acts like a piston, providing input pressure for the nozzle to extrude semi-liquid material. The liquefier is mounted to a gantry capable of moving on the XY plane. The tracks are deposited according to a pre-specified path and solidify upon contact with substrate or previously deposited tracks. After deposition of a complete layer, the build platform is lowered in the Z direction. Schematic of a generic extrusion-based system is depicted in Fig. 1.

Fig. 1

Slip has been modeled according to the generalized Navier boundary condition [1]. Since the force which drives the extrusion is applied by the filament, it is being compressed in the region located between rollers and liquefier entrance. The pivotal point of the FDM system is the liquefier, as it is the assembly where the solid feedstock is melted and pushed through a nozzle to form a part. Due to the unsteady flow of the polymer melt, non-linear dependences of the material properties on the temperature and shear rate and other causes [1] the dynamics of the liquefier are remarkably hard to model.

The force exerted on the melt by the solid filament must be sufficient to overcome the pressure drop across the system, which is dependent on the properties of the melt and geometry of the liquefier. Feedstock materials used in the FDM process exhibit shear-thinning behavior [9], which is modeled mathematically using power law for generalized Newtonian fluids, which is expressed as follows:

(9)

The pressure drop through the nozzle limits the rate at which the filament can be fed into the liquefier and then extruded. The feed rate should be controlled to compensate for the varying gantry velocity. However, as the feed rate changes, the volume of the melt in the liquefier varies, which influences the melt temperature and shear rate, on which viscosity is non-linearly dependent. These variables, along with liquefier geometry, determine resolution of the printed roads and should be taken into account in control systems, especially in transient working conditions.

## 3 Discussion

Models of the pinch roller mechanism provide qualitative description of the process and allow for estimation of motor parameters. However, these models do not take the slip between the filament and the rollers into account, which results in correct model behavior only in the system steady-state operation. Slip between the filament and pinch rollers has been modeled numerically, however, accuracy of this model is yet to be verified empirically [1]. Proposed model of the buckling phenomena in conjunction with experiments allowed for determining bounds of applicable feedstock properties [8]. As for the dynamics of the melt and liquefier, analytical [1, 6] and FEA [1, 5, 6] models have been obtained. Both mathematical and FEA models agree qualitatively, as they are showing increase in the pressure drop as the nozzle diameter and angle decrease or as the feed velocity increases [1, 6]. Additionally, both modelling approaches show that most of the pressure drop takes place near the liquefier nozzle. However, pressure drop obtained with FEA models is considerably lower than that calculated with the mathematical model, which may be caused by more rigorous assumptions made in order to make the mathematical model feasible to compute.

## 4 Conclusions

The models for major components of the FDM system have been developed, although there remains much room for improvement, especially that the degree of experimental validation of developed models is limited. Additionally, there has not been any physical system making use of these models to control the FDM with adaptive control algorithm employing feedback loop. The author plans to develop a physical system which would enable further evaluation of the revised models, especially those related to liquefier and melt dynamics.

# Method for Determining Bucket Chain Drive Loads During Excavation of the Bucket Chain Excavator

Marcin Kowalczyk1  , Jerzy Czmochowski1  , Przemysław Moczko1  and Eugeniusz Rusiński1

(1)

Wroclaw University of Science and Technology, Wroclaw, Poland

Marcin Kowalczyk

Email: marcin.kowalczyk@pwr.edu.pl

Jerzy Czmochowski

Email: jerzy.czmochowski@pwr.edu.pl

Przemysław Moczko (Corresponding author)

Email: przemyslaw.moczko@pwr.edu.pl

Eugeniusz Rusiński

Email: eugeniusz.rusinski@pwr.edu.pl

Abstract

In the paper method for measuring loads acting on excavation unit of bucket wheel and bucket chain excavators is presented. Measurements were performed with the use of strain gauges located on the torque beam of the drive. Analytical and experimental methods were adopted for determination of the torque beam behavior. This method is used for long-term measurements of loads in order to assess remaining life of long term operating excavators.

## 1 Introduction

Currently, open pit mines are operated by machines whose service life exceeds 30 years. In order to assess their current technical condition and forecasts of further exploitation it is essential to obtain actual operational loads acting on the machine during operation. As far as this issue is quite well assessed for bucket wheel excavators [1–4], there is a lack of such studies (methods) regarding the measurement of the loads acting on the bucket chain drive of bucket chain excavators. The paper presents an original method of measuring the load of mining unit with the use of numerical and experimental methods. The method bases on strain measurements in a suitable location of the torque beam of the bucket chain drive. Deformation of the torque beam was determined analytically and numerically (FEM) and by measuring the forces of bucket chain tension during calibration measurements. The paper presents an original method of measuring the tension forces of the bucket chain. The deformations data were recorded with the use of an original stand-alone microprocessor device. The presented method was used during long-term measurements of loads acting on the bucket chain drive, which are the basis of forecasting the further operation of excavators [2].

Long-term measurements of the load on the bucket chain drive were made in the KWB Bełchatów open pit mine during normal operation of the bucket chain excavator shown in Fig. 1. Loads identification was carried out by measuring the strain on the torque beam frame of the bucket chain drive. The 2-channels battery powered recorder was used for data collection. Data were recorded on an SD card with a resolution of 16 bit and the frequency of 235 Hz, which enabled the subsequent tracking of loads waveforms.

Fig. 1

Bucket chain excavaor

## 2 Calibration of the Measuring Set

The bucket chain drive, a motor and other drive components are arranged on the frame (Fig. 2). The frame serves as the torque beam. From one side the drive is mounted on the drive shaft of the chain, and from the other one, connected to the structural support by a link. The frame operates under shear and torque loads. The frame consists of closed box section. Strain gauges were located on two webs between the drive gearbox and the motor in the middle frame height. There were two half bridge strain gauges used to measure the linear deflection caused by shear stress. In this cases sheared cross section of the frame includes webs. The field distortion is fairly uniform, which reduces the measuring error caused by the inaccuracy of measuring point placement. Torque at output drive shaft is linearly depended on the force present on the frame link. The distance from the link to the axis of the output shaft equals 2,800 mm.

Fig. 2

Measuring point located on the drive frame (torque beam)

In order to calibrate measuring system the following works have been done:

  * analytical strain calculations,

  * numerical calculations of the frame (Fig. 3),

Fig. 3

Linear strain in the strain locations direction obtained from the FEM model used for calibration purpose. The 100 kN calibration force was considered in the calculations

  * on site measurements.

An active section of the frame, where the strain gauges were placed, was considered as the product of the sum of the thickness of the webs and the height of the frame. The average strain in the full bridge strain gauge (two rosettes on both sides of the frame) εma_100 kN equals 2.21 × 10−5, for the 100 kN force acting on the link connecting the frame and the supporting structure of the excavator. Considering that the frame is loaded asymmetrically, FEM model and calculations for the 100 kN calibration force were made. As a result of numerical calculations it was obtained:

  * εwFB_100 kN = 2.65 × 10−5—average strain for the full bridge of strain gauges,

  * εwHB1_100 kN = 5.66 × 10−5—average strain for the half bridge of strain gauges on the bucket chain drive side,

  * εwHB2_100 kN = −3.70 × 10−6—average strain for the half bridge of strain gauges on the outer side,

  * ratio εwHB2_100 kN/εwHB1_100 kN equals −0.065.

Strain gauges were placed in areas of relatively homogeneous strain fields on the frame resulting from the shear loads of cross sections. The measured value at each point was the mean value of strain in two orthogonal directions. It varied with the shift of the measuring point, to a lesser extent than is apparent from the strain contour of one of the component (Fig. 3). Analysis of the results of deformations calculations allowed to estimate the measurement error due to the deviation of position of strain gauges and their directions, and also to indicate the required precision of the measuring points.

The higher amount of εwFB_100 kN in relations to εma_100 kN indicates that an active cross section is smaller than assumed in the analytical calculations. The ratio εwHB2_100 kN/εwHB1_100 kN shows, that the use of full bridge causes decreasing of sensitivity and also makes signal level 10 times smaller on the outer side of the frame. The deformations of the torque are similar to the deformation caused by a pure shear, therefore the ratio of εwHB2_100 kN/εwHB1_100 kN is so small. This strain ratio is similar to the ratio b/a (Fig. 4). Shares of torque and shear forces are almost constant. For these reasons, the long-term measurement were made with the use of half bridge only on the chain side (Fig. 2). Thanks to that power consumption was reduced, despite the use of two active strain gauges and at the same time sensitivity was increased.

Fig. 4

Time signals of the bucket chain force and strain obtained during tests

The bucket chain drive is characterized by the following parameters:

  * nominal output torque M n = 240 kNm,

  * nominal output power: P no = 420 kW,

  * the average radius of the driving wheel calculated from the power: RKZ = 0.631 m with consideration of linear speed of the buckets 1.1 m/s.

On the basis of numerical calculations scaling factors of strain gauges were calculated:

  * k M = 1.10 kNm—the scaling constant value of transmission output torque after A/C conversion,

  * k wM = 0.00457—the scaling constant value of overload factor wM after A/C conversion.

The overload factor w M was calculated as ratio of transmission output torque and to nominal torque M n .

Calibration of strain gauges and measuring circuits (Fig. 5) were made with the use of force sensor, as shown in Fig. 6. As a result of almost static load, the deformation was measured on the frame at the measuring points on the chain side of C2 and C3 on the outer side (Fig. 4). The ratio of signals b/a amounted to approx. −0.08 confirmed the validity of the selection point. Friction forces of the chain are very large (Fig. 7), which prevents very accurate scaling of the physical object. The front part of the boom where the buckets move along, is inclined at an angle of approx. 45°, which means that almost 30% of the force F1 is absorbed by the transverse component of the chain force. In addition there are effects of friction and jamming of the chain, which are manifested by the lack of a full strain drop of C2 and C3 points. The full chain unloading was obtained only after buckets chain post movement. The force obtained from the calculation F2 is approx. 32% smaller than the force F1 measured (Fig. 7).

Fig. 5

Calibration procedures

Fig. 6

Force sensor used for calibration

Fig. 7

Force time signals obtained from the force sensor F1 and calculated with consideration of kM i Rkz

Taking into account the type of load case and construction of the frame it was determined that an error in the calculation of deformation on the numerical model and calibration constant values does not exceed 2%.

Time signal of the output torque of the bucket chain drive without material load and digging forces is shown in Fig. 8. The amplitude of the output torque is within the range of 63–71 kNm, which corresponds to 26–30% of the nominal torque.

Fig. 8

Output torque of the bucket chain drive without material load and digging forces

## 3 Long Term Tests

Continuous 21-day measurement of the chain drive loads of the Bucket Chain Excavator was made. Examples of acquired loads waveforms are shown in Figs. 9 and 10. The maximum overload factor obtained during tests exceeds 2.1 times the nominal torque. Analysis of the results was based on the determination of the distribution function of extreme loads above 240 kNm in 17-s periods.

Fig. 9

An example of the output torque of the chain drive during excavation

Fig. 10

An example of overload of the bucket chain drive

The cumulative distribution (Fig. 11) shows that among 22,600 cases of rated torque overloading in the three weeks period there were 2% of the cases with overload factor ranging from 1.6 to 2.1, while the cases of congestion more than 1.8 times of the nominal torque were only 29. Long-term measurements allow to determine the probability of load at a certain level, which is the basis for the assessment of condition assessment and residual life prediction of the machine [5].

Fig. 11

The probability of extreme load presence in the range of overload coefficients of 1.0–2.1

## 4 Conclusions

In the paper a method of measuring the load acting on the bucket chain drive of the bucket chain excavator used in open pit mines is presented. Strain gauges based system was used to measure the deformation of the torque beam, which serve as drive support. Obtained from measurements values were compared with theoretical calculations. The differences between results obtained from both methods were determined and discussed in the paper. The presented method for determining the excavation loads was used for long-term measurements, which were aimed to determine the residual life of the load carrying structure of the excavator.

# Design by Analogy: Synectics and Knowledge Acquisition Network

Sebastian Koziołek1

(1)

Department of Machine Design and Research, Wrocław University of Technology, Lukasiewicza 7/9, 50-371 Wroclaw, Poland

Sebastian Koziołek

Email: sebastian.koziolek@pwr.edu.pl

Abstract

Truly successful engineers and inventors not only use their domain-specific knowledge; they also utilize knowledge from other domains as well as the large body of heuristics and metaheuristics. They are holistic thinkers using both their deductive (rational) and abductive (creative) capabilities. Present computing education mostly emphasizes the utilization of knowledge in the context of analysis. Unfortunately, this limited focus has a negative impact on engineering students as it severely limits their ability to become inventors. In computer-aided design, models utilize attributes only from the used representation space. Therefore, the nature of such space is decisive where innovation of results is concerned. How to build a representation space for the problem-specific knowledge but allowing exploration leading to innovation is a challenge within the intersection of engineering and computer science. This paper proposes a method for building a design representation space capturing domain knowledge and at the same time creating an opportunity to acquire knowledge outside the problem domain. This dual emphasis increases the potential for producing novel designs. The method combines the advantages of heuristic thinking based on Synectics with traditional systematic and analytical thinking and is intended mostly for use in conceptual design. It will allow designers to develop a fundamental understanding how to acquire knowledge necessary for conceptual design while preserving their ability to explore various domains and to expand a representation space.

Keywords

CreativityHeuristic thinkingSynecticsComputing education

## 1 Introduction

Design innovation depends on the novelty of design concepts, products of conceptual design. Unfortunately, very often design concepts are simply a reflection of the past customer needs and the entire design process is focused mostly on satisfying these current requirements without looking into the future. In approach of design for the future the problem-specific knowledge is exploited and it rarely produces truly innovative design concepts, i.e. patentable concepts advancing evolution of engineering systems [1–3].

From the knowledge perspective, conceptual design can be considered as a two- or three-stage process. First, design knowledge is acquired. In the case of conceptual design entirely conducted by humans, the acquired knowledge is used directly in the second stage of concept development. When computers are used, in the second stage the acquired knowledge must be formally presented as a knowledge representation space, in the form of decision rules, and/or of ontologies. Then, in the third stage this formal knowledge may be used for the concept development.

In both cases of human and computer-aided design the nature of acquired knowledge is crucial for the conceptual design process and its results. If knowledge is acquired only from the problem-specific domain, the subsequent development of design concepts can be considered as exploitation of a design representation space prepared only for a specific domain. If knowledge is acquired also from outside this domain, from other engineering or science domains, then the development of design concepts can be considered as exploration. Obviously, this type of conceptual design is much more effective than exploitation-based design as far as innovation is concerned [4].

Presently, engineering design is focused mostly on the analytical aspects of design and does not sufficiently address issues associated with conceptual design. If conceptual design is discussed at all, it usually is considered as an exploitation process, which can be deductively conducted using, for example, various search methods. To advance engineering design education, a much better and complex understanding of conceptual design based on exploration must be developed, including understanding of methods, and tools.

This paper is focused on the fundamental issue how to acquire knowledge to be used in computer-aided conceptual design, knowledge which will allow exploration and ultimately will create opportunities for the development of novel design concepts. Such opportunities are of significant importance in many competitions, start-ups and investments, as in building a pneumatic driven vehicle dedicated for competition, where original solutions for many technical problems are required [5]. As a result of our studies a method is proposed, which is intended for use in design process and engineering education to prepare future designers for their challenges as explorers and inventors.

Innovation and Ideality Ratio. There are many ways to measure innovation in conceptual design [6, 7]. However, in teaching conceptual design an approach based on the concept of ideality ratio [8] seems most useful, as supported by experience with teaching Inventive Engineering. It is a purely qualitative measure but it encourages the designer to consider the system being designed in terms of two classes of functions, or effects. Obviously, these functions, or effects, can be associated with costs to make the measure quantitative, but it is not necessary in the majority of design situations.

The ideality ratio is defined [8] as the ratio of useful functions, or effects, to useless and harmful functions, or effects, (see Eq. 1).

(1)

where:

Fu

useful function of an engineering system

Fb

useless or harmful function of an engineering system.

Also, a concept of an engineering system can be associated with three classes of useful functions in accordance to Kano Model [9] (Fig. 1), when a concept is considered in the context of the market response. In this case, in the class of useful functions three subclasses can be distinguished, including "Attractive Functions", "Linear Quality Functions", and "Must Be Functions".

Fig. 1

The KANO model [9]

(2)

where:

FuAttractiveness

Useful and attractive function

FuLinear Quality

Useful related to performance—the more, the better

FuMust Be

Useful and required function.

Considering the market response to a given new product/engineering system, its sale volume depends on the used design concept and a proper balance of various useful functions (see Eq. 2 and Fig. 2).

Fig. 2

Characteristics of useful functions during product life cycle

When a product's life cycle is considered, in the first phase (Fig. 2) of the cycle [10] the majority of useful functions are perceived by customers as attractive and they contribute to the attribute of attractiveness of the product. For example, when a cell phone is considered, such useful and attractive function would be "taking pictures" (refer to the year 2000 in Fig. 3). In the next phase, the focus shifts to Linear Quality—that is, customers are now interested in better and upgraded performance of the same functions. Eventually, these functions become expected for a given product and the customers now simply require them. This is referred to the attribute of Must Be (refer to the year 2010 in Fig. 3).

Fig. 3

Evolution of an useful function

There is a relationship between the product's ideality ratio and its attractiveness, which is obviously related to the novelty of the used design concept [11]. That means that the key to attractiveness of new products/engineering systems is in conceptual design, not in the market studies. Also, from this perspective, development of design concepts driven only by the market needs is insufficient when our objective is true innovation.

## 2 Inventive Conceptual Design Method

The proposed method is based on the following assumptions:

  * It is intended for inventive conceptual design

  * Inventive conceptual design is a process leading to the development of design concepts, which are new, non-obvious and surprising, as well as potentially patentable concepts

  * A design concept is an abstract description of a given engineering system in terms of mostly symbolic attributes

  * Inventive conceptual design is a process of learning/knowledge acquisition related to the problem and of acquiring knowledge about inventive design concepts [12]

  * It is intended for a team conceptual design

  * It uses Synectics [13] for knowledge acquisition and for generation of design concepts

  * Knowledge acquisition is conducted using "Knowledge Acquisition Network"

  * "Knowledge Acquisition Network" utilizes both internal and external knowledge acquisition processes.

The method is based on a five-stage process (Fig. 4), including such stages as:

Fig. 4

Conceptual design process

  1. 1.

Problem identification

  2. 2.

Team selection

  3. 3.

Problem formulation

  4. 4.

Knowledge acquisition and development of design concepts

  5. 5.

Concept evaluation and selection.

The first three stages are preparation for the most important and difficult Stage 4 [11], called "Knowledge Acquisition and Development of Design Concepts". In the first stage, called "Problem Identification", the Team Leader identifies the problem and presents it in a descriptive form. Next, he/she determines the relative position of the problem with respect to the State of the Art (SOTA). In the second stage, the Team Leader selects team members, called "Synectors". The ideal team of Synectors should be balanced considering at least eight main characteristics, listed below:

  1. 1.

Domain Differentiation: Synectors should represent various domains, for example four engineers and two-three professionals from non-engineering domains (for example, biology, law, history, etc.)

  2. 2.

Emotional involvement: differentiated levels of motivation

  3. 3.

Thinking styles: global and local thinkers, members with legislative, executive, and judicial thinking styles, etc.

  4. 4.

Differentiated Age: optimal age is 25–40, but all ages are acceptable

  5. 5.

Administrative Experience: one or two experienced executives understanding management

  6. 6.

Entrepreneurship: one or two entrepreneurs focused on action

  7. 7.

Job Experience: Synectors should be experienced and successful

  8. 8.

Differentiated Education: as many domains as possible, including Art, Engineering, Biology, etc.

  9. 9.

The "Almost" Individual included: people who are not very successful at work but have potential.

In the Stage 3, called "Problem Formulation", the entire team is building a group understanding of the problem and is working on the formulation of the specific design tasks. In the Stage 4, called "Knowledge Acquisition and Development of "Design Concepts," all knowledge is acquired and design concepts are developed. This integrated process is based on the assumption that human development of new ideas (design concepts in our case) requires knowledge and is inspired by knowledge from various domains. For this reason, the process of knowledge acquisition in the proposed method is conducted using Synectics and both internal and external Synectics sessions (Fig. 5). The idea of using Synectics for knowledge acquisition has been inspired by great inventors, who also learned using unconventional methods. For example, Leonardo da Vinci learned human anatomy using human carcasses to improve his inventions [14] and Thomas Edison sought knowledge in poetry, which his mother taught him while schooling him at home [4]. Another great inventor, Genrich Altshuller [8] learned inventive knowledge studying thousands of patents and looking for patterns in the evolution of various engineering systems.

Fig. 5

Concept of internal and external knowledge acquisition

In the proposed methods, the integrated process of knowledge acquisition and development of design concepts is called the "Knowledge Acquisition Network" (Fig. 5). In this case, knowledge and new design concepts come from internal and external Synectors participating in Synectics sessions. First, an internal Synectics session is conducted. In this session, six-eight Synectors use the problem description and the problem formulation and try to acquire knowledge both from the problem domain and from other unrelated domains. This initial knowledge is then reformulated and its context changed using four analogies (Fig. 6), including:

Fig. 6

Illustration of synectics analogies

  * Personal Analogy

  * Direct Analogy

  * Symbolic Analogy

  * Fantasy Analogy.

When an internal Synectics session is conducted, the most fantastic and infeasible concepts are created. They are not useless because they can be considered as seeds in an evolutionary process, which may ultimately lead to novel and feasible ideas. Next, the initial concepts created using Analogies are transformed by Synectors in accordance with selected metaphors [8, 15–19]. As a result of this, the concepts gradually become better and their feasibility is improved. This part of the session is very important, because the conducted process leads to the seed questions for the External Synectics Session. Then, all Synectors distribute the questions through the entire Knowledge Acquisition Network, searching for new sources of inspirations and concepts, if possible. An External Synectic Session could be something small like a short conversation with friends or family, or something big like an international teleconference or a forum on the Internet. All knowledge acquired from these interactions is then presented in the second internal Synectics Session [13]. In this session the most interesting, novel, and plausible design concepts are produced.

After the development of a class of design concepts, Stage 5, called "Concept Evaluation" is conducted (Fig. 4). In this stage, the produced design concepts are first evaluated and then the best concept, or several comparable concepts in terms of their novelty, utility, or feasibility are selected. At this stage, concepts are usually presented in the descriptive form. Their descriptions are used then to identify symbolic attributes and their values. Next, other possible values for the individual attributes are determined and in this way the entire ranges of variation are obtained for all identified attributes. Finally, these attributes and their values are used to construct the design knowledge representation space for a given problem. The developed design representation space allows the preparation of patent claims and/or of design specifications for the detailed design.

## 3 Case Study: Internal Synectics Session

An Internal Synectics Session was held at George Mason University. There were four team members with different personal and professional backgrounds, who represented various engineering domains, and were at different stages in their respective professional careers. Members of the team included an MS student, a Ph.D. student, a junior faculty, and a 75-year old student and inventor with several patents.

Problem Identification. To reduce the raw sewage and other pollution that the city of Chicago was dumping into Lake Michigan (the source of its drinking water), the Corps of Engineers reversed the flow of the Chicago River from emptying into Lake Michigan to flow to the Illinois River and thus downstream into the Mississippi instead. This was achieved, among other means, by installing navigation locks at the upper mouth of the Chicago River. Barge traffic, and other small boat movement, was permitted through this system through the navigation locks, which can be opened and closed as needed.

The reversal of river flow and installation of navigation locks was done in the early 1900s. The primary cause for reversing the river flow, i.e. reducing pollution in the Lake Michigan, is no longer important because the city of Chicago now has an excellent waste water treatment program and does not release any untreated water. However, there is still a substantial barge industry dependent on moving commodities between Lake Michigan and the Illinois-Mississippi River system through the established system of navigation locks.

Today a threat to the lake fisheries and recreation industry in the Great Lakes is in the form of two related invasive species (Asian Carp and Silver Carp) that escaped into the Mississippi River in Arkansas during the mid-1990s and have been moving upstream through the watershed ever since. Both carps are voracious eaters, and they crowd out native species. They also create hazards to boaters, as they are easily stimulated to jump out of the water by the sound/vibration of motors. These fish may grow to 50 pounds or more, and are dangerous projectiles to boaters when jumping.

The US Army Corps of Engineers has created two electrical barriers in the upper end of the Chicago River for the purpose of blocking the passage of these fish, but recent evidence indicates that the carp have already travelled upstream of the electric barriers. Many of the states bordering the Great Lakes are suing the state of Illinois to close down the Chicago Sanitary Ship Canal and permanently remove any water connection between the two watersheds (Mississippi and Great Lakes). The state of Illinois is opposing this action, driven by the interests of the barge industry.

Problem Formulation. The problem was finally formulated as follows: Keep the Asian and Silver Carp population out of the Great Lakes and satisfy the following requirements:

  1. 1.

Minimal change to the time required for barge transit, and minimal additional operating costs.

  2. 2.

Strong assurance that the new system will prevent the invasive species from entering the Great Lakes through Lake Michigan.

Personal Analogy. Concept development using the Personal Analogy is the third step in the Synectics Session. The first class of concepts developed in this step is presented in Table 1. All concepts developed with the Personal Analogy describe personal ability to keep the Asian Carp out of the Great Lakes. Thus the ideas involve sentences such as "I eat", "I block", "I kill", etc. It is important to use this concept development in the Personal Analogy Stage of Synectics Session. Synectors usually have a tendency to use all analogies at the same time. Direct idea formulation keeps Synectors focused on using one analogy at the time, thereby maximizing the effectiveness of the session.

3 | I block the fish with my hands

4 | I kill the fish

Direct Analogy. In this analogy, Synectors look for similarities in different systems. The most powerful effect of this part of the session is the use of the Direct Analogy in the context of energy. Application of different form or source of energy to keep the Asian Carp out of the Great Lakes was the task in this stage of the session. The selected results from the Direct Analogy Stage of Synectics Session are presented in Table 2.

Symbolic Analogy. One of the most powerful analogies is Symbolic Analogy. This analogy shows a logical unit represented by a symbol. Very often, the symbols in this analogy are the natural objects, such as human body parts, trees, leaves, etc. Often ideas generated by the symbolic analogy could equally well be developed using a direct analogy. But the mere fact of looking for symbols affects the development of new solutions. Thus, despite the seemingly similar results, application of only one of them may be insufficient. The selected results from the Symbolic Analogy Stage of Synectics Session are presented in Table 3.

Fantasy Analogy. It is the simplest analogy for development of the first class of concepts. However, this part of the Synectics Session is the most difficult in terms of evolutionary concepts. The transformation of fantastic ideas from the first class of concepts into the next one is the crucial part of the session. This is because the transformation requires the change of a fantasy into a real, applicable concept. Metaphors. Metaphors are used to generate more classes of concepts. This is a new element of the proposed method of Conceptual Design. It is important to use the metaphors after the first Synectics Session is completed because metaphors fill the gap of limited number of Synectics Analogies. Computational linguistic analysis of over 1 trillion words of text exhibit the most typical words used [16]. These 25 common words have the most powerful effect in the linking of ideas. ## 4 Conclusions

The proposed method is intended to bridge an important gap in conceptual design between engineering focused on the traditional analytical use of computers and design dealing with advanced use of computers, including inventive conceptual design. In both cases a knowledge representation space is a must. However, in the case of analysis, a knowledge representation space is usually known or easy to prepare as a result of repetitive nature of computations. In the case of inventive conceptual design the situation is entirely different. Usually solving inventive problems requires exploration of knowledge and that leads to building a representation of knowledge from the problem domain and from other domains. Also, the nature and extend of such knowledge representation has a direct impact on the novelty of produced design concepts and often also determines if a given problem can be solved.

The proposed method has been developed as a result of extensive research on methods and tools for building design knowledge representation space. It has been tested with a group of students and modified as a result of the provided feedback. The method is not easy to use and it is appropriate only for designers familiar with Inventive Engineering and with Synectics. Also, all team members must be carefully selected and prepared for their participation in the team efforts. During the entire process the team cohesion must be maintained and team members constantly motivated and encouraged to be involved and to contribute to the process. The method is also sensitive to the internal group balance, i.e. no group member is supposed to dominate the team and the Team Leader must constantly react to the changes in the group's dynamics.

The conducted experiments were successful. The team efforts produced a continual flow of concepts and all members contributed in various ways, reflecting their knowledge and personalities. Most likely, the team size (four members) was too small and that might have negative impact on results because all team members needed to be fully engaged all time, sometimes nearly impossible to maintain.

Presented experiments clearly demonstrated that it is possible to develop a transdisciplinary design representation space for inventive conceptual design and that this goal can be accomplished in a systematic manner. Synectics proved to be difficult in use but it helped to acquire a rich body of knowledge. The method still requires refinements but even in its present form it can be used for teaching how to acquire transdisciplinary knowledge and how to use it to develop a design knowledge representation space.

# Correlation of Gears Strength and Methods of Determining the Coefficient of Load Distribution Along the Tooth Width

Stanisław Krawiec1, Michał Krawiec1 and Tadeusz Leśniewski1

(1)

Department of Machine Design and Tribology, Wroclaw University of Science and Technology, Wroclaw, Poland

Tadeusz Leśniewski

Email: tadeusz.lesniewski@pwr.edu.pl

Abstract

The analysis of the impact of the method of determining the coefficient of load distribution across the width of the tooth K Hß on its value and the value of safety factors on pitting SH and tooth fracture at the base of SF were presented. Three methods were analyzed. Described important differences in the methods adopted for analysis. Comparisons analyzed methods made on the example of the calculation of two-stage bevel-helical gear ratio of i = 4.10 and transferring the power of 580 kW. The results of analysis are shown graphically in two drawings and given appropriate proposals.

Keywords

Gear's strengthCoefficient K Hß

## 1 Introduction

The need to generate high torque at low motor speeds in working machines requires the use of mechanical gears which also enable the adjustment of the rotational speed. One of the basic types of mechanical gears are toothed gears, which are widely used. The gears carry the movement through the meshing of their teeth, which is why their durability and ability to work is determined by mechanical properties of the teeth. Damage of the teeth can occur for many reasons, the main of which are pitting and breaking at the base of the tooth. Therefore, calculations of the load capacity in accordance with ISO 6336 include verification of the tooth breakage strength at the base and of the surface pressure on the lateral surface of the teeth. The main objective of the gears strength calculation is to determine the values of the safety factors for pressure SH and tooth breaking at the base SF, as well as their assessment. According to [1–3], the coefficients are calculated from the general strength criterion:

where:

σ Hlim

σ Flim

σ H0

σ F0

Z NT

Y ðrelT

Y RrelT

K A

K Hα , K Fα

K Hß

SHmin

SFmin

The obtained values of coefficients SH and SF should further be assessed due to the fact that the results are affected by a number of errors resulting from the difference of the assumed coefficients occurring in the strength dependencies. One of the factors, relatively difficult to exactly estimate, is the ratio of the face load distribution along the width of the tooth for contact stress K Hß . This coefficient is defined as the ratio of the maximum unit load to the average load per unit width of the rim:

The value of this coefficient can be determined experimentally by measuring the adhesion trace of the teeth under pressure in the final gear or analytically by calculating the effective deviation of the teeth contact line. The accurate calculation of this deviation is difficult because it is affected by a number of parameters, the value of which is dependent on clearances in the bearings, manufacturing inaccuracies, as well as on the elastic deformation, mostly of the shafts. The size of this deviation similarly to the load and the deformation related to it, varies in a random manner. Therefore, only approximate values and statistical data taken as a probability of the occurrence of specific, effective deviations tooth line can be discussed. Precise calculation of it is time and work consuming, so its determination requires the use of various approximation methods. Out of the methods, three major ones should be distinguished, i.e. C2 method recommended by ISO [1–3] and the method described in the manual [4], which differ mainly in the way of calculating the bent and torsional deformations in the shafts and gears, as well as the method given in [5, 6], consisting in the reading of its value from the corresponding graphs.

In method C2 (ISO), coefficient K Hß is calculated from the equation whose character depends on whether the gearing transfers the load over the entire width (pattern a), or only over its section (pattern b).

This state of diversity was the inspiration for the authors to attempt to evaluate the selected methods for the received values of KHß and their impact on the pitting and tooth breaking safety factors. KHß factor, whose values were obtained using the three above-described methods, was analyzed.

## 2 The Analysis Object and the Implementation Method of the Research

To accomplish this objective, a two-stage taper–cylindrical gear shown schematically in Fig. 1 was used. For the solution, the calculations required to analyze the impact coefficient KHβ on the gears' strength were performed. The taper stage was adopted due to the fact that the calculation of the strength of that meshing were carried out for the alternate cylindrical wheels. It was decided that the comparison of the calculated safety factors S H and S f of coefficient K Hß for those significantly different meshing's, increases the validity of the conducted analyses. The calculation of the gears' geometry at both levels, as well as their strength calculations were carried out using dedicated computer programs [6]. In the schematic drawing (Fig. 1) all necessary measurements to determine the values of K hß were entered.

Fig. 1

Diagram of the analyzed gear with the dimensions necessary to perform the calculations

The calculations were made for the following design data and assumptions:

  * engine power P = 580 kW,

  * speed on the gearbox input shaft n = 986 rpm,

  * total gear ratio ic = iz1 * iz2 = 24/19 * 65/20 = 1.263 * 3.25 = 4.10,

  * gear manufacture accuracy class—7,

  * gears made of steel 20MnCr4 of 60 HRC hardness,

  * coefficient of the external dynamic surpluses (application factor) KA = 1.75,

  * durability Lh = 75,000 h as recommended for the drives of the cutting drum wheels of excavators,

  * unbarreled and unmodified gear teeth,

  * coefficients: ZL, ZR, ZV (lubricant factor, roughness factor and velocity factor) were calculated using approximation,

  * the distance between the supports and the gears assumed according to the dimensions plotted on the diagram of the gear illustrated in Fig. 1.

The others, more detailed data adopted for the calculations have not been given due to their irrelevance for the analysis results.

## 3 The Calculation Results and Summary

The results of coefficients K Hß , K Fß and their respective safety factors S H , S F calculated using the three methods for the analyzed gear are shown for level I (taper) on Fig. 2 and level II (cylindrical) on Fig. 3.

Fig. 2

The values of coefficients of the face load distribution along the tooth width KHß, KFß calculated using three methods and their respective safety factors SH, SF for level I

Fig. 3

The values of coefficients of the face load distribution along the tooth width KHß, KFß calculated using three methods and their respective safety factors SH, SF for level II

The analysis of the graphs shows that the values of coefficient K Hß calculated by means of the three methods vary considerably. And so, in the calculation of the first level (taper gear)—of the alternative gear (Fig. 1), the smallest value has factor K Hß taken from the graphs according to L [5, 6]. The increase in the value appearing in the calculations according to the other methods is significant and amounts to 25% for method C2 ISO [1] and 56% for the calculations carried out according to L [4]. A similar growth ratio of the values of coefficient K Hß occurs in the calculations carried out for the second, cylindrical, level (Fig. 2). The increase in the value of K Hß obtained for ISO C2 [1] was 35 and 68% for method L [4].

As to the impact of the obtained values of coefficient K Hß on the strength of the gears assessed by the values of the safety factors on pitting S H and on tooth breaking at the base S F it can be stated that it is also unequivocal and substantial.

The smallest values of those safety factors occur when coefficient K Hß is determined according to method L [4], higher when K Hß is calculated using method C2 ISO [1] and the biggest when K Hß is defined by L [5, 6]. It should be emphasized that the percentage increase of safety factors SH and SF is here smaller than that obtained in the calculating of K Hß . For example, calculating the first level, an increase in the value of the safety factor for pitting S H1 in relation to the lowest value obtained from K Hß calculated according to L [4] taking into account coefficient K Hß from method C2 ISO [1] amounts to 10.5 and 16% calculated using method L [5, 6]. This same safety factor for pitting S H1 calculated for the second, cylindrical, level is increased by 10% taking into account coefficient K Hß from method ISO C2 [1] and 18% using K Hß defined using method L [5, 6]. Similar relationships occur in the values of the safety factor for tooth breaking at the base S F . The smaller differences of the safety factors in relation to the occurrence of the calculating coefficient K Hß are due to different impact of coefficient K Hß on the value of calculated factors S H and S F . The values of both coefficients are inversely proportional to ratio K Hß , whereby in the coefficient for breaking by K Hß its calculated value should be adopted, and when calculating the coefficient for pitting a smaller value i.e. √K hß should be assumed.

In conclusion, it should be emphasized that the condition for carrying out the correct evaluation of the gear strength according to the criterion value of the safety factor on pitting S H and tooth breaking at the base S F , is to determine the values of the coefficient of load distribution across the width of tooth K Hß using the same method. The same evaluation, but conducted on the basis of the values of coefficient K Hß determined by various methods is not correct due to the high dispersion of the obtained values of the safety factors on pitting S H and breaking S F between the analyzed methods.

# The Design and Field Tests of a Box for "Erg" Electric Blasting Caps

PROJEKT I BADANIA POLIGONOWE POJEMNIKA NA ZAPALNIKI TYPU ERG

Piotr Krysiak1  , Ireneusz Lubach1, Janusz Śliwiński1 and Andrzej Wojciechowski1

(1)

Military Institute of Engineer Technology, Obornicka 136, 50-961 Wroclaw, Poland

Piotr Krysiak

Email: krysiak@witi.wroc.pl

Abstract

The paper presents strength analysis and experimental tests aimed at the selection of the optimal geometric and strength parameters of an explosion-containment case used for transporting "ERG"-type electric blasting caps. This box is mainly to be used by the soldiers during mining and demolition operations. Under the technical assumptions, the box is to withstand detonation initiated within and it is also to be resistant to perforation with bullets, hence the two kinds of tests which have been conducted.

## 1 Introduction

During mining operations on the battlefield there is a need for a soldier to be supplied with a set of blasting caps used for of arming of explosive charges. Both mining operations and demolitions require considerable amount of explosives, hence the capacity requirement for 50 electric blasting caps. A key parameter of efficient operation on the battlefield is soldier (force) protection. That is why it was assumed that the box is to be resistant to the possible detonation of electric blasting cap contained within, with additional requirement stating that the detonation would not transfer to other blasting caps contained within the same box. Additionally, the case should be resistance to bullets fired from assault rifle ball ammunition, in accordance with STANAG 4569 level 1.

Military engineers have at their disposal a number of boxes for blasting caps manufactured of various kinds of materials (plastic, wood, metal), varying as far as their capacity and blasting cap shapes which they are to contain is concerned. Several examples of boxes for blasting caps are visible in Fig. 1. Some of those, however, have purely historic value.

Fig. 1

Examples of blasting cap boxes [1–5]

Following the analysis of the boxes available on the market it was concluded that none of them fulfils the requirements specified below.

## 2 Armour Steel Perforation Test

The test has been conducted at the Ballistics Laboratory of the MORATEX Institute of Security Technologies—test certificate No. 031/2015U. An 8.5 mm-thick AM500T armour steel underwent test. This type of steel was used for the designed electric blasting cap box. In accordance with STANAG 4569 level 1, 4 perforation tests using three kinds of bullets have been conducted using a velocity test barrel. The test results are included in Table 1.

Table 1

Fig. 2

Furthermore, additional tests have been conducted with higher bullet striking velocity in order to confirm the safety limit in relation to the thickness of the selected armour plate (Table 2).

This verification confirmed that the increase of velocity by 66.5 m/s (7%) resulted in perforation. Basing on the results obtained it can be said that proper type of steel sheet has been selected and, additionally, the steel sheet is characterized by a slight allowance.

## 3 Detonation Transfer Test

One of the requirements for the box was its high capacity: it is to transport 50 "ERG" electric blasting caps. These blasting caps contain sensitive primary explosives and base charges (such as penthrite, lead azide and lead styphnate), hence the importance of precluding the detonation of additional blasting caps, should one blasting cap explode. In order to fulfil this particular requirement, a number of field tests have been conducted, the goal of which included estimation of the impact of impulse transfer to an adjacent electric blasting cap and perfecting the construction of the space within box.

The trials under field conditions were conducted in the following manner: the electric blasting caps were placed in several configurations in relation to one another and each time only one electric blasting caps was detonated using TZK-100A electric blasting machine. The test results, the explosion itself and all the resultant phenomena have been registered using Phantom V711 ultra high-speed camera. The test area is visible in Fig. 3.

Fig. 3

Test area

Trial No. 1 was conducted at an area, where the distance between the electric blasting caps was being changed from 12 to 40 mm, with step of 4 mm. Then, one blasting cap had been detonated in each test and what followed, was verification of whether adjacent blasting caps detonated (Fig. 4).

Fig. 4

Test area with electric blasting caps during series of tests No. 1

It has been found out that in all the cases there had occurred transfer of detonation from one blasting cap to another. This was the result of the impact of both the blast wave and the fragments of the detonated blasting cap.

The next stage of the test included insertion of the blasting caps into an insert made of polyurethane foam (Fig. 5).

Fig. 5

Test area with electric blasting caps during the series of tests No. 2

The foam applied did not provide sufficient protection and as the result, all the tests finalized with the detonation of the adjacent blasting cap.

Following the analyses, the researches decided to prepare steel tubes (made of grade S235 steel), the diameter of which equalled the external diameter of the blasting cap and the thickness of which ranged from 2 to 7 mm for series of tests No. 3. Then each blasting cap was detonated consecutively (Fig. 6).

Fig. 6

Steel tubes during series of tests No. 3; prior to detonation (on the left) and after the detonation (on the right)

After the series of tests, it was concluded that each time the steel tube had been torn due to the very high explosion energy of the explosive contained in a blasting cap.

According to literary sources [6, 7], pressure at the blast wave front is reversely proportional to the distance of the centre of explosion to the target (with the 3rd power). Therefore, what is vital here, is striving to increase the distance between the blasting cap and the tube wall as much as possible.

Hence for the next verification, a series of systems was prepared. Each of those comprised steel tubes of inner diameter equal 30 mm and the thickness of 2 and 3 mm and the wall thickness equal 2 mm, with the diameter of 15, 20 and 25 mm (Fig. 7).

Fig. 7

Test area with electric blasting caps during the series of tests No. 4

The test bed with all the types of tube systems was put under field conditions and each of those systems has been detonated one by one. Following the trials, it was found out that in order to preclude the transfer of the detonation from one "ERG" electric blasting cap to another, the blasting caps have to be inserted in tubes, whose side wall would be 2 mm-thick and whose internal diameter would equal 15 mm. A system fabricated of this type of tubes should comprise the interior fittings of the box.

A series of tests have also been carried out which utilized tubes made of glass-fibre-reinforced epoxy composite with 2 mm-thick side wall and whose diameter equalled 15 and 20 mm. Each detonation resulted in the tubes being utterly destroyed. Based on this experiment, a conclusion was drawn that the tube/sleeve for the blasting caps should be manufactured out of a material susceptible to deformation on one hand, but on the other hand, out of a material characterized by proper strength. Such properties are exhibited by steel, such as grade S235 structural steel.

Hence elaboration of a box manufactured out of 8.5 mm-thick armoured steel sheet. Holes were drilled in the steel sheets in order to vent the explosive gasses. A system made of steel tubes was put into the blasting cap box, and in order to verify the construction, 50 blasting caps were inserted into the box and then the blasting cap located in the centre was detonated. The experiment was registered using the ultra high-speed camera and the images from the trials are presented in Fig. 8.

Fig. 8

Test area with electric blasting caps during the series of tests No. 4

The practical tests corroborated the initial assumptions. No adjacent blasting cap detonated as the result of the central blasting cap detonation. What can be seen in Fig. 8, is also that the holes made in the side wall of the box fulfilled their task and explosive gasses could have been vented outside freely.

It has also been noticed that significant portion of the gasses was ejected directly under the lid of the box and that causes its significant deformation. In order to eliminate this phenomenon, the final version of the box was fitted with special elongated holes under the lid. Figure 9 illustrates the prototype of the box and its cutaway view.

Fig. 9

Geometric model of the blast cap box and its actual execution

## 4 Summary

The project included manufacture of a conceptual design of type "ERG" electric blasting cap box and a number of perforation tests and internal detonation tests. These were aimed at the selection of a proper construction of the box and also proper structural materials. The tests conducted confirmed the robustness of the assumptions made.

Based on the tests results, several conclusions can be drawn:

  * blasting caps need to be placed in proper sleeves/tubes which would protect the blasting cap adjacent to an exploding blasting cap from the unfavourable effects of such an explosion;

  * the protective tube needs to be manufactured out of a material characterized by proper strength and susceptible to deformations;

  * the box has to be fitted with holes in its walls for the venting of significant amount of explosive gases generated as the result of possible detonation.
