# Airless Tire Conceptions Modeling and Simulations

Michał Kucewicz1, Paweł Baranowski1  and Jerzy Małachowski1

(1)

Department of Mechanics and Applied Computer Science, Military University of Technology, 2 Gen. S. Kaliskiego Str, 00908 Warsaw, Poland

Paweł Baranowski

Email: pawel.baranowski@wat.edu.pl

Abstract

In this paper a modeling methodology and results of Finite Element Method simulations for selected non-pneumatic tires are presented. Additionally, a new conception of airless tire was proposed by the authors. To describe mechanical properties for components of tires a popular hyperplastic rubber constitutive model was implemented. Static radial deflection test was performed and the influence of internal structure geometry was investigated in terms of vertical displacement of rim, deformation shape and contact pressure. Obtained results from all tested tires were compared. For all tested conceptions stress distribution within the area of internal tire structures were analyses. All simulations were performed using explicit LS-Dyna commercial code.

Keywords

FE analysisNPTTire modelingNon-pneumatic tireAirless tire

## 1 Introduction

For the last few years everyone can observe a rapid growth of the automotive, civil and military industries with new trends of development in each of these areas. Such situation caused, that many companies are searching for new, more reliable and safer technology, also in the tire industry sector. One of the results of such researches is a development of an innovate Non Pneumatic Tire (NPT), which does not require the compressed air to work. NPT or airless tires have many advantages such as resistance for puncture, reduced fuel consumption, low maintenance and improvement of passenger's comfort due to better shock absorption [1]. However, there are some disadvantages associated with a difficulty with dissipation of the heat produced by friction and relatively high manufacturing cost, compared to traditional tires. NPTs became more popular in many fields, where traditional solutions are not effective enough,.i.e. in military vehicles [2] (American light armored vehicle Humvee) or in civil and mining industries (wheel excavators and dump tracks).

In this paper the authors present modeling and numerical simulations of selected NPTs, each with different internal structure geometry resulting in different radial load transfer between ground and car suspension system. For this purpose three different tire models were developed based on available commercial NPTs. Additionally the authors proposed the new conception of NPT called KucWheel. All of those structures are tested in the same loading conditions: radial deflection test under 10,000 N load. As a result of the simulations tire behavior, stress distribution for each component and tire deflection were taken into consideration and compared. For numerical simulations Finite Element Method (FEM) implemented in LS-Dyna commercial code was used.

## 2 Description of Non-Pneumatic Tires

In the paper three different NPTs were modelled: Tweel by Michelin, honeycomb airless tire by Resilience Technology and airless tire conception by Bridgestone (Fig. 1).

Fig. 1

Non-pneumatic tires chosen for simulations: a tweel, b honeycomb, c bridgestone airless tire conception [3]

Michelin Tweel [4–6] conception has radially placed flexible spokes that connect inner and outer components of wheel. In the Bridgestone tire spokes are not distributed radially and they are initially curved. Instead of one constant part there is two rows of spokes with the gap in the middle of wheel, from which one is placed in the opposite direction [7]. In both cases spokes are elements that provide load transfer as the effect of deformation during rolling [8, 9]. Airless tire proposed by Resilience Technology was inspired by natural honeycomb structure [10]. This tire is widely used in military due to bullet puncture resistance. Due to its progressive crushing and good energy dissipation properties it can provide a better safety of vehicle crew during mine or IED explosions [2].

Finally, a new conception of non-pneumatic tire called KucWheel was proposed, which was developed taking into account advantages and disadvantages of described constructions. It combines features of all of them. Internal structure close to the rim has a radial spokes which are connected to cellular shape which starts midway between tread and rim. Openwork structure is divided into three parts spaced equally across the tire. One of them is placed in the center and is rotated 5.625° in order to give additional stiffness in each position during rolling.

## 3 Description of Numerical Models

Due to the fact that none of the companies does not provide information about materials used and dimensions, all of executed numerical models were developed based on articles, photos and press reports which are available on the internet [3].

The main purpose of this article was to compare the influence of internal structure geometry for vertical rim displacement during radial deflection test. All other parts: rim, cords, inner and outer layers are invariant—it eliminates additional deformation caused by difference in measurements. Thickness of internal structure layers was determined by the criterion of constant mass for every wheel. Models of the tires were developed using beam elements (cords reinforcement), shell elements (spokes) and solid elements (rim, tread, inner and outer band). Number of elements and nodes in each discrete model is presented in Table 1. Figure 2 shows all three discrete model of tested tires with the solution proposed by the authors. Figure 3 presents a slice of FE model of honeycomb tire.

The mesh sensitivity study was also performed to obtain proper results convergence. Characteristic elements lengths equal to: 5, 10, 15, 20 and 35 mm were used and verified [11]. As a result 10 mm element size was chosen to discretize all FE models due to its relatively low simulation time, good deformation shape projection and no effect on the tire stiffness. For the contact modeling a penalty based contact algorithm implemented on LS-Dyna code is used [12, 16].

For article purposes it was assumed that all of the components except steel rim and steel reinforcement are made of rubber. For each FE model of the tire three constitutive material models available in LS-Dyna code were used [12] (Table 2):

## 4 Boundary and Initial Conditions for Simulations

The radial deflection test under 10,000 N load was performed. This value of force was adopted according to assumption that the tire is working with Humvee vehicle of weight 4000 kg. The load was applied in the center of the wheel and distributed to nodes on edges of the rim hole. Movement of rim was constrained: translational degrees of freedom (DOF) in X and Y axis and rotational DOFs around Y and Z axis (Fig. 4).

Fig. 4

Initial—boundary conditions applied in radial deflection simulation [11]

Due to large deformation and material nonlinearity it was necessary to use nonlinear method to solve FEM equations. Therefore, iterative Newton-Raphson solution was used [12].

## 5 Results and Discussion

Based on performed simulations characteristics of deflection as a function of applied force for each tire were obtained and are presented in Fig. 5. The lowest value of vertical displacement was obtained for Honeycomb cellular tire and is equal to 21 mm. That means this tire is characterized by largest coefficient of radial stiffness. Similar results are obtained for KucWheel conception, which achieved 21.6 mm. Larger values of deflection were observed for Tweel and airless tire conceptions, which are 33.2 and 89 mm, respectively. Deflection curves for KucWheel and Bridgestone tire are similar. The difference between these two compared to the others is a result of the internal structure geometry and consequently different load transfer between ground and suspension, what was described in Sect. 2 of the paper. Looking at stress distribution (Fig. 7) it is clearly visible, that in case of the cellular geometry, concentration of stress is located only in the bottom part, where the deformation of openwork structure is the largest. Maximum stress value for Honeycomb tire is equal to 1.81 MPa and can be observed in the lowest area of the internal structure. In case of KucWheel the maximum value is 2.63 MPa located within a locally buckled free edge of the structure. Comparing that to non-pneumatic tires with thin spokes it can be seen that again maximum stress appeared in spokes buckled due to compression (1.92 MPa for Tweel and 1.75 MPa for Bridgestone conception). Moreover, stress distribution can be also observed in tension areas of the structure (0.25 MPa for Tweel and 0.5 MPa for Bridgestone conception). Based on the results from radial deflection simulations the longitudinal contact pressure distributions for each tire were analyzed (Fig. 6). Rely on those curves, the relationship between deflection and pressure for wheels with high vertical stiffness and small area of tread and road contact are visible—the maximum pressure value are observed at the center of this areas, thus directly under the force loading direction. Such phenomenon but more uniform is common to traditional pneumatic tires [17]. On the other hand, in Bridgestone and Tweel conceptions, where the deformation of tread is larger the maximum contact pressure occurs near the place where tread lost the contact with ground.

Fig. 5

Deflection versus applied load characteristic obtained from radial deflection test for each tire; max. deformations are presented next to the curves [11]

Fig. 6

Distribution of contact pressure obtained from radial deflection test [11]

Fig. 7

Distribution of Von Mises stress on internal structure with maximum values for each tire: a tweel, b bridgestone conception, c honeycomb, d kucwheel [11]

## 6 Summary

The authors presented numerical modeling and simulations of three selected non-pneumatic tire conceptions available on the market which were compared with the tire structure proposed by the authors. Results of radial deflection test was presented. Such quantities as force versus displacement, contact pressure and stress distribution were analyzed and compared. During numerical investigations it was proved that each tire due to different internal structure geometry has given different radial load transfer and stress distribution, despite the fact of the same mass in all four conceptions.

It have to be stated that presented investigations are only a first step of wider study pointed on the development of a new airless tire. The authors wanted to present the possibility of testing several solutions using numerical methods. However, it is known and undeniable that a prototype of a tire needs to be developed and tested. Only when a coupling between FEA and experiments is carried out satisfactory results can be achieved.

The paper describes the part of a project that assumes to developed and test the KucWheel tire idea in actual loading conditions.

# Method of Assessment of Energy Consumption of Forklifts in Warehouses with Specific Operating Conditions

Stanisław Kwaśniowski1  and Paweł Zając1

(1)

Institute for Sustainable Technologies, Radom, Poland

Stanisław Kwaśniowski (Corresponding author)

Email: stanislaw.kwasniowski@pwr.edu.pl

Paweł Zając

Email: pawel.zajac@pwr.edu.pl

Abstract

This paper presents the method for evaluating energy consumption by a forklift with front forks. The model describing the work takes into account the truck's acceleration, driving at a constant speed, braking and the processes of raising and lowering the fork. Power consumption was estimated assuming the efficiency of the drive mechanism and the driving efficiency of the system lifting and lowering the fork carriage. A calculation model, in the form of non-linear differential equation, was solved by the approximate finite difference. On the basis of such a formulated model, the case of the truck work cycle VDI2198 was examined.

## 1 Introduction

In light of the current geo-ecological problems, energy consumption of many business processes is one of the biggest problems with which the international community copes [2, 10]. Reduction of energy consumption, optimization of production and transport processes is now a priority [1, 20]. We strive to realize such goals through various partial objectives consisting in reducing energy consumption and optimizing processes. In the case of warehouses, which are the buffers in logistic systems, where goods are stored temporarily, the energy is consumed to maintain the proper climatic conditions within the warehouses and on work related to the movement of goods stored inside. A sort of an indicator describing the consumption of energy on the storage may be the energy passing a specific stock-keeping unit through the warehouse [J/SKU]. If we assume that the stock-keeping unit is a EUR pallet, then the rate will be expressed in [J/EP]. The index value depends on the type of the stock-keeping unit, the type of product, the storage program, storage technology. The storage is inseparable with internal transport, which, depending on the type of warehouse, can be very simple or complex, depending on the warehouse equipment, required capacity, size, etc. The highest rates of energy consumption are in air-conditioned or refrigerated warehouses, when the temperature difference between the inside of the warehouse and the surroundings are tens of degrees Celsius [5–9]. The heat balance of the warehouse can be improved through a variety of technical and organizational solutions [26–30]. These issues require a comprehensive approach. A warehouse filled with goods can also be a kind of "energy storage" in the form of potential energy stored in stock-keeping units placed on shelves. Modern warehouse management tools enable optimization of many processes to manage energy consumption. One of the important factors of energy balance is energy consumption by the internal transport procedures. The rest of this paper will present a comprehensive model of energy consumption in the warehouse under cycle VDI2198 and a detailed model describing the energy consumption of the forklift during warehousing work [23–25, 31].

## 2 The Energy Balance of a Modern Warehouse

A warehouse as a separate entity needs energy for the implementation of the ongoing processes. It functions in an environment that also affects it back. The walls of the warehouse constitute a kind of a thermal barrier, and also a separate closed space with a certain energy intensity. Depending on the situation, we can consider fixed, quasi-fixed or undetermined energy states. A fixed state—the authors suggest considering situations where the warehouse uses a fixed amount of energy and the thermal state of the interior is characterized by stable microclimate parameters. A quasi-fixed state is a state, where there are small variations in the microclimate caused by the dynamically changing streams of energy consumed by devices performing in logistics processes inside the warehouse. A characteristic feature may be the average value of the microclimate and energy consumption. Undetermined—pronounced changes in the microclimate in time, and large fluctuations in the demand for energy during the processes of storage [19]. The following discussion will raise the issue of the phenomena in quasi-fixed state, where there is a time-varying energy demand. These situations are illustrated in Fig. 1.

The rest of the paper examines forklift movement on the basis of this cycle and energy consumption.

This cycle is divided into 4 stages, with each stage divided into sub-steps of the forklift movement. In the case of raising and lowering the carriage with forks, a constant speed of movement was assumed, significant for the direction and load. The energy consumed in this case was the product of the weight and the lowering or raising height [12, 13, 15, 21, 22].

## 5 Summary

The calculations have shown that energy consumption for traction in a forklift work cycle as per VDI is a total of 68.39 kJ per cycle. The energy dissipated during braking is approx. 43.01 kJ per cycle, which represents about 63% of the energy consumed to drive. The remainder of the energy consumed goes to cover the resistance movement of the truck. The energy required to raise an empty fork carriage requires an energy of 3.92 kJ, and loaded with 1000 kg takes 23.53 kJ. The VDI cycle energy consumption for raising an empty and loaded carriage absorbs a total of 27.47 kJ. A forklift working in a VDI cycle requires the energy of 95.86 kJ. If it was possible to recover the energy of braking and lowering a loaded truck carriage, consumption would amount to only 29.3 kJ, which is only 30% of the energy consumption compared to the truck without such possibilities. Of course, the calculation assumes 100% efficiency of energy recovery devices. In fact, the effects are expected to be somewhat lower. Nevertheless, the results encourage further work and the search for new solutions in the field of drive systems and operational systems. New possibilities are provided by the more and more frequently used super-capacitors, which in terms of current density per unit weight are comparable to conventional batteries, but their advantage is the possibility of fast energy accumulation. The large weight of these devices for forklift trucks is not a negative feature due to the stability of the truck when lifting loads and the need for counterweights.

# Modeling and Strength Analysis of the Specialized Car Trailer

Piotr Ladra1  and Bogdan Posiadała1

(1)

Politechnika Częstochowska, Częstochowska, Poland

Piotr Ladra (Corresponding author)

Email: kolar17@interia.pl

Bogdan Posiadała

Email: bogdan.p@imipkm.pcz.pl

Abstract

The subject of this paper concerns the issue of road transport, often described in literature.

## 1 Introduction

The subject of this paper concerns the issue of road transport, often described in literature e.g. [1, 5]. It is specifically about the difficulty that appear during the carriage of ordinary car trailer loads for one wheel bike specialist, mostly single-purpose, serving often narrowly defined to transport materials. In [6] an attempt to resolve this issue is described. The innovative solution in the form of a trailer has made the project the specialized multitasking, which in its design combines several single-purpose small trailers in one design. The innovation which has been proposed due to the application of innovative solutions applied in this project, namely the equipment trailer in folding frame, which significantly increases its multi-tasking through various settings. Moreover, the front side has been decomposed. The model and some examples of applications are shown in Fig. 1.

Fig. 1

Model of the prototype car trailer—sample applications

The project has been widely described in the literature [6]. Designed construction maintains standards trailer general purpose, but has been modified to combine several single-task car-trailers. The proposed trailer, equipped with innovative solutions, has never been applied in the construction of this type yet.

## 2 Description of the Proposed Solutions

Prior to designing the trailer the following construction and design requirements had been specified:

  1. 1.

Permissible gross weight: 1300 kg (maximum cargo capacity: 1000 kg).

  2. 2.

Dimensions of cargo space:

    * standard: 2200 × 1320 × 400,

    * when unfolded: 2600 × 1320 × 400,

    * with load distribution over the rear side (platform): 3100 × 1320 × 400.

  3. 3.

Non-slip floor sheathing—#3 aluminium, grooved.

  4. 4.

The rear side strengthened by the entrance.

  5. 5.

The folding front side.

  6. 6.

Hinged box.

  7. 7.

Universal multi-task frame.

The construction is intended to provide multitasking and versatility for applications to carriage such things as: scaffolding, garage doors, quads, motorcycles, bicycles, kayaks, self-propelled mowers.

To meet the above requirements a suitable frame construction that uses many innovative solutions was necessary. One of such solution is the use of the specialized rack that meets many of the features among others: creates a structure for the carriage of large dimension objects, such as garage doors. This is possible by applying the special frame (handles) by suitable modification of the mount frame. Normally these jacks are used as mounting brackets. This frame can be modified for other uses and so the rack elements can also serve to secure motorcycles or bicycles during transport with full adjustable spacing at each wheel size. Another functionality is the design and presentation of advertising banners, and through another modification (the addition of a horizontal bar) creates the frame for carrying kayaks (up to maximum of 8), or a long sewer materials e.g. pipes. The frame has handles for extra cargo security. The trailer project has been developed in SolidWorks 2013 [2, 3] with consideration of design standards based on the literature [3, 4, 7] The proposed model of car trailer is shown in Fig. 2.

Fig. 2

The model of the car trailer

The prototype car trailer project has been completely made in SolidWorks 2013 [2, 3]. Created in this program the model frame (Fig. 3) has been used as the model for the calculated static tests carried out by using finite element method [5]. This model contains all the components that were created in this design.

Static analysis has included the following tests: displacement, reduced stress and strain.

The study has been performed for two cases:

## 4 Summary

In the work the prototype project of specialized car trailer is presented. While maintaining the standards of general purpose trailer the proposed trailer prototype combines several individual small trailers in a multi-task trailer. A number of innovative solutions have been showcased in design of the car trailer. The following solutions have been created in design of the car trailer: fold-out sides, multi-functional rack folding, which, after appropriate setting creates all sorts of configurations necessary for the carriage of particular cargoes. Also handles cargo lashing is an innovative solution that perform several tasks in the whole structure, one of them is mounting elements frame. During the transport of long loads, e.g. canoes where the dimension is greater than 4 m, the special retractable panel backlight is used, in which the innovative solution is the way its extension without loosening screws or removing pins.

The project has been developed in SolidWorks 2013. The static analysis has also been completed on the bases of the calculation model in the form of a framework created by using finite element analysis using an additional capabilities of SolidWorks. The analysis have been performed for two different studies, as a continuous load and local load in the place most likely to obtain the biggest strain or displacement. In the work sample results of the two studies are presented.

The conclusion of the obtained results is that the structure of the trailer has been designed properly. All values obtained during the tests are in many times smaller than the allowable stress of the material from which it was made.

# Application of Reverse Engineering Methods in 3D Wide Area Measurements

Mateusz Lebiedzki1

(1)

Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, Wrocław University of Technology, Wrocław, 50-370, Poland

Mateusz Lebiedzki

Email: mateusz.lebiedzki@pwr.edu.pl

Abstract

In recent years we have witnessed a rapid development of Reverse Engineering. It significantly improved the process of machine designing. Its another application is creating three-dimensional models of areas (3D mapping), which provides some necessary information for constructors of machines that are to work in these areas. As far as RE methods of measuring small and big size objects are advanced and their precision known, approach for surveying larger areas is still being developed. This article presents a review of available Reverse Engineering techniques that are potentially applicable for 3D area scanning, as well as an attempt to connect them to a mobile platform. Therefore, advantages and disadvantages of a few such platforms are discussed in the paper. Position and orientation tracking systems of the whole device are also considered. Finally, a comparison of obtainable measurement uncertainty is provided with selection of the best solution for subsequent researches.

Keywords

Reverse engineeringMobile area measurements3D mapping

## 1 Introduction

Reverse Engineering is a field of science and technology focused on methods and means for creating digital models of real objects based on their 3D measurements. It represents a reverse approach to the standard process of designing machines, devices, buildings or other objects, which begins with creating a model and then continues to manufacturing a real product. There are plenty of Reverse Engineering applications—making datasheets for objects that do not have them, archiving monuments, quality control, designing personalized products or 3D mapping.

Modern methods of machine constructing include Reverse Engineering. Usually it is used for obtaining a 3D model of an existing part which subsequently is modified to create a new element or is a base for designing a part that is to cooperate with it. However, Reverse Engineering enables 3D mapping of areas. The results of it provide some necessary information for constructors of machines that are to work in these areas. For example a model of mine tunnels can be useful for designing road header machine.

Reverse Engineering methods for measuring objects are advanced and precise. It is slightly different when it comes to surveying larger areas. These methods are less developed what is also easy to see in publications (Fig. 1). This article focuses on application of Reverse Engineering in mobile 3D area measurements.

Fig. 1

Subjects of reverse engineering articles in 2015

## 2 Materials and Methods

### 2.1 Reverse Engineering Technologies

The most appropriate Reverse Engineering techniques for 3D area measurements are contactless methods. The first of them is triangular laser scanning. The principle of operation is based on transmitting a low-power focused laser beam and receiving it after reflection from an obstacle. For calculating the position of a measured object triangulation is used. The angle at which the beam returns to the scanner corresponds to the distance to the obstacle as it is presented in Fig. 2.

Fig. 2

Triangulation method used in laser scanning

For geodetic application there was a special kind of laser scanners created—Terrestrial Laser Scanners. It is characterized by a wide measurement range. For instance, Faro Focus 3D X330's range is from 0.6 to 330 m at the precision of ±2 mm [2]. Environmental scanning is performed with the use of infrared laser light directed by a rotary mirror system [1].

Laser scanning is used in many fields. Stationary TLS measurements are used in geodesy. A good example is 3D mapping of forest inventories [4], with Mobile Laser Scanning it is possible to detect and classify cars in big cities [11] or in agriculture to map watersheds [7].

Another measuring technique involving laser light is LiDaR (Light Detection and Ranging). The device transmits light pulses which then are dissipated and observed via embedded telescope. It is applied in various geological surveys, such as analyzing landslide conditioning factors [3].

Photogrammetry is one of the oldest methods in Reverse Engineering that enables creating 3D models. A series of images recorded with a photo camera is oriented in space based on common points or other geometric features [1]. With the right amount of photos and positions from where they are taken it is feasible to generate a 3D model of a test object or area. Photogrammetry is used among others to preserve information about historical or cultural sites [6], make 3D maps of mines [5], or in precision agriculture [10].

The accuracy of photogrammetric systems depends on such factors as resolution and calibration of the camera, scene lighting and proper arrangement of reference points. When it comes to wide area measurements, photogrammetry is usually used in aerial projects. The most basic parameter that describes the spatial resolution of taken pictures is Ground Sampling Distance (GSD)—it is the distance between two adjoining pixels in a photo, measured on the ground Pix4Dmapper support site [8]. GSD depends on internal camera parameters and distance to measured object according to the formulae (1):

(1)

GSD [cm/pix]

Ground Sampling Distance,

d [mm/pix]

pixel size in focal plane of the camera,

f [mm]

focal length,

h [cm]

distance between camera and ground (obstacle).

This relation is illustrated in Fig. 3. The usual values of GSD in aerial photogrammetry projects are between 0.1 and 10 cm/pix.

Fig. 3

The relation between Ground Sampling Distance GSD, interior camera parameters: d—pixel size, f—focal length, and distance between camera and ground h

With an appropriate overlap of taken photos, the accuracy of a reconstructed 3D area model in some systems reach the value of 1 GSD. For instance in Pix4Dmapper expected horizontal accuracy is 1–2 GSD and vertical accuracy—1–3 GSD Pix4Dmapper support site [8]. Vertical precision is usually worse than horizontal while taking nadir photos (axis of the camera is vertical). It can be increased by using oblique imagery techniques instead.

### 2.2 Mobile Platforms for Reverse Engineering Measurements

To make surveying of larger areas possible a scanner, camera or other measuring device needs to be moved. Additionally, in order to automate the whole process it is necessary to integrate it with a mobile platform. Attempts of mounting scanners on agricultural machines so that they are able to work autonomously or camera systems on cars for mapping are well-known. Latest example of using cars as mobile platforms is cited in a project of monitoring parking lots [11].

In recent years airborne measuring methods have gained popularity. The main reason of that is a rapid development of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAV). Muñoz-Nieto et al. presents three main types of UAVs: multirotor (Fig. 4), mini-helicopter and fixed-wing.

Fig. 4

Unmanned aerial vehicle, multirotor type [9]

A great advantage of multirotors and mini-helicopters over fixed-wings is the ability to vertically take-off and land as well as their lower flight height. Multirotor is also the most convenient one when it comes to controlling. These kinds of platforms were used in archeological area scanning [6], precision agriculture [10] and photogrammetric registration of gravel pit [9]. However, fixed-wings allow to cover greater distance at higher speed what was used for 3D mapping of mines in [5]. An important issue connected with airborne platforms is their payload. Scanners, especially TLS, are often too heavy to carry.

### 2.3 Position and Orientation Measurements

Having selected a Reverse Engineering method and a mobile platform, there remains one concern—determining the position and orientation (and scale in photogrammetry) for each single measurement. Geo-referencing of the generated 3D model is also worth considering [9].

The most popular technology connected with location systems is the Global Positioning System (GPS). Positioning is based on triangulation and time-of-flight of a radio signal from satellites to a receiver. Using the standard civilian C/A code, the precision of localization is ±10 m [12]. This unsatisfactory result can be improved by using GPS-RTK (Real Time Kinematic) technology. This system requires two receivers—one of them is fixed, with a known location and is used as a reference station for the other. This results in sending real-time corrections for GPS readings. If there is access to at least 5 satellites, precision of GPS-RTK positioning is ±2 cm [12]. GPS is used for geo-referencing of geodetic measurements and for routing of drones [5, 6]. However, there are places where GPS signal is inaccessible or impeded.

One of methods used in those situations is placing Ground Control Points (GCP) around the measured area. After geo-referencing these markers they become reference points for combining data during post-processing. This method was used both in [5, 6].

Another method is inertial navigation, with the use of Inertial Measurement Units (IMU). This system was used in 3D mapping of mines in [5]. Location and orientation of an object is calculated based on accelerometer and gyroscope measurements in 3 axes. Sometimes additionally the system includes magnetometer for better calibration. The major disadvantage of the IMU method is the fact that it suffers from accumulated error. Proper integration of data collected by a 3D scanner or photogrammetric camera would need correction of this kind of errors.

## 3 Discussion

The above description of Reverse Engineering methods, types of mobile platforms and navigation systems generates a question: how to connect these components to achieve optimal solution. When it comes to mobile platform, a multirotor drone seems to be the most suitable for large area measurements. The main arguments for it are its very good controllability and possibility to get to hard-to-reach places.

Due to limited payload of most available UAVs, the author proposes to focus in subsequent researches on photogrammetry. The precision of mapping with this technique may be a little worse than with laser scanning but the weight of necessary equipment is significantly smaller.

Error in determining the position and orientation, assuming the use of GPS-RTK is ±2 cm, which is 1–2 orders higher than the uncertainty of measurement of a photogrammetry system. Therefore it has the greatest impact on the precision of the whole system. For the purpose of 3D area mapping this result is satisfactory. However, to avoid losing orientation during measurements, the system should also include an inertial navigation unit and should cooperate with the Ground Control Points method.

## 4 Conclusions

This article provides a review of available Reverse Engineering methods that potentially can be used in large area 3D measurements. There are also mobile platforms presented and navigation techniques necessary for proper functioning of the whole measuring system.

Based on the collected information, the author of this article is developing a system consisting of photogrammetry equipment, airborne multirotor platform, GPS and inertial navigation.

# Experimental Analysis of the State of Stress of the Axisymetric Perforated Plates Loaded With Hydrostatic Pressure

W. Ledwoń1  and H. Achtelik1

(1)

Technical Opolska, Wydział Mechaniczny, Opole, Polska

W. Ledwoń

Email: w.ledwon@doktorant.po.edu.pl

Abstract

The subject of the work is the experimental analysis of the state of stress and deflection of a simply supported on the perimeter, the perforated plate rotationally symmetric loaded hydrostatic pressure. For this purpose a special test stand designed and developed research methodology perforated plate. To measure the deformation of plates used strain rosettes. The load plate was determined by bending its center of plate. The research obtained the radial stress, and peripheral to be reduced as a function of the radius of the circle perforation plate and load. The topography of the stress distribution to be reduced disclosure allowed zones of maximal effort perforated plate.

Keywords

Perforated platesStressDisplacementExperimental studiesDeflectionHydrostatic pressure

## 1 Introduction

In engineering structures are often used panel components comprising a plurality of holes forming a regular, dense grid. Such structures are used in chemical apparatus, e.g. A tube sheet heat exchanger [1, 2], or as components of shakers bulk material [3]. In heat exchangers important issue is the analysis of the complex interactions of the perforated plate (sieve plate) connected thereto to coat chemical apparatus and related schedules stresses in the jacket, tubes and the actual perforated plate [4–9]. In working example. [5] shows the approximate method of analysis of the state of stress in the perforated plates, involving the adoption of substitute stiffness plates, Poisson's ratio and stresses in bending sections thick plate perforated with hexagonal grid of holes. A perforated plate was taken as the isotropic plate of the same thickness but analyzed as a plate without perforations made of a material having a Poisson's ratio of substitution. Adopted by the backup plate stiffness value determined by comparison of the elastic deformation energy for the tri-armed slice (rod) for the load bending moments in a single direction. The influence of lateral forces on the size of the backup plate stiffness omitted. A similar approach to the determination of elastic parameters in replacement of perforated plates is proposed in [10]. For thin perforated plates whose diameter holes perforation is significant in comparison with the thickness of the plates the problem of finding alternative elastic parameters taken in [11]. To determine the effect of the concentration of normal stresses in the bent sections of perforated elements and the stress distribution in the cross section shown in studies [6, 7]. Based on the results taken adequate, but a simplified calculation model perforated plates. In order to determine in thick plates perforated substitute values \u200B\u200Bof Poisson's ratio and the stiffness of the plate were also conducted experimental studies by R. C. Sampson [7], W.J O 'Donella [12]. The results of these tests satisfactorily confirmed the results of calculations made on the basis of a model adopted by M. Bijak-Żuchowski [5].

## 2 Objective of Work

The aim of this work is to present the results of the diagnosis topography deformation pattern on the entire surface of the model adequately prepared circular loaded axially symmetrical perforated plate. Another objective is to calculate the value of principal stresses to be reduced and cross-sectional plates.

## 3 Experimental Research

### 3.1 Object of Investigation

Experimental tests were performed on a model of a circular plate with dimensions: outer diameter D = 300 mm and thickness h = 5 mm, supported freely on the whole circumference, the load plate was distributed circularly symmetric, is perpendicular to the surface of the pressure plate q uniform over the entire surface. Experimental perforation plate made in the form of holes of varying diameters suitably selected across 10 circles with radii as shown in Fig. 1 in the number of openings 20 on each circle.

Fig. 1

Load the perforated plate loaded hydrostatic pressure q, simply supported

Selection of the diameters of openings made in such a way that the opening cross-sectional weakening factors for both radial and circumferential each section were the same plate. Means providing circularly symmetric configuration stiffness sections. The attenuation coefficient of the radial cross-section will thus be the same for all sections, but different from the coefficient of stiffness sections. In the prepared plate coefficients they were adopted as follows:

  * Extinction coefficient section in the radial direction   is 0.5.

  * Extinction coefficient section in the circumferential direction   is 0.6.

Details of hole diameters shown in Fig. 2.

Fig. 2

View experimental model of perforated plates with decomposition perforation made in the form of holes and visible measuring points S1-S7, R1-R7

On thus prepared model were taken measuring points placed on the bridges between the holes, which have been stuck equiangular strain rosettes delta (Fig. 3).

Fig. 3

Diagram of the applied strain rosettes delta of Tokyo Sokkia Kenkyujo Co 'Ltd

Was used to measure the deformation strain rosettes of Tokyo Sokkia Kenkyujo Co 'Ltd, FRA-1-11-1L on the basis of measurement equal to 1 mm and resistance of 120 Ω strain gauge and a constant k = 2.14. These strain gauges were stuck in two mutually perpendicular measurement zones (Fig. 2), with 7 points. Details are shown in the pictures (Fig. 4). The scheme of the studies prepared for perforated plate rotationally symmetric loaded hydrostatic pressure is shown in Fig. 5.

Fig. 4

Strain gauge rosettes delta of Tokyo Sokkia Kenkyujo Co 'Ltd glued to test a perforated plate

Fig. 5

The scheme of the prepared test circularly symmetric perforated plate, loaded hydrostatic pressure over the entire surface

### 3.2 Research Position

To carry out the measurements of the topography of strains in the plate had to prepare suitable test stand. To this aim a special tooling to ensure that the rear plate of this apparatus as a support freely around the perimeter. To ensure that the load applied to the plate onto a disc of a thin, supple, homogeneous intermediate sheet on which was placed a closed container filled with a liquid, which is placed on top of a steel, respectively rigid plate. The whole thus prepared (Fig. 5) was placed on the universal testing machine ZDM 2.5 of Werkstoff Pruefmaschinnen Leipzig. The apparatus was placed on the machine in such a way as to ensure during the test also measured the bending displacement of the central point of the disc. Uses a dial gauge with a scale 0.01 mm. The load has been applied to the upper, rigid steel plate located on the machine pressing die. The value of the clamping force steel plate was read on a dynamometer testing machine, set the scope of 10 kN. View of bench prepared to study the perforated plate is shown in Fig. 6.

Fig. 6

The test for the experience with perforated circularly symmetric-loaded hydrostatic pressure over the entire surface, where indicated: 1—stamp of pressure, 2—along with the tooling plate, 3—the dynamometer, 4—the dial gauge, 5—bridge strain gauge, 6—distributor box

## 4 Methodology Of Research

Program strain measurements at specified points operates as follows:

  * Adopted the preload of 400 N, you reset all the indications strain gauges and dial gauge, and then measured the strain for in turn increasing the load by controlling the deflection plates in increments of 0.5 mm, reading at the same time the amount of force on a dynamometer machine. 6, a total series of measurements for the following displacement sizes: 0.5 mm, 1.0 mm, 1.5 mm, 2.0 mm, 2.5 mm, 3.0 mm.

# CAD/CAE Applications in Mill's Design and Investigation

Marek Macko1  , Józef Flizikowski2  , Zbigniew Szczepański1, Krzysztof Tyszczuk1, Grzegorz Śmigielski1, Adam Mroziński2, Jacek Czerniak1 and Andrzej Tomporowski2

(1)

Faculty of Mathematics, Physics and Technical Sciences, Casimir the Great University, Chodkiewicza 30, 85-064, Bydgoszcz, Poland

(2)

Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, University of Technology and Life Sciences, Al. Prof. Kaliskiego 7, 85-793, Bydgoszcz, Poland

Marek Macko (Corresponding author)

Email: mackomar@ukw.edu.pl

Józef Flizikowski

Email: fliz@utp.edu.pl

Abstract

CAD/CAE are crucial in supporting structural design shredders, as well as the management of the acquisition test data. These tools, but also the AI has been used to search for the best solution of shredder. Implementations of this method and verification of shredding on many edges improve operational performance. Selected results and analysis have been verified with the results of the laboratory tests.

## 1 Introduction

The dynamic development of computer technology and CAD/CAE systems creates new opportunities in design, manufacture and operation of the machines. The advantages of their use are well known and can be seen even by reducing the time of the performance of the technical documentation and strengthening the creative possibilities constructor [3, 4, 10–12]. Basically, the design process using CAD/CAE systems begins with building a geometric model without the detailed implementation and technical documentation. This makes it possible to pay more attention to the characteristics and relationships of the final solution. It also enables to present even physically non-existent product and makes it easier to elaborate analysis on the implementation of the production by taking into account the effects of the market economy. In addition, implementations of applications such as artificial intelligence (AI) contribute to the improvement of the final solution [8, 10, 11, 14]. The paper proposes methods for testing the grinding process of polymer plastics which use computer tools. The reason for taking such formulated task is an unsatisfactory solution to the problem of effective shredding materials both in laboratory and industrial applications, and correct materials (like polymers or vegetable) preparations [1, 2, 5–7, 9, 13]. Each new research approach can contribute to more thorough knowledge of the complex process. If in additional way acquisition and data management are conducted in a controlled manner, then these data can be effectively used to build a base for the construction of grinders. Currently, the aspects of computer-aided grinding process of polymer materials can be observed not only on the acquisition and development research or laboratory results but also on the virtual model of the mill, which was built as a mechanism followed by strength and kinematic analysis. For the purposes of virtual modeling applications we used SolidWorks Simulation and own applications in the field of AI.

## 2 Objectives and Description of the Simulation

The object of the research system is described as a working universal grinder in the lab of the Department of Mechatronics and built using our own multi-edge shredders [15–24] [Fig. 1].

Fig. 1

The laboratory-stand grinder view

In the proposed methodology provided for research, which is based on source collecting data from the experimental chopper, then creating a relationship angular velocity and linear, torques, and kinematic relations by SolidWorks Simulation conducting model corresponding design features as a real chopper laboratory in the methodology provided further implementation of simulation tests—durability verified arrangement of working elements compared to the sample. The purpose of this step is to analyze the possible cases of disintegration of the sample material at low and high speed, taking the following criteria into account:

  * sample dimensions,

  * the type of research and related settings,

  * the properties of the material,

  * load and boundary conditions.

In SolidWorks Simulation and SolidWorks Motion Simulations we carried out kinematic assemblies preparing earlier in the SolidWorks environment. With this application we verified a virtual 3D model of the mill. It was verified that there are no collisions during movement assembly and it defines the relationship between the elements of the chopper and shredded samples. It presents a graphical and hierarchical model of assembly.

Following phases for defining and simulation mechanisms grinder.

In order to establish and analyze grinder mechanism properly we have to specify, which elements of assembly are fixed and which are movable, and continue an analysis by the proposed criteria (Fig. 2):

  * the assessment of the concept of the project—identification of components, links between elements and the determination of driving components,

  * the identification of the elements of assembly, which will participate in the moving model,

  * adding movement in bond mechanisms—the use of bonds degrees of freedom (the movement in this case may be of the rotary or the linear function of time),

  * optional addition of external forces,

  * running the simulation model—using SolidWorks Motion—the calculation of displacements, and reaction forces in some parts of the mechanism

  * the development of the simulation results—in the form of charts, analysis and animation.

The laboratory investigations were conducted, based on the measurement system, where we obtained transient values of rotary moment and angular speed. The results from investigations were used to calculate necessary energy onto disintegration of sample from material. The value of minimum expenditures of energy served for criterion of suitable solution selection for the multiple-edge milling system. Such cases were studied: grinder with drums with holes (one of them rotary the inner one—motionless) and discs with holes. The analysis of the results let us observe differences of range and phenomenon of rotary moment as well as shape and dimension of shredded material for different values of velocity solutions.

## 4 Implementation of Genetic Algorithm Application

The algorithm (CutMAG) uses hybrid approach to optimisation, i.e. a combination of classic genetic algorithms (GA) with morphologic optimisation (M) by creating innovative approach to optimisation of cutting disk design (Cut) for the multi-edge grinder. The input data include population of individuals. Each individual is represented by a set of cutting disks. The fitness function of an individual is calculated as the fitness average of each disk supplemented by information describing the relationship between both disks. The method for calculating function values was selected to ensure its maximisation in the process of evolution (Eq. 1, 2).

The modified roulette wheel method was used as a way of selection. This will allow for further improvement of the algorithm efficiency by using more optimum methods. The algorithm is terminated when the population includes the individual with the fitness function value not lower than the assumed one. If there is no such an individual and the algorithm stops at a relative extreme, the algorithm will be automatically terminated when 10000 populations are exceeded. It is also worth mentioning that the proposed approach meets J.H.Holland's postulate and represents classic algorithm without memory, characterized by overwriting (replacement) of the parent population with the population of children. The figures below show four stages of processing for the same disk. Point A shows a "raw" result of the crossing. It includes small holes, which, although technologically feasible, do not make any difference for the structure. Point B presents the disk after morphological optimisation (i.e. after closing operation). The smallest holes disappeared and the disk geometry seems to be proper. The figure C, on the other hand shows places (holes) which were eliminated as a result of mutation applied to the disk. The effect of that operation can be seen in the figure D (Fig. 4).

## 5 Description of CAD/CAE in Measurement System

The system design of the measurement module is described as an universal structure of utility, postulated states of shredding: product quality, efficiency process, the harmlessness of the product and the global process. Collection, analysis and processing of data state indicators are based on computer support in an environment of LabVIEW. The grinding requires to deliver not only feed but also the given the nature of the structure and process air with the specified parameters. Figure 5 explains to us a schematic representation of the process for grinding precision grinder.

The modular—mechatronic system of shredding based on AI algorithm

## 6 Summary and Conclusions

Common stages of CAD/CAE and AI (AG) integration of grinding systems give us some possible solutions for better efficiency of the process thanks to the preparation the new solutions of discs geometry. From that point of view, minimizing the standard deviation of a selected conception, e.g. value of disintegration intersection for a group of data, may be easily transformed into a problem of maximization—it is consistent with the assumed mode of application/interpretation of the accommodation function: the bigger the value, the better the solution, especially for GA results. Because of that, worse solutions (characterized by a bigger standard deviation which holds smaller value of an accommodation function) shall be slowly removed from population (natural selection) and individuals that shall remain, should be characterized by desirable—from the point of view of criteria—features of construction.

The average value of the intersection for all the iterations in a single simulation is the additional measuring instrument of a solution's quality in case of the construction's optimisation of disintegration intersection. It means that a potentially interesting solution should be characterized by minimum intersection fluctuations in the "total time of living" and its high average value. In order to improve the time of convergence in implementation, it was decided to apply the function of reward and penalty. Each solution for which the accommodation function is negative or equal to zero, has a chance to survive to the next generation, which renders it possible to preserve the population's variety important in genetic operations by setting the value of accommodation value to a very small number.

Some analysis of the implementations proved that the CAD/CAE GA methods optimising design of grinder can facilitate a choice of the specific geometric features for grinders. Finally, for grinders the specific energy of milling depends not only on the method and parameters of the processing, but also on many features of the tools, including shape of its active surface. It has been developed that there is a correlation between the parameters of the topography of the active surface and the energy consumed during the processing. The simulation comparison tests allowed to determine the features, for grinding tools of various micro- and macro-topographic parameters, for which the amount of the consumed energy was the least. Additional tasks were important and have influenced on final energy requirements.

The purpose of the development, which consists in design and implementation of methods for CAD/CAE subsystems AG and modern computer-aided research is to: process efficiency, product quality, innocuousness of the product and the grinding process of high complexity has been achieved. Having sold the problem of measurement, collection and analysis of the characteristics of utility, the state postulated grinding. The collection, analysis and processing of data on the state indicators were based on computer support in an environment of LabVIEW. The measuring system can support any stand shredding technology. Apart from determination, the characteristics of utility allows us to examine, develop, apply and explore ideas and designs, technologies shredding.

# The Method of Artificial Organs Fabrication Based on Reverse Engineering in Medicine

Marek Macko1  , Zbigniew Szczepański1  , Dariusz Mikołajewski1  , Emilia Mikołajewska1 and Sławomir Listopadzki1

(1)

Institute of Mechanics and Applied Computer Science, Kazimierz Wielki University, Kopernika 1, 85-067 Bydgoszcz, Poland

Marek Macko (Corresponding author)

Email: mackomar@ukw.edu.pl

Zbigniew Szczepański

Email: zszczep@ukw.edu.pl

Dariusz Mikołajewski

Email: darek.mikolajewski@wp.pl

Abstract

The paper presents the concept and implementation of innovative methods of producing artificial organs and prosthesis based on 3D printing technology. These organs possess physical and mechanical properties similar to human organs and bodies part. As a result, using such organs, it is possible to conduct training and workshops, especially in the field of urological surgery, under the conditions close to real operations. Due to the fabrication of 3D models can also lead so-called pre-operations in order to better prepare surgeons to carry out complex operations and post-operation e.g. observers proper operation. The proposed method enables the production of artificial human organs whose consistency, plastic properties, hardness, elasticity are close to the real organ of specific patient, because it can be made on the basis of the data from MRI and CT. The process of preparing 3D geometry is prepared in applications in the field of CAD, but also through advanced applications designed for editing in vector geometry environment.

## 1 Introduction

Many advances in medicine have been achieved as a result of advances in other fields, including rehabilitation engineering, medical IT and robotics. This makes biomedicine open to novel approaches and technologies, which can increase effectivity of the therapeutic interventions. 3D printing, 3D scanning and associated technologies can constitute another step toward better application of the medicine and rehabilitation engineering principles in current clinical practice.

Current medical applications of 3D techniques cover many areas including:

  * learning, including customized anatomical models, individual and team training in medical simulation centers,

  * scientific research, concerning e.g. bones or soft tissues modeling and testing,

  * 2D or 3D diagnostics (CT, MRI, 3D scans, clinical motion analysis, etc.)—2D images can be converted to 3D images,

  * 3D scanning (including fast face/head scanning and fast whole body scanning),

  * 3D printing in surgery, drug fabrication and rehabilitation engineering,

  * reverse engineering (digitizing of real objects, partly for replication purposes),

  * additive manufacturing, which allows for geometric flexibility of printed products (e.g. implants) and customization to suit individual needs.

Traditional manual design and manufacturing of personalized therapeutic solutions can be changed thanks to computer-aided design (CAD), rapid prototyping (RP), and computer-aided manufacturing (CAM) of physical models or even final products directly from 3D computer data. Joining various methods and techniques (e.g. within reveres engineering) allows to significantly shorten track between measurements in particular patient and ready-to-use personalized equipment. Expensive, high-end 3D technologies are currently replaced by much cheaper commercial technologies that have proven much cheaper, offering the same quality, geometric accuracy, and shape reconfiguration possibilities. Each 3D copy reflects the same original (or modified by therapists/manufacturer) data—there is lack of e.g. plastic mold or wrap destroyed irreversibly in the process of fabrication. Modification of geometrical parameters and material features of the model or final product is possible on almost every stage of the manufacturing. In selected cases, where more specialized knowledge and experience is required, rapid prototyping can be regarded only as quicker alternative for contemporary approaches. Another problem constitutes application of proper materials in particular cases—there is need for development of novel materials for 3D printing, dedicated to the medical applications (e.g. in anti-allergic, water-resistant, non-fragile, etc.). Despite efforts of scientists traditional natural materials (wood, leather, and metals) may be hard to replace, and there will be necessity to incorporate these materials [1].

The paper presents the concept and implementation of innovative methods of producing artificial organs based on 3D printing technology. These organs possess physical and mechanical properties similar to human organs and bodies. As a result, it is possible to conduct training and workshops in the field of urological surgery, under the conditions close to real operations. Due to the fabrication of 3D models can also lead so-called pre-operations in order to better prepare surgeons to carry out complex operations and post-operation e.g. observers proper operation.

## 2 Genesis

Early studies by Wilson and Boland showed a cell printer placing cells in a shape similar to their respective positions in organs. This way printing of two-dimensional (2D) tissue constructs has been possible. Three-dimensional (3D) organ printing has been possible thanks to generation sequential layers for cell printing using thermo sensitive gels. Cells have been placed on previously printed successive layers. Researchers demonstrated optimal thickness of the gel, size of cells ensuring a direct contact between printed cell, and aggregation of the closely-placed cells in two types of thermo sensitive 3D gels [2, 3]. Several devices for:

  * creating stable, functional protein arrays,

  * positioning organic molecules, molecular aggregates, cells, and single-cell organisms onto solid supports,

  * dispensing protein or cell solutions instead of the ink,

  * creation of cell libraries as well as cellular assemblies that mimic their respective position in organs, have been developed using inexpensive high-throughput technology, fully automated and computer controlled [4]. Further development recognized four basic categories of jet based approaches to printing cells.

  * laser guidance direct write (LG DW, since 1999)—to print formed embryonic-chick spinal-cord cells on a glass slide,

  * modified laser-induced forward transfer techniques (LIFT),

  * modified ink jet printers,

  * electro-hydrodynamic jetting (EHDJ) method [5].

Direct neural tissue printing technique in a 3D multilayered collagen gel harness a layer of collagen precursor printed as a scaffold for the cells, and embryonic neurons and atrocities were subsequently printed on the layer. Sodium bicarbonate applied to the cell allowed the gelation of the collagen, and aforementioned process was repeated layer-by-layer [6]. Producing of the soft scaffold and placement of various cell types should be possible using a single 3D printing device. Boland et al. described spatial and functional controlled structure: simultaneous printing of cells and biomaterials with precise placement of cells and proteins within 3-D hydrogel structures. Various types of cells can be used, and capillaries and vessels can be also constructed within the scaffolds [7]. In the study by Kundu et al. multi-head deposition system was applied to fabricate 3D cell-printed scaffolds using polycaprolactone and chondrocyte cell-encapsulated alginate hydrogel [8]. Ex vivo 3D engineering of functional tissues by laser-assisted bioprinting was also presented by Koch et al. (there were printed fibroblasts and keratinocytes embedded in collagen) [9]. The Zhang et al. printed human umbilical vein smooth muscle cells [10]. Inclusion of a vascular network to support cell viability required fabrication of printable vessel-like microfluidic channels supporting mechanical integrity ad enabling fluid transport [11]. In the study by Christensen et al., 3D printed vascular-like trees were fabricated thanks to liquid support-based inkjet printing approach (with calcium chloride as cross-linking agent and supporting material) [12]. Optimization of printing parameters allows for increased cell viability and mimics physiologically relevant attributes (e.g. cells density) of printed implant such as human skin [13]. 3D bioprinting technique may offer new possibilities for neural tissue regeneration. Next step is integration of 3D printed biological tissues with functional (micro- and nano-) electronics, such as bionic ear by Mannoor et al. [14]. Concept of 3D printed modular lung assist device was recently proposed by Rochow et al. [15]. Taking into consideration recent advances in brain-computer interfaces and neuroprosthesis, limitations of such approaches development are hard to overestimate. Study by Faulkner-Jones et al. showed printed human induced pluripotent stem cells [16]. Novel technologies represent 3D bioprinting of living soft tissue with cells on nanofibrillated cellulose. It is characterized by fast cross-linking ability of alginate and relatively high cells viability [17].

Current 3D bioprinting offers many possibilities to build functional biological tissues. In the future it may provide quick development toward on-demand individualized biological organs. Such situation will allow for optimization of complex therapy, even requiring modification or re-designing organic compounds for patients. Computer modeling and just-in-time production will extend aforementioned possibilities (Fig. 1).

Fig. 1

Enlarged 3D reconstructions of trabecular bone, PolyJet 3D printing (made in Institute of Mechanics and Applied Computer Science)

## 3 Requirements

Regenerative medicine aims at:

  * improvement,

  * restoring,

  * or replacement of damaged tissues/organs.

This aim is achieved using a combination of materials, cells, and growth factors. There are observed discrepancy between needs and possibilities. First of them is a gap between transplantation needs and tissues/organs shortages. High number of elderly, severely ill and disabled people requires novel solutions, quicker and cost-effective. Artificial tissues and organs may deal with this problem. Future clinical use of 3D printed organs shaped the main requirement use on a large scale to manufacture tissues and whole organs. Detailed requirements are following:

  * cell viability (requiring appropriate conditions cell dispensing and optimum concentration of alginate),

  * retained genotype and phenotype,

  * minimal stresses and forces encountered by cells during printing (cells should not be harmed by the printing procedure),

  * precision, shape, structure, and function fitted to the original organ (e.g. investigation of cell localization and proliferation, and other characteristics),

  * direct bioprinting of complex media exchange networks,

  * (bio) mechanical properties and their change in time,

  * as minimal as possible risk of graft rejection (including pre-programmed biocompatibility and biodegradability similar to the natural tissues), minimal adverse effects caused by biomaterial degradation,

  * high precision, including minimal axially-varying deformation and uniform diameter along axial directions of 3D printed vessels,

  * high automation and high flexibility of production,

  * lack of post-fabrication procedure.

  * Development of 3D organ printing generated three main directions of theoretical and practical (clinical) research:

  * replicas (surrogates) of the tissues for learning and medical simulation purposes (e.g. preparation to the rare or complicated (neuro) surgical intervention),

  * artificial implants of bones (including their complex internal porous structure),

  * artificial implants of soft tissues—complex 3D organs (exact replicas of the natural organs of the particular patient or improved versions) with computer-controlled, exact placing of different cell types, completed even in several minutes, useful in applications relating to medical interventions and organ replacement [2, 3, 7].

Development of engineered tissues can be based on anatomic geometries derived from medical imaging modalities (microcomputer tomography and magnetic resonance imaging). The aforementioned approach provides precise artificial patient-tailored solutions (so called custom-printed), even characterized by very complex geometry [18]. They are regarded as easier to use than conventional brain atlases, often difficult to interpret, interface with printing system, and shape to the particulate patient needs [19]. Preoperative planning and in constructing personalized prostheses for patients are crucial for life-saving interventions [20]. Such phantom surrogates are often made from agarose gels of variable concentrations [21]. Complex structures based on a digital blueprint can be created using patient imaging data, so precision is guaranteed, even despite therapeutic modification and use of diverse materials. Both metal and synthetic implants, as far as 3D printed combinations of cells, growth factors and biomaterials (bioprinting) are currently used in clinical practice, but number of limitation is huge and aforementioned technology still remains during its initial stage [22]. Chang et al. showed 3D-printed scaffold coated with mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) seeded in fibrin for the repair of shape and function of reconstructed trachea [23]. Hsieh & Hsy showed 3D bioprinting neural stem cells embedded in the thermoresponsive biodegradable polyurethane [24]. 3D printers may be also useful for initiation of pre-programmed therapeutic chemical reactions purposes [25].

## 4 Technological Challenges

Bio-mimicked tissue/organs (including vasculature, muscle, cartilage, and bone) may be printed with capacity of single cell manipulation, digital control, high throughput even thank to the most popular bioprinting based on thermal inkjet. Biphasic or triphasic tissues are also available [26]. Computational modeling complexity may vary depending on many factors. Wang et al. studied such parameters of 3D printing as concentration of synthetic polymer solution (optimal: 12%), nozzle speed, and extrusion rate critical for implant quality [27]. Gao et al. studied the concentration and flow rate of the sodium alginate and calcium chloride during bioprinting. Higher concentrations of sodium alginate accompanied by smaller distance between adjacent hollow filaments allowed for printing high-strength structures with built-in microchannels [28].

Suy et al. described an agent-based modeling method, which uses the kinetic Monte Carlo algorithm as efficient time-dependent simulation tool to study the evolution of the multicellular aggregate system [29]. Cheung et al. developed a 3D printed realistic pediatric pyeloplasty simulator for educational tool (laparoscopic training and skills acquisition) [30].

The main technological problem is the process of tissue self-assembly and extracellular matrix deposition. Another technological barrier to overcome is building 3D vascularized organs. Skin, cartilage, or bladders are characterized by relatively simple structure, morphology, low oxygen consumption, and low requirements for blood vessels. More complex organs (heart, kidney, liver) are huge challenge for tissue engineering due to their complex cross-sectional vascular structure, diverse small diameter, unique mechanical properties and organization. Vascularization provides enough nutrients, waste removal, and gas exchange, required for maturation during perfusion. Thus many technologies were developed for vascularized tissue engineering, including cell sheet conduits, biodegradable synthetic polymer-based constructs and natural biomaterial-based blood vessel constructs (biomimetically fabricated bifurcated vessels, embedded micro-fluidic networks). Traditional scaffolds provide mechanical support of extracellular matrixes, but novel approaches provide both mechanical supports to cellular assembly and controlled fluid transport to and from the cells. Tissue spheroids or cell-encapsulated micro-beads may be used. Establishing connection of the implants to the host's vasculature maintaining implant' cells viability is also challenging task [31].

Precision is limited, but current achievements allow for 3D printing of millimeter to micrometer structures. With an development of the technology may be observed increase in the demand for increased precision of tissues and organs, especially printed form various materials (even mixed, e.g. biocells, plastic and metal) in room temperature. Moreover increases of aforementioned precision have to be accompanied by the novel miniaturized, biocompatible 3D systems (even joining printed and traditional technologies) [32].

Integrity is key value in the case of bio-implants. Very useful are compartmental studies analyzing analyze the successful interaction between the cells and the biomaterials (number of cells attached to scaffold) [33].

Two another major technical challenges have to be overcome:

  * limited variety of 3D printable biomaterials not covering physical, chemical, and biological complexity and diversity of tissues and organs,

  * combining of the scaffold structure with various in vitro and in vivo materials [34].

## 5 Own Research

3D printing can use various materials (plastic, metal, ceramics, living cells) in layers to produce a 3D object. There are many technologies, their features (speed, resolution) and materials, but general rule is the same: object is build vertically layer by layer allowing creation of the complex structures. In our investigation we have been using plastic as primary material, using FDM and PolyJet technology.

The proposed method enables the production of artificial human organs whose consistency, plastic properties, hardness, elasticity are close to the real organ of specific patient, because it can be made on the basis of the data from CT, MRI and 3D scans. The process of preparing 3D geometry is prepared in applications in the field of CAD, but also through advanced applications designed for editing in vector geometry environment (Figs. 2 and 3).

Fig. 3

These organs possess physical and mechanical properties similar to human organs and bodies. As a result, it is possible to conduct training and workshops in the field of urological surgery, under the conditions close to real operations. Due to the fabrication of 3D models can also lead so-called pre-operations in order to better prepare surgeons to carry out complex operations and post-operation e.g. observers proper operation (Fig. 4).

Fig. 4

3D printed skull reconstruction based on 2D cross sections CT technique (made in Institute of Mechanics and Applied Computer Science)

We started to build digital library of particular human "spare parts", primarily bones, starting from bones of spine and breasts geometry form 3D scans. Such libraries (equivalent of the traditional anatomical atlases) are necessary for further developing the technology toward simplified and automated process accessible for non-professionals. Pre-programmed natural- or large-scale models of bones will be also useful for learning purposes, especially within medical simulation environments. Physiological and pathological models can reflect various age, deformations, and stage of the disease. Colored parts make easier recognition of particular bones. We hope open-source scientific libraries, inexpensive software, hardware and technology cause medical specialists familiar with this technology, and will have wide-reaching effects on the practice of medicine (Fig. 5).

Breast geometry from 3D scan and CAM visualization of mold geometry, with supports

## 6 Discussion

We are aware that replacement of the organs within human body has its own limitations. Its main aim is life saving. Even fully artificial bionic body (or body replacement) may not provide immortality due to nervous system degeneration.

Main limitation of the recent studies is usually initial stage of research and development. Proposed solutions are effective, but rather need for further research allowing for unification, automation, quality assessment, clinical trials (especially randomized controlled trials engaging huge groups of patients), compartmental studies with concurrent approaches, and finally clinical guidelines and commercialization. Their full clinical introduction may last at least several years (if will be cost-effective). We aim at early preparation of medical staff and current education system to novel solutions. Introduction of subsequent novel approaches may be this way regarded rather as procedure similar to the introduction of the novel surgical tool, but not novel approaches at all. Moreover application of 3D printed solutions may shape social awareness and make this solution familiar and expected both by clinicians and patients. Aforementioned situation may stimulate intensive research, quicker development, and earlier clinical application of the particular solutions. Maturation of the used technologies will foster increased publish confidence.

Limitations of the own concept is high initial cost of the whole system for clinical purposes, but low-cost 3D printing solutions may cause revolution concerning prices and provide better cost-effectiveness of the proposed solutions. Medical specialists seem be prepared for such novel technologies. Study by Jones et al. showed, that models fabricated using reverse engineering was useful for 95.8% (82.6% required models' price less than $500). Opinion that the models may be useful into the medical school curriculum was common [35].

There are still a few studies and publications. Recent review by Beuermeister et al. identified 1092 articles concerning clinical applications of 3D printing, but only 103 (9.43%) were included in the review. Despite strict selection topics of the selected papers were diverse as follows: general issues, surgical planning, training and patient education, upper extremity and hand prosthetics, bone reconstruction, breast reconstruction; nose, ear and cartilage reconstruction, skin [36] (Figs. 6 and 7).

## 7 Direction for Further Research

3D printing if tissues and organs has emerged as a new solution solving problem of increasing demands for organ transplants. Current findings are promising, 3D in vitro models and tissue substitutes may be useful for many clinical applications. But this way of tissue engineering still needs for further development. No doubts further challenges are:

  * learning system of medical staff and translation technical solutions into clinical language,

  * comparing and contrasting the different techniques and their properties,

  * comparing and contrasting the different materials, including complex, heterogeneous tissues, monitoring of gap junctions, critical for tissue morphogenesis and cohesion,

  * vascularization of the tissues, including planning and assessment of the fluid diffusion rate across the printed channels,

  * innervations of implants,

  * regeneration/replacement of complex tissues (heart, kidney, liver, etc.),

  * survival rate of ex vivo cells in tissue grafts [37],

  * accessibility and cost efficiency,

  * indications and contraindications, adverse effects,

  * specific therapy, rehabilitation and care guidelines concerning patients with various syndromes and injuries with diverse kinds of 3D printed implants,

  * task division and co-operation within multidisciplinary therapeutic team.

The complicated nature of the 3D printing technologies and human organs require also:

  1. (1)

legal regulations,

  2. (2)

ethical regulations,

  3. (3)

patenting and licensing issues (e.g. who is the owner of rights to the particular additional copy of tissue/bone/neuronal structure: patient or anyone else) [38].

## 8 Conclusions

Artificial organs fabrication based on 3D printing technology is an innovation that is transforming the clinical practice. Its application expanded dramatically over the last 20 years. Many technologies were intensely investigated for possibilities to produce implants, tissue scaffolds, organs, and even surgical tools. Printing of heterogeneous 3D scaffolds built cell-by-cell may advance tissue engineering. Future, commercial techniques need to be better known, developed, and optimized toward printing the fully clinically functional tissues.
