# Analysis of the Use of Biogas as Fuel for Internal Combustion Engines

Mariusz Ptak1  , Sebastian Koziołek1  , Damian Derlukiewicz1  , Mateusz Słupiński1 and Marek Mysior1

(1)

Wrocław University of Technology, Department of Machine Design and Research, Lukasiewicza 7/9, 50-371 Wroclaw, Poland

Mariusz Ptak (Corresponding author)

Email: mariusz.ptak@pwr.edu.pl

Sebastian Koziołek

Email: sebastian.koziolek@pwr.edu.pl

Damian Derlukiewicz

Email: damian.derlukiewicz@pwr.edu.pl

Marek Mysior

Email: marek.mysior@pwr.edu.pl

Abstract

The article presents the opportunity to power internal combustion engine by treated and non-purified biogas. Internal combustion engines may be operated only within a certain range of parameters of fuel due to the design and method of operation. Furthermore, they are sensitive to changes in chemical composition of the fuel. The aim of the work described in the studies was to test the quality of biogas that can be obtained by methane fermentation of the test material. Considering the treatment of biogas as a consumable in vehicles, its physicochemical properties can be very diverse. It is reasonable therefore to analysis biogas composition of samples from various biogas plants, in the context of the possibility of its use in a motor vehicle with an internal combustion engine. The article presents an analysis of the chemical composition of untreated biogas collected from five representative biogas plants. Then it summarizes the data received with the requirements of the standards referred to European countries and set out the possibility of direct use of untreated and untreated biogas during the operation of vehicles with combustion engines.

Keywords

BiogasBiogas composition analysisOperation of internal combustion enginesThe characteristics of fuels

## 1 Introduction

Biogas is a mixture of combustible and non-combustible compounds resulting from the fermentation process. The most desirable component of biogas is methane (CH4). The use of biogas only to produce electricity at current economic conditions is highly unprofitable [1]. Implementation of a system of distribution of biogas directly to factories, farms and special objects is a chance for more efficient use of this environmentally friendly fuel, where the biogas will be used to produce electricity, heat and cooling. Any surplus of biogas can then be used to power motor vehicles (fleet or private) equipped with an installation dedicated for the supply of gaseous fuels. It implies, that biogas can become one of the best renewable energy sources and efficient alternative fuel used in transportation in the nearest future. Combustion of biogas in a classical internal combustion engine has to be safe and economically reasonable mostly due to exploitation and maintenance of engines.

The oil crisis in 1973 provided the impetus for engine designers to look for solutions that could guarantee the elasticity in control of the propelling unit, which will provide good parameters of internal combustion engines and low consumption of fuel. Currently one can observe a trend among vehicle manufacturers to introduce new vehicles that are originally adapted to combust CNG (Compressed Natural Gas) and LPG (Liquefied Petroleum Gas). This results in increased safety of exploitation, reduction of the homologation costs and ensures professional maintenance of gas propelled vehicles what leads to fulfillment of more restrictive requirements. Research in exhaust emission in internal combustion engines shows that the gas propelled engines have an advantage over oil or gasoline engines [2, 3]. Significant development of gaseous fuels in the world took place in the last 20–25 years. The main factors of this development are environmental reasons, the improvement of security of fuel supply by diversifying the fuel and cost-effectiveness [4]. Currently, there are more than 17 million vehicles in the world that are propelled by CNG or purified biogas and the number is still growing [5, 6]. There are various mechanisms that support development of natural gas as a fuel for cars in various countries [7–10].

Compared to other gaseous fuels as LPG and CNG, the composition of biogas varies not only due to a way of production, but also due to a place from which it was obtained. Manufacturing and processing of biogas are oriented to obtain the highest content of methane. All other components of biogas increase its mass being either neutral like CO2 or aggressive like sulfur compounds. Aggressiveness of constituents of biogas can lead to damage of tanks, power systems, combustion chambers and also to irregularities in the functioning of some terminal equipment and the emission of harmful compounds as a result of the combustion of biogas [11, 12].

Therefore, considering the biogas as a consumable for vehicles, its physicochemical properties can be varied depending on the chemical composition. Therefore, it is vital to analyze the composition of multiple samples of biogas from various biogas plants in the context of the possibility of its use in a motor vehicle with an internal combustion engine.

## 2 Implementation of Purified Biogas in Motor Vehicles

The use of biogas as a primary source of energy in vehicles is inherent to the costs that one need to invest in the modernization and adaptation of the engine to the gaseous fuel or buy a car that is originally equipped with a power supply system [13].

Indirect cost is the purification and treatment of biogas. The crude biogas formed in the methane fermentation process in addition to methane contains non-combustible carbon dioxide, hydrogen sulphide, water, water vapour and small amounts of nitrogen and oxygen. Due to the fact that the biogas and CNG are similar in composition (see Table 1) it is possible to use existing fuel supply systems dedicated originally to Compressed Natural Gas.

Table 1

Comparison of the composition of the purified and conditioned biogas and compressed natural gas [12]

(%) | Natural gas | Purified biogas

---|---|---

Methane, CH4 | 55–75 | 97.4

Carbon dioxide CO2 | 25–45 | 0.07

Nitrogen, N2 | 0–0.3 | 1.22

Water, H2O | 1–5 | –

Hydrogen sulfide, H2S | 0–3 | –

Oxygen, O2 | 0.1–0.5 | –

Ethane C2H6 | – | 0.94

Propane, C3H8 | – | 0.22

Noble gases (Argon, Helium) | – | 0.13

The greatest advantage of the vehicles propelled with biogas compared to gasoline vehicles and other conventional fuels is that the environmentally harmful emissions are greatly reduced. Therefore, the main reason for users to invest in gas vehicles are economic and ecological considerations [12–16]:

  * limiting exhaust emissions, primarily carbon dioxide (CO2).

  * vehicles powered by biogas compared with those driven by petrol emit up to 90% less carbon monoxide (CO), 80% less hydrocarbons—the main factor responsible for smog and 50–86% less nitrogen oxides (NOx)—rules for calculating the impact of biofuels, bio liquids and their fossil fuel emissions of greenhouse gases are presented in Table 5.

  * reduction to a minimum the release of sulphur compounds and soot, which has a significant impact on reducing their emissions to the environment and improving the microclimate of large urban agglomerations.

  * the cost of biogas and CNG are lower than the prices of gasoline and show significant stability compared to oil prices.

Disadvantages of biogas to power vehicles are as follows:

  * the use of biogas as a primary source of energy in vehicles is inherent to the costs that one need to invest in the modernization and adaptation of the engine to the gaseous fuel or buy a car that is originally equipped with a power supply system;

  * less space (e.g. in the trunk), and increase the weight of the vehicle;

  * a limited number of refuelling stations;

  * extended refuelling time;

  * increased maintenance costs;

  * shorter range of the vehicle (including gas supply only).

## 3 Testing of Biogas Captured from 5 Different Installations

The aim of the study was to measure the composition and quality of biogas, which can be obtained as a result of methane fermentation of test material. Biogas is a medium that is difficult in analysis due to its composition and properties. It requires knowledge and analytical experience, especially in terms of sampling. The representativeness of the sample determines both the correct choice of the point of consumption, and the method used in testing. It is important to avoid "dead" space, places in which the condensate accumulates and areas subjected to temperature fluctuations and flow distortions.

The study consisted proper placing of prepared batch of raw material in the bioreactor containing the bacteria involved in methane fermentation. Subject of measurement was a daily increase in the volume of biogas formed and its composition. The obtained results are then plotted as a kinetics of biogas creation. Selection of the initial conditions of the process takes place on the basis of the physio-chemical analysis of the raw material and the information received from the supplier of the substrate. In specific cases, the individual results are given as average values \u200B\u200Bof a minimum of three independent and parallel repetitions.

In order to verify the selected properties of biogas in chosen plants that process waste and biomass, the collection of 30 samples from 5 biogas installations was analysed:

  1. 1.

Active municipal waste landfill located in the town of Lubin operated by MUNDO Ltd.

  2. 2.

Closed and reclaimed municipal waste landfill in the town of Grudziadz.

  3. 3.

Installation of biogas usage produced in closed sewage treatment plant digesters "Łyna" in Olsztyn.

  4. 4.

Periodically active anaerobic bioreactor that process anaerobically municipal waste and sewage sludge located in the town of Kosiny Bartosowe wheel Mławy operated by Uskom Ltd.

  5. 5.

Active agricultural biogas plant located in the town of Swidnica operated by Bioelektrownia Swidnica Bio-watt.

Samples of biogas were taken in March 2014. In all samples, percentage of: CO2, CH4, O2, H2S, NH3 was analysed. Analysis was performed on-site using a portable biogas analyser GA 2000, in which the measurement principle is based on, in the case of CH4and CO2 on infrared absorption method and in the case of O2, H2S and NH3 on electrochemical cells. In five samples, each one obtained from different biogas plant the content of the siloxanes was assessed for each sample. The content of siloxanes was determined by the use of gas chromatography method with mass spectrometry (GC-MS).

The acquired data, after verification and statistical processing, was summarized and presented on Fig. 1. It is noted that the results represent the crude biogas (untreated and non-purified). The most beneficial quality of the biogas showing potential for the use in internal combustion engines was measured in the Regular Anaerobic bioreactor in Kosinach Bartosowych processing anaerobic waste. It should be noted that the percentage of methane (CH4) is more than 60%. The samples taken from the indicated biogas plants are characterized by the smallest total content of CO2, O2, N2. However, biogas from Kosin Bartosowych shows adversely greatest amount of sulphur compounds of approx. 200 mg/mn3 (Fig. 1) Fig. 2.

Based on the summarized results it was proven that despite significant progress in the technology of biogas acquisition, it is not currently recommended to use it in motor vehicles without prior purification and treatment. The collected samples of biogas do not meet the requirements of the minimum level of methane content and an acceptable level of sulphur content. To reduce the possibility of corrosion in the intake system of the internal combustion engine it is necessary to include getting rid of the sulphur compounds from biogas (desulphurisation). It should be noted, however, that the samples taken from the biogas plant in Swidnica are characterized by relatively low levels of sulphur compounds—an average of 45.2 mg/nm3. Despite the lack of opportunities in the context of these requirements, the use of raw biogas in internal combustion engines states great potential in biogas production technology and the future of its direct application as an alternative fuel.

## 5 Conclusions

In comparison to other alternative sources of renewable energy biogas production takes place in a continuous manner and is not affected by atmospheric conditions, such as the energy of the sun, wind or water. The crude biogas formed in the methane fermentation process apart the desired content of methane contains also non-combustible carbon dioxide, hydrogen sulphide, water, water vapour, and small amounts of nitrogen and oxygen. Manufacturing processes and biogas processing are oriented to obtain the highest methane content. All other components of biogas increase its mass being either neutral like CO2 or aggressive like sulphur compounds. Aggressiveness of constituents of biogas can lead to damage of tanks, power systems, combustion chambers and also to irregularities in the functioning of terminal equipment and the emission of harmful compounds as a result of the combustion of biogas.

It is emphasized that in practice almost every piston engine designed to power gasoline is ready to be supplied by gas of suitable composition. The aim of the work described in the studies was to test the quality of crude biogas (untreated and non-purified) which can be obtained in modern biogas plants, and its potential in application as a fuel for vehicles without purification and enrichment. The result of the research is a summary of parameters of biogas that are relevant for the operation of internal combustion engines for 5 representative biogas plants. The data obtained were compared with the standards of some European countries, which establishes the required composition of biogas for use, among others, in internal combustion engines. It has been proved in this way, despite significant progress in the technology of biogas acquisition, it is not currently recommended to use it in motor vehicles without prior purification and treatment.

# Calculations with the Finite Element Method During the Design Ballistic Armour

Dariusz Pyka1  , Krzysztof Jamroziak2  , Wojciech Blazejewski1  and Miroslaw Bocian1

(1)

Departament of Mechanics, Materials Science and Engineering, Wroclaw University of Technology, Smoluchowskiego 25, 50-370 Wroclaw, Poland

(2)

General Tadeusz Kosciuszko Military Academy of Land Forces, Czajkowskiego 109, 51-150 Wroclaw, Poland

Dariusz Pyka

Email: pykadariusz@gmail.com

Krzysztof Jamroziak (Corresponding author)

Email: krzysztof.jamroziak@wso.wroc.pl

Wojciech Blazejewski

Email: wojciech.blazejewski@pwr.edu.pl

Miroslaw Bocian

Email: miroslaw.bocian@pwr.edu.pl

Abstract

For protection against projectiles with higher impact speed (up to 1000 m/s) a type of a ballistic sandwich shield can be used—which is a monolithic combination of ballistic laminates with additional materials, typically hard layers made of ceramic in the form of plates or spheres of oxides, carbides and nitrides. The authors of this paper, by using FEM to optimize defined material sets to fire the cartridge 7.62 × 54R mm, give a range of results which are compared with tests of ballistic firing on the shooting range.

## 1 Introduction

Currently, composite materials have gained great popularity. Especially those made on the basis of high-fiber artificially obtained by man [1–3]. Said fiber composites are characterized by several properties which make them ideal for applications ballistic shields. They have a low weight, a programmable structure, high specific strength and high ability to absorb energy of a ballistic impact [4–7]. For this reason, these materials are preferable used to carry light shields for military vehicles and civilian, such as vests, helmets or shields. Monolithic materials for the content of ingredients such as a fabric-resin, resistant only to fire small firearms ammunition with a low speed up to 400 m/s. Because of the current capabilities of firearms resistance becomes insufficient.

In order to protect against bullets of higher velocity (up to 1000 m/s) layered shields are used a combination of monolithic ballistic laminates with additional material, usually hard layers made of ceramics in the form of plates or balls with oxides, carbides and nitrides. This is not the only material used for ballistic plates. Because of low density are also used aluminum alloys, titanium or plastic also can be used [1–7].

The use of a variety of materials in a single cover is dictated by using their specific properties. Thus obtained shield can have various configurations of layers, including the use for this purpose other additional materials, which include composites based on glass, carbon or aramid fibers [5, 8, 9]. An interesting idea is to use the geometry of the sphere as a factor in changing the flight path of the projectile. Ideally, this may be suitable made of hardened steel ball bearings. Such armour can be used as a personal protection as a vest or an additional protection placed on a military vehicle.

This work is focused on different configurations of systems verified material resistant to small firearms ammunition with a speed of at least 700 m/s with regard to the quantitative efficiency of existing solutions.

## 2 Objectives and Description of the Simulation

Simulation of ballistic shields composite was carried out with ABAQUS software. This simulation is primarily designed to generate solutions of the material setup, which in the end will be tested with live round shots. Due to the workload and cost effectiveness initial research process of puncturing is performed by using numerical methods, which are an orderly methodology of seeking appropriate solutions to design armor that could stop the shelling effectively. A positive test result can help improve the ballistic simulation. Simulation is a simplification of the subject and does not contain all the variables that occur on impact, this is due both to the complexity of the process itself, as well as the capabilities of the program. The source of data on the mechanical properties of the various "elements" of the cover are usually the data acquired from scientific studies [10–14]. When resorting to the programs which use FEM, it is adviced to average calculations accuracy and time to obtain them, which is mainly related to the computing power of the computer on which the simulation is performed.

After an initial simulation there was no significant effect of the bullet cover on the puncture of the shield, so further research is omitting this element to streamline calculations. The simulation is set at Step on Procedure Type: General, then Dynamic, Explicit, and time in the range of 0.0005–0.00005 s, depending on the particular simulation. Interaction Property is set to Contact, then on Hard Contact. Penetration energy has been set by the velocity of the projectile.

## 3 Material and Its Parameters

For accurate modeling of the behavior of the resin-composite fabric FEM simulation is needed to determine its mechanical properties, depending on the percentage of the fabric laminate. For this purpose a homogenization method, which allows to determine the state of stress in the composite of both micro and macro scales, based on rigorous mathematical theory, enabling the description of the boundary problem in a local and global scale, using the method of an asymptotic expansion, if you enter the periodic conditions for the so-called boundary, representative cell.

Thus it was assumed that the selected composite structure is statistically uniform and periodic, such that the asymptotic method of homogenization may be used, if the representative cell is large enough [15]. The sample for testing was performed by the same method as core samples (see Fig. 1a).

## 4 Geometrical and Numerical Models

In order to implement the relevant models, the analysis of ballistic material guard and ammunition was conducted. The study used the bullet of 7.62 × 39 mm and 7.62 × 54R mm Polish production coming from production facilities "MESKO". Geometrical models were made on the basis of touch-scanning on a Cyclone II scanner with indexer, then performed numerical models (see Fig. 4).

Fig. 4

The numerical models: a the bullet 7.62 × 54 mm with core-type LPS, b the steel thickness 10 mm with a superimposed grid, c the steel bearing ball ϕ 7 mm

## 5 Description of Numerical Tests

By entering the numerical tests several modeled were considered, which were then subjected to a thorough analysis. First simulations were conducted with rifle bullets. In the following simulation a puncturing composite plate (Kevlar 49) and a titanium plate (Ti6Al-4 V) for a rifle bullet core-type LPS (see Fig. 5) was introduced.

As a result of the simulation a dissipation graphs of impact energy in a bullet-plate setting was also obtained. The results are summarized in Fig. 6. As noted for the steel and titanium, a linear relation of energy losses can be determined. In case of Kevlar the thickness of the tested object proved to be insufficient.

Fig. 7

## 6 Summary and Conclusions

As a result of numerical experiments and tests on the ballistic field appropriate procedures for numerical models based on software ABAQUS could be developed. As demonstrated, an essential element of the development of numerical models is to prepare the necessary material constants, which could be obtained through the study of characteristics of mechanical properties in specific tests [16–18]. Due to the verification of numerical models obtained the important issue was to conduct tests at the shooting range, which concluded:

  1. (1)

the verification for the use of zirconia as a ballistic material is negative. Spheres of 1 mm are too small to affect the flight path of the projectile. There was no structural damage to the ceramic balls which may suggest that the energy of the bullet was taken over by the resin proving insufficient results,

  2. (2)

the sample made from ball bearings has passed tests with ammunition 7.62 × 39 mm the bullet type PS. The degradation of the disc was minimal, no chips or splinters. While having the lowest curb weight and low profile.

In addition, it was found that:

  1. (1)

the homogenization process allowed to obtain results similar to those in the literature simultaneously in an easy and fast way allowed to determine particular characteristics of the laminate obtained by the process of shielding production,

  2. (2)

the results of the ballistic simulation are similar to those obtained on the sample,

  3. (3)

the use of PE-UHMW as the last layer outcomes as positive. The ammunition 7.62 × 39 mm the bullet type PS was retained in the shielding. The structure of PE has not been influenced in the case of the bullet type PS. With the ammunition 7.62 × 51 mm the bullet type Ball and 7.62 × 54R mm the bullet type LPS proved to be insufficient,

  4. (4)

the analytical methods allowed for preliminary estimation of the thickness of the shielding layer.

In summary, numerical methods must be validated experimentally, their usefulness in ballistic protection comes down to optimize the shielding and illustrate the physical phenomenon. A prerequisite of the verification are still trying physical penetration tests.

# Experimental Tests of Pressure Pulsation of Gear Pumps

D. Rabsztyn1  and K. Klarecki1

(1)

Gliwice, Poland

D. Rabsztyn

Email: dominik.rabsztyn@polsl.pl

Abstract

The paper presents results of experimental tests regarding pressure pulsation of the gear pump with external gear design. A cycle of measurements was carried out in relation to the selected parameters of system's operation such as temperature of hydraulic fluid (viscosity) and pressure of the pressure line. The obtained results of pulsation measurements were analyzed in terms of time and frequency. The time analysis was carried out in order to determine the peak-to-peak value of pumping pressure that is responsible for generating increased levels of vibration and noise, as well as influences fatigue wear of the hydraulic system elements. The frequency analysis was carried out in order to identify the pressure values not related to periodical changes in pump capacity, which may be used to diagnose the operation condition of the pump. Research has shown that increase of pumping pressure and temperature of the oil causes significant increase of the pressure pulsation amplitude resulting from the eccentricity of gearwheels.

## 1 Introduction

A phenomenon of pressure pulsation of pumps used in power hydraulics is a result of periodic changes in working fluid flow rate, which results from the cyclical nature of operation of displacement pump elements, as well as external force in the form of mechanical vibration that impacts mechanical elements of the hydraulic system. Another source of pressure pulsation is the changeable nature of loads on hydraulic receivers (motors and cylinders), as well as acceleration and braking [1–3, 7, 9]. Pressure pulsation has influence on the limitation to accuracy of positioning the receivers, accelerated wear of hydraulic systems elements and the increased emission of noise [4, 5].

In hydraulic systems with fixed displacement pumps, the most commonly used are gear pumps with external gear design. This type of pumps is characterized by simple and space-saving design, high density of transmitted power, relatively high durability and low price [6, 8, 10]. These pumps are widely used both in stationary system (machining tools, injection molding machines, molding machines) and in mobile machine drive systems (construction, municipal and transport machinery). The scope of the tests covered a series of experiments allowing identifying the relation between pressure pulsation of the gear pump and the pressure in pressure line as well as hydraulic oil temperature (oil viscosity).

## 2 Pump Capacity Fluctuation Model of External Gear Pumps

Pumping pressure pulsation of gear pumps result from periodical capacity changes connected with changes in the position of gearwheels. According to [5, 10] capacity fluctuation of external gear pumps with identical gearwheels, results from the change in temporary flow output Q, as expressed by the formula:

## 3 Measuring Station

Measuring system (Fig. 3) has been composed of a gear pump with external gear design with specific capacity of 5 cm3/rpm, powered by asynchronous AC motor with P = 1.5 kW and nominal rotational speed n = 1420 rpm, throttle valve 9N600S (regulation of pressure in the circuit) and pressure reducing valve.

A measuring system comprising HDA 4748-H-0250 pressure transmitter, EVS 3108-H-0020 flow rate transmitter and ETS 4148-H-006 temperature transmitter was mounted in the pressure line of the pump. Results of the experiment were saved using HYDAC HMG 3010 measuring and data-loggind device.

Analyzing the measurement results for pressure pulsation it has been observed that the pressure amplitude resulting from rotational speed of the pump shaft increases simultaneously with increase of pumping pressure and temperature of the oil.

## 6 Conclusions

Teeth damage was not observed on when analyzing time courses of pressure pulsation. The fact is supported by the lack of periodically recurrent (one shaft rotation) significant pressure drops.

Amplitude of pressure pulsation resulting from temporary change of pump capacity caused by the teeth engagement is much higher than pulsation resulting from the pump gearwheel eccentricity.

Value of the average pumping pressure practically does not influence the pulsation amplitude. It follows that pump leakage within the limits specified by the producer does not influence pulsation of the examined pump.

Temperature of hydraulic oil (and at the same time—viscosity) does not influence the changes in pumping pressure pulsation. Increase of internal leaks resulting from the drop in fluid viscosity also does not influence the change of pressure pulsation.

Increase of pumping pressure and temperature of the oil causes significant increase of the pressure pulsation amplitude resulting from the eccentricity of gearwheels. Authors of the article favour the thesis that the increase of pressure causes "stiffening" of the elastic hose connecting the pump and valve block. The higher the pressure is, the more deformed is the inner layer of elastomer (no possibility of applying the Hook principle). Thus, it is observed as the increase of substitute value of elastic modulus of the fluid (taking into account the stiffness of the hoses).

# Analysis of Blood Flow Through the Pathologically Changed Main Artery

Alina Rudiak1  , Jakub Słowiński1 and Maciej Zawiślak1

(1)

Wrocław University of Technology, Wroclaw, Poland

Alina Rudiak (Corresponding author)

Email: alina.rudiak@gmail.com

Maciej Zawiślak

Email: maciej.zawislak@pwr.edu.pl

Abstract

During the examination a Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) analysis of blood flow through the physiological and pathologically changed aorta was performed. The model used in the Fluid—Structure Interaction analysis (FSI) has been enriched by a variable thickness of the wall in the section being subject to lesions. The influence of the occurrence of pathological change in the descending section of the thoracic aorta on the nature of blood flow, the value of flow parameters of fluid and endurance parameters of the wall of an arterial vessel, was demonstrated.

## 1 Introduction

The aortic aneurysm, i.e. pathological local widening of the arterial vessel can be classified among one of the most dangerous diseases of the cardiovascular system. The main problem accompanying the process of the aneurysm coming into being is its asymptomatic development usually ending with a rupture which results most often with immediate death [2]. Blood flow in the main aorta especially in its thoracic section is the most complex as far as hydrodynamics in the cardiovascular system is concerned. It is connected primarily with irregular geometry of the arterial vessel within which stenosis and branching (aortic arch) can be observed. Such specific character of the system causes that phenomena taking place in the aorta during a pulsating blood flow are extremely difficult to be interpreted.

Thanks to the dynamic development of numerical methods, modelling of biological phenomena accompanying blood flow becomes more and more popular. The aorta, being the place with specific flow, has repeatedly been examined, both in a laboratory and in the examination supported by computer methods [3, 6, 7].

The CFD analysis of blood flow through the physiological and pathologically changed aorta was carried out. Additionally, the response of the aorta wall to irregular pressure resulting from the blood flow was examined (FSI).

## 2 Geometrical Model

The basis for creating a geometric model consisted in a real CT image (Computed Tomography) of the aorta subject to pathological changes in the descending section. Processed CT image was a demonstrative model and the data of a patient were not made public. Isolations of the image of the arterial vessel were made with the use of InVesalius 3.0. programme. Examples of the cross-sections of thoracic aorta have been presented in Fig. 1.

Fig. 1

CT image of the thoracic section of the aorta: a side cross-section, b 3D image

## 3 Numerical Simulation of Blood Flow Through the Thoracic Aorta

The numerical simulation of blood flow has been conducted with the use of ANSYS Fluent 14.0 programme. During the analysis it has been adopted that blood was a homogenous Newtonian fluid. Blood flow in the examined section is turbulent and deformations of the wall of the vessel are insignificantly small and they can be neglected. The model of a turbulent flow has been enriched by the influence of gravitational field. The direction of the operation of the gravity force was in line with the patient being in the standing position. A simplified blood model has been defined, described by density and dynamic viscosity at a body temperature of 37 °C. Considering the referenced data [1] the following values have been adopted: density (ρ) = 1050 kg/m3 and dynamic viscosity (µ) = 4 · 10−3 Pa s.

  1. A.

Steady Blood Flow Analysis

Method

Simulations of the steady flow have been carried out for two cases of the phase of the cardiac cycle: systole and diastole.

The discrete model consisting of tetragonal and pentagonal (boundary layer) elements has been created with the use of ANSYS Workbench 14.0 programme.

In the model the area of given velocity (v) of the flow and the pressure were defined. For the individual phases the following values have been adopted [7]:

  * Systole phase: v = 0.9 m/s, p = 13,800 Pa

  * Diastole phase: v = 0.1 m/s, p = 11,704 Pa.

Results

The results have been compared as regards the impact of the pathological change on the velocities and the pressures distribution obtained during the systole and diastole phase of the cardiac cycle (Table 1). It has been stated that the analyzed parameters for the model of thoracic aorta being subject to disease changes, increased. The dependence has been observed in the two analyzed phases of cardiac cycle.

Table 1

Set of maximum values of analyzed parameters for the model of physiological and pathologically changed aorta

Phase of the cardiac cycle | Pathologically changed aorta | Physiological aorta

---|---|---

Velocity (m/s) | Pressure (Pa) | Velocity (m/s) | Pressure (Pa)

Systole | 3.8 | 20691.7 | 3.2 | 18607.2

Diastole | 0.4 | 11799.2 | 0.4 | 11704.2

Exemplary results (showing velocity distribution) achieved for the systole phase have been presented in Fig. 2.

Fig. 2

Fluid streams showing velocity distribution obtained in case of the model of physiological and pathologically changed aorta. The results obtained for the maximum velocity at the entrance to the aorta occurring during systole phase (velocity v = 0.9 m/s for the time t = 0.302 s)

Obtained results (Fig. 2) indicate significant blood flow disturbances resulting from pathological changes of the descending section of the thoracic aorta. In the place of pathological narrowing, an increased velocity of blood flow can be observed. In the area of enlarged diameter (aneurysm) fluid starts circulating and decelerating (with the velocity drop even to 0 m/s). This phenomenon causes regular thinning of already weakened walls of the aorta. The area of aortic arch is the place where highly turbulent flow can be observed. In aortic arch arteries the increased velocity of blood flow can be observed resulting from significant narrowing of vessel diameter.

  1. B.

Analysis Considering Pulsating Character of Cardiac Activity

Method

As a part of the analysis, simulation of blood flow through the arterial vessel has been conducted in six time cases. The analysis has been conducted for one cardiac cycle (0.8 s) [5].

For the purpose of the simulation based on the reference data [1, 7, 8] the velocity profile of blood flowing in the aorta has been created. The analysis was conducted for six successive time variants: t = 0.05 s, t = 0.25 s, t = 0.302 s, t = 0.37 s, t = 0.45 s and t = 0.7 s. For each analyzed case velocity of blood flow was defined.

Results

The obtained results have been compared as regards velocity, pressures and propagation of vortexes as well as intensity of turbulences, depending on the phase of cardiac operation. Distributions of analyzed parameters show the existence of maximum value of pressure and velocities in the systole phase for t = 0.302 s (Figs. 3 and 4). Dependency has been observed both for the model of physiological and for pathologically changed aorta. Sample results of the process of velocity profiles for the model of pathologically changed aorta in two extreme cases have been presented in Fig. 5.

Fig. 3

Distribution of maximum velocity observed within one cardiac cycle for both pathologically changed and physiological aorta model

Fig. 4

Distribution of maximum pressure observed within one cardiac cycle for both pathologically changed and physiological aorta model

Fig. 5

Comparison of the blood flow stream distribution in the model of the pathologically changed aorta depending on the phase of cardiac cycle for two selected time steps (t = 0.05st = 0.302 s)

## 4 Fluid—Structure Interaction Analysis

Method

Fluid—Structure Interaction (FSI) analysis combines flow simulation and the structural analysis. The impact of pressure exerted by blood flow on the walls of arterial vessel was examined.

The model of pathologically changed aorta was enriched by different thickness of the wall in the place of a disease focus (aneurysm). The change in the range of 0.6–2.0 mm of the wall thickness in the aorta model was adopted. The discrete model consisting of SHELL181 elements has been created with the use of ANSYS Workbench 14.0 programme.

Models of the aorta have been loaded both by intravascular pressure and the tensile force exerted during the systole and diastole phase. It was assumed in the analyses that the aortic wall is a linear elastic material. Considering the reference data, [4] the following values were adopted: Young modulus (E) = 6 MPa, Poisson's ratio (ϑ) = 0.45 and density (ρ) = 2000 kg/m3.

Results

Selected results obtained as part of FSI analysis have been presented in Fig. 6.

Fig. 6

Comparison of the von-Mises reduced stress distribution obtained in case of a the model of physiological aorta, b the model of pathologically changed aorta

The results of a structural analysis show the existence of significant differences between von-Mises stress distribution in the wall of pathologically changed and physiological arterial vessel. In case of the model with aortic aneurysm in the descending section (Fig. 6b) the existence of the highest stress in the pathologically changed area has been observed, where we deal with widening of the arterial vessel and pathological thinning of the aortic wall.

The stress concentration is also observed in aortic arch carotid arteries, brachiocephalic trunk and subclavian left artery. Increased stress in this area is caused by a sudden change of vascular geometry.

## 5 Summary and Conclusions

The impact of the existence of pathological change in the area of descending section of thoracic aorta on the nature of blood flowing through the arterial vessel was demonstrated. The results obtained as part of FSI analysis showed differences in the stresses distribution observed in the pathologically changed aortic wall with reference to the results observed in case of the model of physiological aorta. Pathological change of geometry of the arterial vessel causes significant increase in von-Mises reduced stress observed in the area of the pathological change in the descending section of the aorta. It has been shown that the value of obtained parameters, both in case of the analysis conducted for the model of pathologically changed and physiological aorta depends strictly on the phase of cardiac operation.

Further progress of research towards the combination of calculation methods with a modern medical imaging may have a great influence on diagnostic possibilities. If clinical procedures assess thickness of vascular wall in the place of a pathological change it could provide new opportunities of real assessment of a patient's condition and his/her being qualified for a surgery.

# Some Aspects of Numerical Calculations of Specialized Vehicle's Load Carrying Structure for the Transport of Dangerous Materials by the Requirements of the European ADR Agreement

Eugeniusz Rusiński1, Artur Górski1  , Michał Paduchowicz1  and Marcin Pondel1

(1)

Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, Department of Machine Design and Research, Wrocław, Poland

Artur Górski

Email: artur.gorski@pwr.edu.pl

Michał Paduchowicz (Corresponding author)

Email: michal.paduchowicz@pwr.edu.pl

Abstract

There are being presented the issues of the load carrying structure of specialized vehicle for transport dangerous materials by the requirements of the European ADR agreement. There are shown requirements and researcher's methodology of design and calculation issue using numerical methods on the example of specialized vehicle used in surface mining. Methodology of complex systems calculation are presented in the paper, in particular joint of main frame and sub-frame with liquid's tanks. The whole of issue are supported by example of vehicle's calculations results, deployed into production.

## 1 Introduction

One of the many issue in surface mining related industry is design and production specialized vehicle. Such vehicle is known MEMU (Mobile Explosive Manufacturing Unit) used to transport components of explosives used to crashing rock. The main issue is determining geometric form of liquid's tanks with the main frame of basic vehicle. The basic of the design's guideline is the ADR agreement (Fr. L' Accord européen relatif au transport international des marchandises Dangereuses par Route). The agreement relates generally understood regulation and a series of standards for the transport of hazardous materials. The purpose of these is to minimize or substantially reduce the likelihood of accidents and the extent of possible damage caused mainly unsealed containers. Development of this laws allowed to systematize the transport of hazardous materials and gave clear guidance how this should be carried out. At the same time, they define guidelines for the same vehicles and equipment are carrying the traffic service [1].

## 2 Technical Requirements According to ADR

The ADR is amended every two years in odd years. It consists of the relevant agreement and annexes A and B, which are an integral part of it. The agreement determines the proper legal relations between the participating countries, while the appendices contain provisions governing a wide range of conditions of carriage of particular hazardous materials in international road transport. Annex B are defined [1]:

  * the conditions of carriage of particular hazardous materials,

  * the technical conditions of automotive vehicles,

  * technical conditions trailers (semi-trailers), tanks and containers—tanks,

  * the conditions for marking vehicles and their additional equipment

  * conditions of loading and unloading of various materials,

  * bans charging load together in one vehicle,

  * requirements for persons participating in the carriage,

  * necessary documentation of these operators.

There has been defined geometric characteristics of the vehicle using numerical calculation methods based on the requirements set in the article.

## 3 The Concept of Transport Set

The output element of the research has become a target concept vehicle MEMU based on the conventional chassis (Fig. 1). The vehicle was characterized by a relatively long mainframe supported on four axes. On it there is a sub-frame to which are fixed the various tanks. In Fig. 1 shows the geometric view of the vehicle with clamped MEMU tanks.

## 4 Loading

Determination of the real loads acting on load-carrying structure support elements in vehicles is a complex issue [1]. The complexity stems from the movement of the vehicle on different pavement, from carrying the burden of the suspension components on the support structure and the interaction between the various units.

Body of vehicle is charged during its motion by inertia forces proportional to the weight of its load and associated accelerations [3].

It was defined the following loads to strength calculate of the vehicle on the basis of the EN 13094:

  * Case 1 (DOWN)—twice load of the frame's gravity and the filled tanks in the respective contents of 90%, oriented in the vertical downward direction.

  * Case 2 (FRONT)—load twice the force of gravity of the frame and tanks filled in 90% of relevant content, oriented in the direction of travel.

  * Case 3 (LEFT)—load gravity frame and the filled tanks in the respective contents of 90%, oriented in a direction perpendicular to the direction of travel (to the left).

  * Case 4 (RIGHT)—load gravity frame and the tank filled with 90% relevant content, oriented perpendicular to the direction of travel (left right).

  * Case 5 (UP)—gravity load of tanks filled to 90% of the relevant content, oriented vertically upwards.

Calculation models consist essentially of a discrete model of each sub-frame tanks. It should provide the most reliable, burdened with as little error results.

Geometrical models (sheet body models) of the individual tanks and sub-frame developed on the basis CAD models of these elements (Fig. 7). The tanks are structural elements of thin-walled profiles and sheet, so discrete models are constructed primarily of shell elements. On the basis of sheet body geometric model, finite elements mesh was generated with specific geometric characteristics (Fig. 8) [4, 5].

## 7 Summary and Conclusions

There were made calculations of emulsion matrix, saltpeter, petroleum, reagent tanks and the sub-frame using the finite element method as part of the research work. Commercial calculation code NX-Ideas 6.1 was using for the calculation. The maximum resulting stress were equal to 166 MPa, and were higher than allowable value for the petroleum tank (equal to 143 MPa) only in the case of the vertical acceleration load directed to down. The maximum equivalent stresses were lower than limits for the remaining elements, i.e. emulsion matrix, saltpeter, reagent 1 tanks, and the sub-frame. In order to reduce the equivalent stresses on petroleum tank, butt straps are proposed in place of high equivalent stress of the tank. The results after modified showed stresses reduced to 117 MPa less than the limits amounting to 143 MPa for the case of vertical load down [9, 10].

# The Numerical and Experimental Vibrations Analysis of WLS Series Fans Designed for the Use in Underground Mines

Eugeniusz Rusiński1, Przemysław Moczko1  , Piotr Odyjas1  and Jędrzej Więckowski1

(1)

Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, Department of Machine Design and Research, Wrocław University of Science and Technology, Łukasiewicza 7/9, 50-371 Wrocław, Poland

Przemysław Moczko

Email: przemyslaw.moczko@pwr.edu.pl

Piotr Odyjas

Email: piotr.odyjas@pwr.edu.pl

Jędrzej Więckowski (Corresponding author)

Email: jedrzej.wieckowski@pwr.edu.pl

URL: http://www.kbm.pwr.edu.pl/

Abstract

The modal analysis of technical objects undergoing variable load intensity is an important task, thanks to which the safety in terms of resonance vibration phenomenon can be measured. This paper concerns the aspects of testing the new WLS series fans, used for local mine ventilation, which provide safer underground conditions resulting in more efficient work. The use of numerical methods in the calculations of natural frequencies and the comparison of numerical and experimental results calculated with the use of operational modal analysis have been emphasized.

## 1 Introduction

Specifying the modal properties of the technical object is recommended when it is affected by variable loads. The example of such a load, in terms of fans, is the rotational frequency of the electrical engine used to power the rotor. It is not the only type of load occurring during the utilization of machines and devices, yet it is usually linked with the power transmission system generating certain multiplicated frequencies, for example, the transmission ratio or the impulses of the system cooperating with the medium, where the work takes place. The standards concerning individual types of devices define ranges, in which there should be no natural frequency. If they are not met, the object can start resonating, possibly leading to failures or even catastrophes [3, 4, 7, 8, 12].

The resonance vibration phenomenon is exceptionally dangerous to technical objects, which can even lead to the destruction of the object itself. It is for that reason why testing whether the machine operates in the range of resonant vibration is crucial. The term resonance refers to the increase of vibration amplitude at particular frequencies of excitation. The most spectacular example of the danger linked with resonance is the American Tacoma Narrows Bridge. It collapsed four months after its opening because of the resonant vibration caused by the wind. The Fig. 1 presents the bridge's behavior during the occurrence of resonant vibration.

Fig. 1

Tacoma Narrows Bridge resonating [14]

The following paper concerns numerical-experimental method of defining the frequency of natural vibration of the new WLS series of axial flow fans used for local ventilation of mines. A whole series of these fans was designed due to diversified airing demands and various local flow resistances occurring in mines. Despite the relatively easy adjustment, one axial flow fan is not capable of providing appropriate local ventilation in all conditions encountered in mines. The designed series of WLS fans consist of four fans of different sizes. Their technical and operational parameters are presented in Table 1.

The current stage of development of numerical methods makes it possible to conduct such research even on virtual prototypes; thus, it is possible to introduce all necessary modifications before assembling the actual prototype. Such research in terms of virtual calculations and verification measurements conducted on the real object with the use of operational modal analysis will be presented later on [1, 2, 5, 11, 13].

## 2 Defining Excitation Parameters

The crucial part of verifying whether resonance will occur in the technical object is defining the frequency of excitation. As mentioned above, it can come from various sources. In terms of fans, it comes from the transmission of the electrical engine (usually without the additional gearing), whose rotor spins with certain rotational speed. ## 3 Numerical Modal Analysis of the WLS Series of Fans

Due to the development of the finite element method [6, 9, 10], it is now commonly used for supporting scientific and engineering research. It also finds use in modal analysis. Appropriate algorithms contained in modern computational systems make it possible to calculate modal parameters of the analyzed object in terms of consecutive modes and frequencies of natural vibration. The additional advantage of numerical methods is the possibility of obtaining detailed visualization of every vibration mode. The fact, as mentioned above, allows introducing necessary modifications in the project at the stage of virtual prototype if there is a stated risk of resonance occurring during utilization.

As part of this paper, a complex numerical modal analysis of the new WLS series fans was conducted. In the first stage of the research geometrical models of each of the fans were prepared. Figures 2, 3, 4 and 5 present the models of individual fans.

## 4 Determining Natural Frequency Using Experimental Methods

There are many techniques for measuring natural frequency of real objects. For the sake of this publication, the operational modal analysis was applied using a laser scanning vibrometer for measurements. The operational modal analysis is characterized by the fact that all excitation comes directly from the utilization of the object. It means that the value of the excitation frequency is unknown, as opposed to the experimental modal analysis, when the value is known.

The goal of the research was to verify the correctness of numerical calculations. Measurements were done during the utilization of the fan at flow measurement site. The use of laser measuring techniques allows registering even the slightest displacements expressed in micrometers, providing a pinpoint accuracy of measurement of the speed of waves expressed in micrometers per second. The disadvantage of this techniques is the capability of registering only the displacements perpendicular to the detector of the measuring optical head if only one head is used. There is, however, the possibility of tridimensional identification of vibration modes if more measuring heads are used. Another important criterion for using this technique is the condition of the surface of the material of which the tested object is made. Its surface must be capable of reflecting the laser beam.

In the paper, the results of research conducted on the prototype of WL-S 500 fan are presented. Figure 14 shows the tested object with a defined net of measurement points. They were made of a special material capable of reflecting laser beams because the signal reflected off the fan's surface oscillated around the minimal values acceptable for conducting a correct measurement. Figure 15 presents the view of the measuring site during the measurement.

Fig. 14

WL-S 500 fan prepared for the measurement using a laser vibrometer

Fig. 15

WL-S 500 fan at the measuring site

On the base of the research, magnitude frequency spectrums were obtained in the analyzed measurement points. They present characteristic values for the WL-S 500 fan, such as rotational frequency, blade pass frequency along with values linked with natural vibration. Graphs Figs. 16, 17 and 18 show exemplary curve trajectories for various operational parameters. The air flow through the fan was regulated with the use of a damper in front of the fan and an outlet reducer behind it. A characteristic frequency of 10 Hz can be observed which is the natural frequency of the tested object. A confirmation of this is the fact that the frequency is the same for various measurement conditions. Figures 19 and 20 additionally show the visualization of this vibration mode obtained with the use of measuring software.

## 5 The Analysis of Test Results

Comparison of the experimental and numerical results is aimed at testing whether the discrete model of the object provides correct values. The correctness of restraints and loads can be verified in this way. The first numerical analysis concerned operational conditions in which the fans is going to be used in mines. Boundary conditions, which were applied to the operational analysis of operational conditions, were completely different than those obtained during the measurements at the measuring site. It is for this reason why an additional modal analysis of the WL-S 500 fan, taking into account the real boundary conditions at the measuring site, had been conducted. ## 6 Conclusions

The results of tests and numerical analysis exhibit confluence. It means that the values obtained from calculations conducted on the virtual objects correspond with the real ones. The difference between the former and the latter equals 2.8%. The fact indicates that numerical methods can be used for the verification of the prototypes in the virtual environment. It allows making all the necessary changes as soon as at the state of documentation. The changes are dictated by the risk of potential resonant vibration. Thanks to that, the amount of prototypes which have to be built is reduced to the bare minimum.

# Computer-Aided Process of Selecting Technological Features for Machine Design Series of Types

Rafał Rząsiński1  and Piotr Gendarz1

(1)

Institute of Engineering Processes Automation and Integrated Manufacturing Systems, Silesian University of Technology, Konarskiego Street 18a, 44-100 Gliwice, Poland

Rafał Rząsiński (Corresponding author)

Email: rafal.rzasinski@polsl.pl

Piotr Gendarz

Email: piotr.gendarz@polsl.pl

Abstract

The basic concept described in this paper is the application that enables generating technological data for machine design series of types. The data is generated in the traditional form (operation and instruction sheets) and codes for numerically controlled machine tools. The model of transformation is based on the developed theory of technological similarity using relational databases [1, 5]. The method is based on the susceptibility to algorithmic presentation of quantitative construction data. Technological structure for each product in the series remains unchanged (with possible small changes). Only processing parameters are subject to changes. The method enables creating a few variants of technological plans for a given element and the differences between these plans result from the fact of different construction forms of the elements.

## 1 Introduction

Requirements of industrial production over the years have shaped the models that technological processes are based on. Very often, these models are burdened with the necessity to design a complex production process in spite of some small, insignificant changes within the given construction. In times of market economy, time and financial resources are the critical factors for the future development of the company. For that reason, research has been carried out focused on the development of production process design methodology that would help reducing the time needed to design and modify processes in workplaces. This mainly concerns aiding production for series of types and modular construction systems. The result of this research are programs aiding the selection of technological process components that are based on similarity and analogy [3–5]. These programs allow designing technological process in a reasonably short period of time, at the same time maintaining high efficiency of the solution to the problem. Some limitation, however, is the subjectivism of the person solving a given problem. Just like construction engineers, who solve a given problem, also technologists are susceptible to their own previous experience. Assuming that a technologist has introduced a given solution for the process according to good engineering practices, we face the problem of time needed to introduce changes. In case of standard procedures, a technologist must calculate parameters from the place where the change was introduced. If we use the computer-aided option of generating documentation, we have the possibility of obtaining the ready process in real time. For that reason, it is sensible to create and develop programs that aid the design of technological processes. So far, all attempts [2, 5] at solving this problem have provided direction for the development of the application for creating technology series of types.

## 2 Method of Technological Similarity

In case of constructional similarity, when we create a new construction we use a number of rules for creating similar constructions [1, 4]. Analogical procedural algorithm is used in case of designing technologies for series of types and modular constructions [6, 7].

Unknown values are determined based on the data included in the so called model construction, described in an unambiguous, comprehensive and experimentally verified manner. This way, similar technologies are created. The value of new variables is determined based on the assumed similarity value in relation to the parameters for the model construction. Newly determined parameters may be subject to further modifications if it is necessary to adjust them to the standardized values [2]. The above mentioned steps are applicable for generating the entire technology series of types.

The method is based on the susceptibility to algorithmic presentation of quantitative construction data. Technological structure for each product in the series remains unchanged (with possible small changes). Only processing parameters are subject to changes.

The method enables creating a few variants of technological plans for a given element and the differences between these plans result from the fact of different construction forms of the elements.

Another step is the selection of qualitative technological features:

  * selection of the technological structure,

  * selection of the form of the input semi-product,

  * selection of the tool,

  * selection of the equipment.

Depending on the type of production process, using similarity theory requires obtaining specific similarity conditions [2, 8]. They are determined by assigning the discrete value of calculated technological parameters, which reflects the degree of similarity of these parameters and the corresponding quantitative technological features. There is a distinction between construction similarity and technological similarity [3, 4].

## 3 The Concept of the Application

In order to generate the appropriate program operation algorithm, it is necessary to develop relational databases [6]. The value of parameters for the given position in a database influences the values of parameters for the further selected positions. Thanks to such assumption, the relation between all modules of all series of types will be maintained. This approach forms the closed structure of creating technologies, so it prevents the incompatibility of quantitative features of the selected process (e.g. choosing a plate size E for the holder size F, or choosing the 20 mm knife holder for the tool holder with a frame of max 16 mm). The detailed concept of the algorithm of generating technologies is presented in Fig. 1.

Fig. 1

The concept of the algorithm of generating technology series of types

### 3.1 Description of the Application

Application "Generating technology series of types" is a program that gives the opportunity of defining a technological process, and compiling process documentation at the same time (in the form of operation sheets), Fig. 2. Furthermore, for the process entered into the application, it is also possible to generate the NC (Numerical Control) code for the numerically controlled machine tools. The program was written in the language Visual Basic 2010 operating within the programming platform VisualBasic.NET.

Fig. 2

The general algorithm of the program

For proper functioning, the application requires MX Excel that is a part of MS Office suite (version min. 2007). For the verification of the CNC code, a CNC Simulator was used that is intended for the visualization of simple operations within broadly defined turning. The program includes the executable file of the application (*.exe), Excel files (*.xlsx). In order to verify the obtained CNC code, one may use CNC Simulator.

### 3.2 Databases Used in the Application

For the proper functioning of the application, a number of technological databases have been established, aiding the process of selecting technological properties on the basis of the design features. Figure 3 presents the schematic diagram of the established databases included in the application.

Fig. 3

The general algorithm of the program

Each of the bases is represented in the program as Excel spreadsheet:

  * Similarity spreadsheets—they are intended for keeping the dimensions of the model and the entire series of types, calculating machining parameters both for the model and modules from the series of types, as well as for saving the control variables of the program characteristic for a given procedure.

  * Sheets (model sheets)—they are used as the model of instruction sheet. The program copies the layout of the sheets in order to later complete them,

  * Allowance database—the database of allowance values for the calculated semi-finished product,

### 3.3 Stages of the Application

The application generates technological data for new elements, but for the purposes of presenting the capabilities of application development, a few other technological processes have been shown (elements MLD, MDU, MTU).

  * Definition of a new process

Selecting the element position "new" results in displaying empty process landscape and the button "Add process". After selecting this button, we get the proper window of defining the name of the process (Fig. 4). In this window, the following process parameters may be defined:

Fig. 4

The dialog box of project

  * Name of the process,

  * Type of the semi-finished product,

  * Dimensions of the ready element (model element),

  * Production volume,

  * Material used to make the element.

As the name of the process, you may enter any string of characters describing the created technological process. The program verifies the dimension values and displays error message if there are any irregularities.

  * Adding mounting and operation group

After adding the process, you need to add mounting of the element. In the window of adding the operation group, there is only one drop-down list, and you should select the proper position (group). The window of adding operations is presented in Fig. 4. Selecting the operation from the list and confirming the selection results in adding the operation to the technological process landscape.

  * Adding machining process

  * Defining the features of series of types

For each of the operations, a series of types for dimensions of construction modules need to be defined

  * Generating parameters for the modules of series of types

After defining series of types, sheets for particular modules of each operation need to be defined. In order to generate the module sheet you need to click on the "Generate parameters of the n element" button in the main window of the program. This window is similar to the window of defining series of types, with the exception that we do not enter any dimensions here. All you have to do is select the module number of your choice and click OK. Then, the program, according to the similarity algorithm, will perform the calculations of parameters and create the instruction sheet for this module. A helpful feature of the program is displaying previously defined values of dimensions for the specific operation. In top left corner, a number of the operation, for which the sheet will be generated, is displayed. In order to generate sheets for other operations all you have to do is click on them on the process landscape and analogically to the previously described method—click on the button "Generate... ", choose the number of the other module and click OK.

  * Generating the simplified CNC code

In order to generate the NC code you need to previously generate at least one instruction sheet for any operation. In case when the operations and procedures were added according to the described method of entering the process, all you have to do is click on the button "Generate CNC code". In case of any interference with the process landscape (displaying process sheet, displaying instruction sheet of the process) the program may display the window of generating CNC code without parts of the columns of the entered processes. Proper display of the window is presented in Fig. 5.

Fig. 5

View of the window generating CNC code and series of types

In the newly opened window, you may see the layout of 10 columns (corresponding to the procedures), and each of them has 19 buttons (corresponding to the number of elements in series of types). Status of the activated button is equal to generating the CNC code for a given module. The generated CNC code consists of sub-codes generated for particular procedures and blocks of the beginning and end of the program.

The example of the model of generating the CNC code presented Fig. 5.

Values of the variables obtained while generating the code are downloaded from the instruction sheets (modules) and similarity sheets of a given procedure. Sub-codes generated for particular procedures are created as a result of entering the values of variables in proper places of the defined model of the code for a given procedure. Each of the procedures has got at least one model code, which is generated while the program is in operation.

## 4 Summary

The developed application aids the process of selecting technological features. It aims at the selection of features for the elements saved as series of types and modular systems. The process of selecting the features is carried out via transformation on the basis of practically verified model technology; the data for transformations is downloaded from databases. The application may be used as a tool to generate traditional technological documentation in the form of operation and instruction sheets. The rules of transforming the features included in the developed application are a form of verifying the theory of technological similarity.

# The Assessment Method of Operation Fuel Consumption of Underground Machinery

Lech J. Sitnik1  , Monika Magdziak-Tokłowicz1  and Monika Andrych-Zalewska1

(1)

Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, Department of Vehicle Engineering, Wroclaw University of Science and Technology, 164 Street, 51-640 Wroclaw, Braci Gierymskich, Poland

Lech J. Sitnik (Corresponding author)

Email: lech.sitnik@pwr.edu.pl

Monika Magdziak-Tokłowicz (Corresponding author)

Email: monika.magdziak-toklowicz@pwr.edu.pl

Monika Andrych-Zalewska

Email: monika.andrych@pwr.edu.pl

Abstract

It was presented method of assessing operational fuel consumption of underground machinery. The method is based on the theory of cumulative fuel consumption developed in the Department of Vehicle Engineering Wroclaw University of Technology. It has been given the investigation manner into a mathematical model and a procedure for determining the constants of the model describes consumption. Attention was drawn to the characteristics of the cumulative fuel consumption. Using the operating data e.g. Working time machine moto hours and corresponding to that time fuel consumption, it was possible to develop a curve of the cumulative fuel consumption and intensity of consumption. These curves may be used to evaluate the method of operation of the machine as well as e.g. A prediction fuel consumption. This information could be used to optimize the selection and use of machines to the task [1, 2].

Keywords

Machine operationFuel consumptionTheory of cumulative fuel consumption

## 1 Introduction

It was presented method of assessing operational fuel consumption of underground machinery. The method is based on the theory of cumulative fuel consumption developed in the Department of Vehicle Engineering Wroclaw University of Technology.

It has been given the investigation manner into a mathematical model and a procedure for determining the constants of the model describes consumption. Attention was drawn to the characteristics of the cumulative fuel consumption.

Using the operating data e.g. working time machine moto hours and corresponding to that time fuel consumption, it was possible to develop a curve of the cumulative fuel consumption and intensity of consumption. These curves may be used to evaluate the method of operation of the machine as well as e.g. w prediction fuel consumption. This information could be used to optimize the selection and use of machines to the task.

## 2 Theory of Cumulative Fuel Consumption

Fuel is injected into the combustion chamber in a "quantum". Quanta of fuel, also called fuel doses has the magnitude of the random. This randomness is a kind of intended, as the result of the need for producing motor energy necessary to cover the demand in a random arrangement of its use, e.g. in the underground systems of the machine or not intended when the value of the dose determined random processes implemented in the apparatus of the fuel engine.

Quanta of fuel can be characterized by volume or weight. Traditionally, and most frequently used measures of volume.

The sum of the volume (or weight) of quanta of fuel supplied to the engine in order to obtain energy, is known as fuel.

Summing quants of fuel leads to determine the cumulative fuel consumption.

The size of the cumulative fuel consumption can be determined at any time engine operation, and therefore the cumulative fuel consumption could be recognized in the generally understood operation time the engine. The time may be understood literally, e.g. by stating the operating hours of engine operation or administered indirectly as an example mileage. Each time while the engine is possible to determine the size of the cumulative fuel consumption. It is the sum of the fuel used since the introduction of the motor into operation for the selected time corresponding to the time of his work be analyzed [3].

The cumulative fuel consumption referenced to engine run time, is the intensity of the cumulative fuel consumption after a given period of engine operation [4, 5].

To be distinguished the cumulative fuel consumption from the instantaneous consumption. The instantaneous fuel consumption is consumption which has occurred during a given, relatively short period of time at any time of the overall engine operation. If time of engine works is regarded as indirectly mileage of the vehicle in which the engine is the source of power, popular size characterizing the instantaneous fuel consumption is the instantaneous intensity of the fuel consumption given liters per 100 km.

## 3 Example Operating Data of Underground Machinery

The study of underground machinery are conducted from their introduction into operation. Fuel consumption of these machines is particularly important not only because of the obvious economic aspect but also the environmental aspect. Every liter of fuel burned is a specified quantity of toxic compounds emitted in the exhaust. These toxic compounds must be scrupulously removed from the mine [5, 3].

## 4 Conclusion

  1. 1.

The paper was presented the theory of cumulative fuel consumption.

  2. 2.

Examples of operating data of the mucker was shown how an investigation into the mathematical model of cumulative wear and intensity of consumption.

  3. 3.

  4. 4.

The results can be used to build the corresponding mathematical models (after further verification of statistical data covering multiple operating machines) aimed at testing the simulation analysis of the current and forecasted fuel machine park mining but it is necessary to obtain data from the operation of the corresponding natural park underground machinery.

# A Comparison Between Two Different Methods of Blast Modelling

Grzegorz Sławiński1  , Piotr Malesa1, Tadeusz Niezgoda1 and Marek Świerczewski1

(1)

Department of Mechanics and Applied Computer Science, Military University of Technology, 2 Gen. Sylwester Kaliski Street, 00-908 Warsaw, Poland

Grzegorz Sławiński

Email: grzegorz.slawinski@wat.edu.pl

Abstract

This dissertation consists mainly in a comparison of different methods of load modelling relative to the blast wave coming from the detonation of a bursting TNT charge and the impact of this wave on a shield.

## 1 Introduction

This dissertation consists mainly in a comparison of different methods of load modelling relative to the blast wave coming from the detonation of a bursting TNT charge and the impact of this wave on a shield. Numerical simulations were carried out with the use of the LS-Dyna calculation code [1].

The aim of the presented study was to investigate the impact of a bursting charge on a shield, in various configurations, with the use of two calculation methods. To solve the problem, the ALE algorithm and the CONWEP function, implemented in the LS-Dyna environment, were selected. The model investigated through the numerical analyses consisted of a spherical bursting charge having a 10 diameter and with the centre arranged at a distance of 170 mm from the top of the loaded object. The detonation begins in the centre of the bursting charge when t = 0 s. In case of the analyses solved with the use of the ALE algorithm, 2D axially symmetrical models were used, while in order to stimulate, using the CONWEP code, the system's quadrant was modelled after being divided into 3D elements (Fig. 1).

Fig. 1

Picture of the numerical model for one of the cases of the analysis

## 2 Validation Studies of Numerical Models

All work within the numerical analyses began by checking the correct functioning of the ALE calculation algorithm for the given parameters of material constants, describing the bursting charge and air, as well as the state equations assigned to those centres.

To describe the material of the bursting charge in the LS-Dyna calculation system, the model of the MAT_HIGH_EXPLOSIVE_BURN material was used. The corresponding state equation, which was described through the use of the EOS_JWL card, is necessary. The material constants, needed for the correct presentation of the phenomenon, were taken from the literature [2]. To describe the air material, the MAT_NULL model, completed by the EOS_LINEAR_POLYNOMIAL state equation, was used. Even in this case, material data were taken from the literature [3] (Table 1, 2).
